MAD RIVER, IN THE WHITE MOUNTAINS. The following poem, from the Atlantic Monthly for May, is Vie last Longfellow ever wrote. -He revised the proofs only a few days before his death. In view of this fact, the craving for rest which finds expression in the second stanza is touch- ingly significant. TB avnLyER Why dost thou wildly rush and roar, Mad River, 0 -Mad River? Wilt thou not pause and cease to pear Thy hurrying, headlong waters o'er This rocky shelf for ever? What secret trouble stirs thy breast? Why all ibis fret and flurry? Dost thou not know that what Is beat In this too restless world is rest . From overwork and worry? VTR BITER: What wonld'st thou in these mountains seek, 0 stranger from the city? Is it perhaps some foolish freak Of thine, to put the words I speak Into a plaintive ditty? TE WELLER : Yes; I would learn of thee thy song, With all its fl3Willg numbers, And in a voice as fresh and strong As thine is, sing it all day long, And hear it in my slumbers. TFIE RIVER : A brooklet nameless and unknown Was I at first, resembling A little child, that all alone Comes venturing down the stairs of stone, Irresolute and trembling. Later, by wayward fancies led, For the wide world I panted; Out of the forest dark and dread Across the open fields I fled, Like one pursued and haunted. I tossed my arms, I sang aloud, My voice exultant blending With thunder from the passing cloud, The wind, the forest bent and bowed, The rush of rain descending. heard the distant ocean call, Implcring and entreating; Drawn onward, o'er this rocky wall I plunged, and the loud waterfall blade answer to the greeting. And now, beset with many ills, A toilsome life I follow; Compelled to carry from the hills These logs to the impatient mills Below there in the hollow. Yet something ever cheers and charms The rudeness of my labours; Daily I water with these arms The cattle of a hundred farms, And have the birds for neighbours. Men call me Mad, and well they may, When, full of rage and troubke, I burst my banks of sand and clay, And sweep their wooden bridge away, Like withered reeds or stubble. Now go and write thy little rhyme, As of thine own creating. Thou seest the day is past its prime; I c3u no longer waste my time; The mills are tired of waiting. —HfrainT WArswoavw LONGFELLOW.

A starved tramp said he was se thin that when he had a pain he couldn't tell whether it was a stomach-ache or a back-ache. Mrs. Ramsbottom dropped off to sleep at church last San- day evening. She says she supposes it was on account of the soothing effects of the full chloral service.—Punch. Mahomet says that when a man dies, people ask, "What property has he left ehied him ?" But the angels, as they bend over his grave, inquire, "What good deeds haat thou sat before thee?" "'Dive MISSCTSSES" AGAlN.—Applicant for Situation as Housemaid: Well, eou see, mum, the rniasis at my last place was a very nice person, but I couldn't get on with the lady as was cook, so I was obligated to leave.—Judy. THE DIVIDED SEIRTS. I'll wear," she said, "and surely it won't hurt, My Lady Harberton's 'divided skirt' ;" But he the silly fashion much derided, And so the house was like the skirt, divided.—Punch. "MEANT SAREASTIC.”—Waiter (who has just brought bin his sixth cup) : You don't like coffee, sir I—Guest : Ca, yes, I do; I'm very fond of a little coffee, but I have to drink such a confounded lot of water here to get that ' litile.—Judy. EISARTS OF OA:T.—Angelina (who has never seen a revolv- e ing light before) : "How patient and persevering those sai- lors must be, Edwin! The wind has blown that light out six times since they first lit it, and they've lighted it again each time !"—Punch. "I remember," says the celebrated Wesley, "heating any father say to my mother,' How could you have the patience • to tell that blockhead the same thing twenty times over?' Why,' said she, if I had told him nineteen times I should have lest all my labour.'" WE'RE IMPROVING.—Young Lady: Oh, aunty! did you see that man stare at ma? How rude the men are! Aunt: Oh, they're getting much better now, my dear! Why, ten years ago they used to actually come up and talk to me; now they only look! [Yon don't say so !—Eo.]—Judy. The.examp'e of a worthy Scotch baronet of old might have bean valuable lately as regards the only safe method of proceeding to arbitration. Sir John louse, after discussing the preliminaries of an arbitration, was asked, "But will ye abide by my award ?" Sir John replied, "Faith, I would ` like to ken first fat it is." "Ticket, air," said an inspector at a railway terminus in the city to a gentleman who, having been a season.ticket holder for some time, believed his face was so well known that there was no need for him to show his ticket. "My face is my ticket," replied the gentleman, a little annoyed. " Indeed!" said the inspector, rolling beck his wristband and displaying a most powerful fist; "well, my orders are to punch all tickets passing on to this platform..." Lord Seaforth, who was born deaf and dumb, was to dine one day with Lord Melville. Just before the time of the company's arrival, Lady Melville sent into the drawing- room a lady of her acquaietarca who could talk with her ficgerd to dumb people' that she might receive Lord Sea. forth. Presently Lord Gaildford entered the room, and the lady, taking him for Lord Seaforth, bean to ply her fingers • very nimbly. Lord Guildford did the same, and they had been carrying on a conversation in this manner for about ten minutes when Lady Melville joined them. Her female • friend immediately said, ." Well, I have been talking away - to this dumb man." "Dumb!" cried Lord Gnildferd ; "bless me, I thought yen were dumb!" ONE OF Olen 13E2EDITART RIILERS.—There is a Curious and well-authenticated story about a deceased peer which is worth repetition. When just of age, he bad not the uncom- mon mania cf falling in love on the slightest provocation, and the less common habit of making offers of marriage, which, as hog as he confined his addresses to ladies of his own rank, was of tro consequence, as they were treated as jokes. But one day his fancy fell on a strapping dairy-maid about twelve inches taller and six years older than himself, and it was shortly afterwards reported to his mother, the countess, that big Polly had shown a fellow' servant a written offer of marriage 'from the little lord. Immense ex- citement, at the end of which the confidential housekeeper was sent on a mission of inwiry, with full powers of corn- promise to the strapping Cinderel'a of the dairy. The ambassadreee offered her an excellent situation at great wages and a handsome present in hand if she would go to a distant estate and promise to have no more to say to her noble lover. The damsel accepted the offers without hesita- tion—indeed with eagerness—answering," Make your mind easy, Mrs. —; as I wouldn't mary the little creature if every 'air on hi 3 'ed was hung with diamonds. I'm keeping company with a young man as stands six feet in his stock- ing soles, and can jump a gate without putting a finger on it." "All right, my good Mary, I knew you were a good girl, and you had better start before his lordship comes back from Londontand there'd something to pay expenses," pro- ducing a nicernew crackling Bank of England note for fifty pounds. "And now, Mary, you will give up his lordship's letter ?" "No, indeed I shan't," was the answer; "my young man is willing to marry me as soon as I can get ready, but I shall keen this letter to show him, if ever he's saucy, that ill liked I might a' married a heart !" Tits TORTOISE.—Few animals seem more sluggish than the common land tortoise. In truth, all its motions are, as Gilbert White says, " ridiculously slow," and its most active pace is but a hobble. But all this gravity of movement is not peculiar to all the members of this extensive order. The marsh, river, and sea species are very active in their motions, and make long journeys with the greatest ease, turtles having been found at sea more than two 2,000 miles from land. Some of the huge land tortoises of tropical isles do actually manage to travel at the rate of four miles a day. No trifling jotirney either for an animal with such crutch- lake legs, and so heavy that six men are required to lift one from the ground. Let no one suppose that such limbs are a defect; all this slowness of movement is evidently a result of the remarkable structure which distinguishes them ani- mals. The reader will see this in a few minutes; in the meantime let us pause to note how this absence of rapid movement is compeneated. An animal requires the gift of speed in tee) cases only—either to escape from foes or to pursue its prey. But tortoises need not run from their ene- mies, most having an impregnable fortress in which they may bid defiance to nearly every animal. When the tor- toise has shut itself up within the shell even the hungry tiger can only grate his teeth in vain against the solid armour. The boa-constrictor may, indeed, swallow the rep. tile, shell and all, but this is an extreme case. The most remarkable defensive armour is that of the box-tortoise (pyris), the under shell of which is furnished with a mov- able plate, and this being drawn up by powerful muscles completely closes the opening through which the reptile's head and forte feet have been withdrawn. The hind feet and tail are protected by the overlapping shell beind. While danger remains the besieged tortoise has only to remain quiet and patient, keeping its box firmly clesed. The ani- mal cannot be starved into a surrender, as it can fast for months without suffering much. When the foe retires the ehelly trapdoor is let down, upon which the heed and feet are again thrust out, and the victorious tortoise has time to dine. Creatures furnished with such a defence have no seed for rapid flight, and therefore the unnecessary power is withbeld.—Cassell's " Popular Educator."

AoarcurrunAt EDUCATION.—The Lord President of the Committee of Council on EduCation has appointed Professor Wrightson' President of the Collego of Agriculture, flown ton, near Salisbury, as the first Professor of Agriculture in the Normal School of Science, and Royal School of Mines, South Kensington. Professor Wrightson has for many years been well known as a scientific agriculturist, and is the occupier of a large mixed farm. RATS.—A writer in the Scientific American says :—" We clean our premises of these detestable vermin by making whitewash yellow with copperas, and covering the stones and rafters in the cellars with it. In every crevice in which a rat may go, we put the crystals or the copperas and scatter it in the corners of the floor. The result was a perfect stam- pede of rats and mice. Since that time not a footfall of either rats or mice has been around the house. Every spring a coat of the yellow wash is given to the cellar as a purifier and rat exterminator. At the recent Farmers' Alliance meeting at York, Mr. J. E. Backhouse cited a striking instance of the injustice of the Law of Distress. Ile instanced the case of a farmer in the county, who took a farm at the rental of £5OO a-year, but paid nothing to his landlord for three years, while at the same time he incurred other debts amounting to £2,000. Under the Law of Distress the landlord sold the tenant's goods for £1,600, and after deducting the £1,500 due for rent, £l.OO was left for division amongst the other creditors. A HUGE FARM.—Oar American relatives have a lofty contempt for what in England we term "large farmers." An American friend once told us, in an inimitable access of patriotic pride, that even our largest farmer at home would be looked upon in the States "as a cottier—a mere squatter: sir!" In truth, the race of great farmers seems to grow apace on -the other side of the water. Mr. E. C. Sprague, of Fargo, for instance, farms on a leviathan scale. This enter- prising agriculturist has under cultivation over 13,000 acres, and he is the actual possessor of nearly half a million acres. He has now 3,000 acres ready for crop, and is preparing 10,000 more. The land under culture is mostly in Clay County; but Mr. Sprague has 200,000 acres in Texas, and supoo in Minnesota, the rest of his property being distri- buted through many other parts of the States. Like a shrewd Yankee that he is, Mr. Sprague has selected the most fertile of the States for his investments in real estate. —Land.

RABBIT BREEDING.—The West Henley Rabbit and Poul- try Company, Limited, have enclosed over 100 acres in wire netting, which was stocked with rabbits in April last. The rabbits are doing exceedingly well, and it promises to be a most successful enterprise. In selecting a spot to establish a rabbit warren it is not absolutely necessary that it should be all sand, but the soil must be light and perfectly dry. If on a bed of chalk, so mach the better, for rabbits are less liable to disease and generally grow quicker. Clay must be avo-ded under any circumstances. The ground should be undulating, and the greater portion covered with gorse, which should be in patches. This is most conducive to the health of the stock, and it would be advisable to sow fresh patches of seed in places, should the bushes which are standing be very old; but wire netting would have to be. pat round the places, and kept there until the young plants get their thick rough stalks, which the rabbits would not eat unless very hard pressed for food, which should never be the case. LIABILITY OF RAILWAY COMPANY TO REPAIR FENCES. —A correspondent complains that a railway company whose line abuts upon his land neglects to maintain an adequate fence to their line; that thereby a horse belonging to him has strayed on the line, and has been injured. He adds that the company decline to make any reparation. A railway company are bound to fence against the cattle of all adjoin- ing land. This under the General Railway Act, 8 and 9 Vice, c. 20, sec. 68. Bat though they are bound to prevent cattle that are lawfully on adjoining lands from straying on to the line, they are not similarly responsible where cattle are trespassing on the adjoining land. Eg. Sheep strayed from land which did not adjoin a railway, and got into land which did abut it, and which was held by a different occu- pier, and they got on the line and were killed. The com- pany were held to be not liable, because plaintiff was not the occupier of the land whence they immediately reached I the railway. He was bound to fence his cattle against his neighbour's land, and not having done so it was his fault that the sheep ever got on to land adjoining the line. (Ricketts v. East and West India Docks Rail. Co., 12 C. B. 174). And again if cattle stray on a highway, and thence get on to a line, the railway company are not liable. But if the cattle are being driven on the highway, and while so driven get on to a lice, the company will be responsible. (Mid. Rail. Co. v. Daykia, 17 C. B. 129). We are not sur- prised that in our correspondent's case the company decline to pay. It is 3 common practice with most lines to resist all claims, just as well as unjust, on principle. They find that the fear of litigation which these tactics produce among the public pays them in the long ran, even though they have to pay with costs when defeated on a just claim. How- ever, if our correspondent is sure of his facts, we recom- mend him to sue them without ceremony. They will have to pay, and will have virtually no defence to the action, if the horse strayed direct from the owner's land through a fence and on to the line, and was thereby injured.—Agri- cultural Gazette. RENTS IN LINCOLNSHIRE.—As a sample of the sticking-up -oats may be mentioned a farm of 375 acres one-third grass in the south-eastern marsh district, of which the rent, fres-11'1824 to 1830, stood at 235. per acre. By two revalua- tions it has jumped up to 40s. per acre rent, the figure for the last fifteen years. All that the landlord has done to- wards earning this handsome increment is the outlay of about £6OO in renewal or replacement of some of the old buildings, an addition to the house, a few bricks for sinking wells, and some pipes for draining, beside keeping the build- ings in repair, and painting outside work (which has of late years been thrown upon the tenent). An increase of £3lB to his income, or about 74 per cent., is a good haul for the landlord for his share in developing the improvement. How much the tenant contributed to the permanent improvement of the farm is not stated; but he built three root and chaff houses; he paid the labour (the heaviest item) in draining GO acres; he sank four yard and field wells; he carted earth for filling in 3 acres of creeks or open drains; he gravelled the road through and about his farm yard; he planted some long lines of new quick badge; he dug some new outran ditchee and planted an orchard of fruit trees. On the self- same estate, another farm of similar soil was, at the latest valuation, scarcely raised at all—at any rate, not to half the extent to which the rent of this improved holding was put up. The occupier in that case was a poor manager, spent little in feeding stuffs and manures, and his land was fairly set by the professional valuer (who "walked over") at its proper figure, much below the rent of the improved farm on which he found big root crops and strong stubhles. The first tenant felt, and feels still, that he was robbed of the just fruit of his work and outlay in being taxed on his own improvements, which, though answering his purpose, had, in equity, not ceased to be his by the effiaxion of time. Enjoyment of his own works had peid him a low commer- cial profit; but those very works helped the landlord to enhanced rental at the rate pf a new fortune. And this is not equity in division of profit from investments under the so-called partnership in farming.—Mark Lane Express. AGRICULTURAL DECLINE.—Under this heading The Times lately published a very striking and exhaustive article, showing the serious decline in the agricultural wealth of the United Kingdom that has taken place since the year 1863, as gauged by the large reduction in the stock of sheep. The figures are taken from the Agricultural Re- turns of 1863 and 1881. In every county in England, in Wales, in Scotland, and in Irelan 1 there is a large reduc- tion in the number of sheep, and this is only in a few cases eounterbelanced by the increase in the number of cattle. For the United Kingdom the decrease in cheep amounts to 7,712,000, or 21 65 per cent.; the increase in cattle being 822,000, or 904 per cent. Taking each head of cattle as equivalent to six sheep, the writer in The Times next shows the net decrease in cattle and sheep all reckoned as sheep and this he finds to be 3,268,000, or 7.49 per cent. for Eng- land; and 111,000, or 082 per cent. for Scotland. For Wales there is a net increase of 171000, or 274 per cent. ; and for Ireland 440,000, or 165 per cent. The net decrease for Great Britain is thus 3,202,000, or 506 per cent.; and for the United Kinedom, including the islands, 2,780,000, or 303 per cent. The money losses he!sets at £8,170,000 for England, and £277,000 for Scotland; the gains at £427,000 for Wales, and £1,100,000 for Ireland; the net loss for the United Kingdom being £6,950,000. What ren- ders these depressing figures all the mere alarming is the fact that the decrease in our live stock has occurred not upon the same, but upon a larger area of cultivated land; and not upon a smaller area of land devoted to feeding crops, but upon a much larger acreage. Thus, the number of acres in the United Kingdom under permanent pasture, clovers, grasses and green crops, including roots, was in 1868, 31,135,600 ; and in 1881 34,512,000. This is an increase of 3,377,000 acres, or 10 8 per cent. Therefore, up to the present time, the flourish of trumpets in reference to the supposed salvation of our agri- culture by means of converting tillage land to pasture' and corn land to land devoted to feeding crops, has ushered in a dead loss. We have devoted more land to less live stock. Rot and other epidemics have undoubtedly helped to diminish our stock of sheep; but the chief cause of the disease has been what may be termed" purse-rot," a waqing disease of a kind most disastrous to all branches of agricul- ture. Thousands of farmers who formerly kept breeding flocks have been unable to keep them lately on account of want of capital. Many who lost their flocks by liver-rot were unable to replace them; and many more who sold their flocks to relieve themselves from what they hoped was only a temporary embarrassment find that the embar- rassment was permanent, and as yet have not been able to replace the sheep they sold. It is obvious that the only possible relief for those who have no sheep and but few cattle would be a prolific harvest. The very fact that sheep are selling well is an additional disadvantage to men who have no sheep, but who would be glad to possess flocks again. If they are to regain their former position of prosperity, a good harvest must he the first step. The re- placement of their flocks should be the second, as on farms well suited to sheep nothing otn make up for the lack of these animals. We fear, however, that with too many the result of the best of harvests would be merely the wiping off of arrears of rent, and 'that we must not count on the restoration of the number of sheep kept in 1868 until we have been blessed with several fruitful years. Then, if the Process of filling tee the great gap in our sheep stock will be so slow and difficult, it is impossible for our rulers to exercise too stringent a provision aa tinst such decimation of our flecks as has too often occurred in the past through the devastation of imported disease.—dfctrk Lane Express.

ceived a generation ago. Thirty years ago stories of plants whose flowers were furnished with the means of enclosing flies or even pieces of meat, as a spider seizes on its prey, and quickly surrounds it with a network of gauze, and which then actually proceeded to eat the prey thus secured almost as a spider would eat the fly—such stories, thirty years ago, would have bean relegated to the category of "travellers' tales." But we have the authority of Mr. Darwin, and anyone may easily have the evidence of his own eyes, to prove that the possession of such properties by certain fl ewers is no fiction, bat an undoubted fact. The same authority who first brought prominently into notice the remarkable properties of the Drocera has shown that other plants have actually the power of progression, within certain limits, from one snot to another. With such in- stances it requires little effort to believe the correctness of the report ancere alluded to, that some plants are endowed with the faculty of picking up loose articles from the ground. Lieutenant Houghton, who recently visited New Guinea and several other islands and groups of islands in the Pacific, was the first, we believe to report the existence of such a tree, though he did. not explain the means by which it accomplished this unusual feat. It appears to be a species of Ficue, allied to the well-known banyan tree, which throws out from its branches air roots that eventu- ally reach the ground, take root there, and in their turn be- come new stems which perform the same function, so that a single tree eventually extends so far in all directions as to form a complete forest, in which all the stems are united by the branches to each other. The prehensile tree in question similarly throws out from its branches long flexible tendrils which, touching the ground, do not take root there, but twine themselves round any article that may lie within reach. Eventually these quasi-branches contract so that they fail to reach the ground; but the finger-like processes continue to closely grip the substances round which they have twined themselves, and which are consequently sus- pended in mid-air. In this way articles of considerable weight may be literally picked up from the ground by the tree, and so held in suspension.

THE RACE FOR THE CHAMPIONSHIP OF THE WORLD. • The race for the championship of the world and £5OO a side took place on Monday between Edward Hanlan, of Toronto, Canada, and Edward Trickett, of Sydney, cham- pion of Australia. The day was fine with a good deal of cloud and a moderately strong breeze. Laycock and Mr. Innes tossed for choice of stations. The former won for Trickett, who chose the Surrey shore. Harry Kelly was Trickett's pilot from the bows of an eight-oared cutter, and the same office was performed for Hanlan by Spencer. The champion took 38 strokes in the first minute, and was soon in front of his opponent, who, though he started well; was not equal to Hanlan's dash. At the Steps, Hanlan was neatly and easily in front, rowing easily. Trickett was pretty close to him, but not going so easily in the wind. Iranian's time for the mile was 5 min. 17 sec. He was then a length clear. Soon after this Hanlan stopped dead and looked round. There was a good deal of laughter at this, and again the cheers and laughter rang out when the champion once more stopped for at least a couple of strokes. It was quite evident before this that Hanlan was, as usual, winning with consummate ease. Trickett was rowing very well indeed, but Hanlan went away from him as he liked, and was 10 seconds in front at 'Hammersmith Bridge, which he reached in 9 min. 31 sec. There was a great crowd of people here, and something like excitement and enthusiasm, but Hanlan was too far ahead for the spectators to feel any doubt. Off Thorneyeroft's works a barge lay across the scullers' path, and Hanlan lost a lot of ground in getting out of the way. There was a very strong wind blowing, and both men were a great deal bothered by the rough water. There were 17 seconds' difference exactly off Thorneycroft's. The water was very rough, and Hanlan was in a regular serf in Carney Reach. He made for the Middlesex shore to get shelter. When he got shelter he deliberately stopped and baled the water out of his boat with his right hand. Trickett was powerless in the waves, and Kelly had to take him into shelter also. When they were approaching Barnes Hanlan was nearly 200 yards in front rowing strongly and grandly. He was, under the bridge when Trickett was at the Bull's Head. So hollow a race has seldom been witnessed, even with Hanlan winning. There were tl3 seconds' difference at Barnes, even though Hanlan stopped for 10 seconds. The champion fairly made a show of Trickett, and won with ridiculous ease by too many lengths to count.
THE ABRAM COLLIERY EXPLOSION.
COUNSEL'S REPORT TO THE HOME OFFICE.

Mr. A. Young, the counsel who attended the coroner's inquiry irate the cause of the recent accident at the Abram Collieries, has forwarded two reports to the Home Secretary, and these have been presented to the House of Commons within the last few days. In his first report Mr. Young says:—" In my opinion it was conclusively proved that the explosion arose from the ignition of a quantity of gas which had been given off as the direct result of a weighting or crush, and that nothin; could have been done on the part of the owners to prevent the gas being given off. The jury came to the conclusion that there was not sufficient evidence before them to show how the gas was ignited. There was, however, a body of evidence to the effect that, in a well- ventilated colliery such as this was, the gas would be carried along with the air, and the air playing upon an ordinary unprotected Davy lamp would blow the flame upon the gauze, raise it to a white heat in a few seconds, and thereby at once ignite the gas. As a matter of fact, the body of a boy with a securely-locked Davy lamp was found at the spot fixed by the jury, the mining engineers, and her Majesty's inspector, Mr. Hall, as being the place where the gas was ignited. Sitting as a juryman, I should arrive at the conclusion that the gas was ignited by coming into con- tact with the boy's lamp, when being carried rapidly against the current of air. Assuming this theory to be a correct one, it follows that, to prevent the recurrence of a like dis- aster, the ventilation must be reduced or a more perfect lamp must be adopted. Having heard the whole evidence, I feel bound to state that, in my opinion, a similar explo- sion may occur at any time, and will occur almost certainly if another outburst of gas takes place when the men are at work. I quite concur with the jury as to the unsatisfactory character of thei'egulations at the colliery in question with regard to the lamps generally; and especially to the re- lighting of lamps which have been accidentally extin- guished."

BOILER EXPLOSION AT RADCLIFFE. TWO MEN KILLED AND TWO INJURED. A boiler explosion, attended with fatal consequences to two men and severe injuries to two other persons' occurred on Monday morning on the premises of the Irwell Vale Dye Works, Radcliffe, in the occupation of the trustees of the late John Walker. The explosion occurred a few minutes after six o'clock, when only a few of the hands were on the premises. These included Thomas Chadwick, watchman; Robert Chadwick, mechanic; William Froy, day fireman; and Charles Burton, a boy. The two Chadwicks were killed on the spot, while Froy was so badly scalded that he is hardly expected to recover. Burton was also scalded by the escaping steam and 'hot water, and sustained some bruises from the falling material. The boiler which burst was built alongside another. Both were 30 feet long by 6 feet in diameter. By the force of the explosion the boiler was moved about five yards from its position, one end being embedded in the ground and the other piled up on the top of the other boiler. The centre plates were blown in all directions, one piece crashing through the roof of the weav- ing shed of the mill of Messrs. John Bentley and Sons, 50 yards distant, and destroying four looms. The dye works cover an area of 20 yards by 30 yards, and the buildings erected thereon were wrecked, and now lie in a confused heap of bricks, beams, &c. The wood and cotton got on fire, but the flames were speedily extinguished by the Rad- cliffe Local Board Fire Brigade, which was promptly on the spot. The noise of the explosion attracted a good many people, many of whom assisted in removing the bodies of the victims of the explosion, though some two hours elapsed before the body of Robert Chadwick was discovered. The boiler was put down in 1860. ,The damage is estimated at £2,000. The cause of the explosion is unknown, as un- fortunately the only persons who were likely to be able to throw light upon the subject are killed. It is stated that the boiler had not been inspected internally for two years.

TR /IDE NOTES, Cornish tin smelters on Wednesday reduced the in standards 3s. per cwt., making the present prices Ole. and 025., according to quality. The painters and yaperhangers of Southport, who have been on strike, have decided to go back to work at the old rate of wages, and on Saturday the strike was brought to an end.

Some time ago the operative shoemakers of Liverpool re- quested an increase of 25 per cent. in their rate of wages. A conference took place hetween tho workmen and their em- ployers, and the result is that an advance of 15 per cent.has been granted. A mass meeting of miners, held at Wrexham on Tuesday, decided to send deputations to the meeting of masters which is to be held in a few days for the purpose of discussing the wages question. It was also decided to establish a miners' union in the district. Mr. Pease, M.P., the arbitrator for the iron trades opera- tives in the North of England, decides against the men's claim for 7i per cent. for the three months ending April 29th, but for the three months beginning in August they are entitled to 3d. per ton, and 2 per cent. on all other wages. The award is not satisfactory to the men, and at some of the works in the Stockton and Darlington district strikes have t ommenced. About a hundred engine drivers and firemen employed by the Lancashire and Yorkshire Company have held a meet- ing, at Walton, to decide upon the course of action to be pursued c*nsequent upon the Rolling Stock Committee of the company having refused to restore their wages to the rate current prior to the year 1874. A resolution was unanimously adopted, pledging the men present to proceed further in the matter, and it was also decided ta ask the various railway associations to join in a mass meeting to be held in Manchester. , DURHAM COLLIERS.—On Saturday, at a meeting of the Durham coalowners' representatives and members of the Durham Federation Board, the offer of the coalowners of an advance of WI per cent. on current prices for May, June, and July was accepted, and also a sliding Ec.ile based on an ad- vance of 2tl per cent, on the old scale was agreed to throughout. The offers came from the owners at the last meeting, held a week ago, and the representatives of the workmen requested that an adjournment should be made before they notified their acceptance or otherwise. The re- sult of the week's d-liberalion has been the acceptance of the terms offered by the owners,and thus they have a settle- ment of wages disputes in the four branches concerned, for the next two years. • THE Coaer TRA.DE.—The Ilfark Lane Express says:— " The weather during the past week has been for the most part rough and stormy with clear cold nights. There has been considerable rainfall, and clay lands now lie cold and wet. On sound well-cultivated soils wheats are showing indications of regaining colour, but as yet there has been no general improvement. The month of May is now before the crops and much will depend in the nature of the weather which may characterise it. With genial weather the spring corn is in a position to come away very fast. No further reports of rust are to hand. The eupply of native wheats to last week's markets has been rather more liberal, but the proportion of tine qualities is very small, and all damp and inferior samples are more difficult to quit. With this ex- ception the trade for breadstuffe has not shown any change during the week, and values of all other descriptions of native grain remain practically as before. The trade for foreign wheats off stands in London has been very quiet throughout the week, but values have been steadily main- tained, assisted probably by the very moderate arrivals of wheat and the small receipts of flour at the port of London." THE LABOUR MARKET.—The labour market remains on the whole in a satisfactory condition. In the North of England the finished iron trade continues brisk, and the award of Mr. Pease in the Cleveland district not being re- trospectively in favour of an advance of wages will, it is feared, not give satisfaction to the operatives. Ship builders and marine engineers remain specially busy, and few of the , great trade societies now complain of many members un- etnployed. At Birmingham the hardware branches are fairly employed, and Most of the minor industries have an average amount of activity. At Newcastle-on-Tyne and Lincoln the building trades are again tnore than usually busy, but in the Metropolis few large contracts have recently been entered on. At Coventry both the ribbon and the watchmaking trades show a satisfactory revival. The textile trades are on the whole fairly employee., and several classes of opera- tives are again being advertised for. The boot and shoe trades at Leeds, Leicester' Norwich, and Bristol are again brisker, and in London the same industries are in a less un- settled state. Canadian advices indictte a good demand for railway constructive hands, and also for some classes of mechanics. Meanwhile the immigration to the United States continues on an unprecedented scale, and strikes in ninny industries are reported. Great distress on the Coast of Labraceer is announced. Prospects at the Cape of Good Hope are genteelly encouraging.—Labour News. THE LANCASHII2 IRON AND COAL TRADBS, MANURES.. TER, Wednescley.—Notwithstanding the reports of a firmer tone prevailing in the speculative markets of Glasgow and Middlesborough, the tendency of the iron market here em- tinues downwards, and business, as arnie, can still only be done by concessions upon current rates. Lancashire makers of pig iron have been doing little or nothing during the week, and with stocks accumulating at the works would now be open to low offers for good orders, akout 40s. less 21, the average price Tutted for Lancashire fo7ge and foundry iron delivered equal to Manchester. In district brands small sales are quoted at little over this figure, but both Lincolnshire and Derbyshire irons are competing keenly with the local brands. Finished iron makers are still for the most part working on old contracts, with but a few new orders corning in, and although in some cases they are hold- ing for £6 155., local bus here can be bought at as low as £6 10s. per ton delivered into the Manchester district—Al- though the general tone of the coal trade of this district is ; still decidedly dull, business his shown an improvement I rather than otherwise since the Easter holidays. House-fire coals meet with a moderately fair demand for the time of the year as compared with the extreme depression through- out this branch of trade during the preceding winter months, and common round coals for iron-making and steam pur- poses move off tolerably well. Prices consequently have j not given way this month to the extent anticipated by ' buyers, and beyond a slight rec:Alication of prices in the Manchester district, there has been no generally announced alteration of list rates. There is, however, a good deal of underselling, and prices are very irregular. In some excep- tional cases 9s. per ton is still obtained for best coals at the pit, but the average is more nearly Bs. to Bs. 6d., seconds, 63. 61. to 75., and common coal from 4s. 9d. to ss. 6d. per I ton. Engine classes of fuel still move off pretty freely, but supplies keep up with the demand; burgy at the pit month averages 4s. ed. to 49. 9d., best slack 3s. 9d. to 4s. 3d., and ordinary qualities 3s. to 3s :6d. per ton. In shipping there is rather more activity. Coke is in less demand.
