THE NEW EDUCATION CODE.—Earl .PENCER, referring to the circumstances of recent occurrence, which would render it impossible for him to bestow time and attention to the discussion of the Education Code asked Lord Norton to postpone for a time the notice he had given on the subject. The noble Earl thanked the Vice-President of the Council and the officials of the Education Department for the able assistance they had rendered him in the revision of the Education Code.—Lord NORTON replied that it was impos- sible to resist the appeal of the noble Earl, but added that he had not intended to make an attack open the Lord Presi- dent of the Council, but to acknowledge a debt of gratitude to him and his colleagues for the great attention they had given to the subject.—The Marquis of SALISBURY remarked •that he supposed the subject was to be postponed until Lord Spencer returned from Ireland, and he asked how long it would be before his Lordship returned.—Earl SPENCER ex- plained that his object in asking for a postponement was that the Lord Privy Seal, who would undertake his duties in his absence, might be able to inform himself sufficiently upon the matter before he dealt with it, and an adjournment of a week or ten days might suffice. IRELAND.—A petition was presented by the Earl of LONG- FORD, and warmly supported by Lord SALISBURY, asking that the principle adopted by the Land Commissioners in the assessment of fair rents might be made public.—Lord CeoniNetuonD showed that the Government had no power to comply with the wishes of the petitioners, but gave his view of the course adopted by the commissioners, which he had derived from observing their proceedings.--Earl GRAN- VILLE joined in the discussion to show the unreasonable- ness of the request, and the subject was allowed to drop.— Answering the Marquis of Salisbury, Earl GnAesevlLLE said Lord Frederick Cavendish had been appointed to succeed Mr. Forster in the Irish Chief Secretaryship, and that he would not retain the office of Secretary to the Treasury.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THuBsDAY. MR. SMITH'S SCHEME OF PEASANT PROPRIETORY.—'r. W. H. SMITH announced that under the changed circum- stances he did not propose to proceed with his resolution on the subject of the land question in Ireland. MICHAEL DAVITT.—Ia answer to Mr. Cowen, Sir Wm. HARCOURT said the same reason that had induced the Gov- ernment to release the suspects had induced them to release Mr. Davitt, the announcement being received with loud Irish cheers.

THE NEW CHIEF SECRETARY.—A new writ was issued for the northern division of the West Riding of Yorkshire in the room of Lord F. Cavendish, who has accepted the post of Chief Secretary for Ireland. THE "No RENT" MANIFESTO.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to Sir H. D. Wolff, said it had been intimated to him that the "no rent" manifesto would be withdrawn. Several Irish members asked what communication the Prime Minister had received on the subject. Mr. Gladstone indi- cated that the intimation had come frcm Mr. Parnell. MR. FOSTER'S STATEMENT. Mr. Pons= then pi oceeded to give his reasons for having severed his connection with the Cabinet. He stated that the Prime Minister had rightly informed the House that he did not think it right to share the responsibility of the re- lease of the three members. He had tried to work the Act according to the repeated promises and assurances he had given to the House. He had only detained the Queen's sub- jects in prison without trial for the purpose of preventing crime, and not for punishment. He felt that the same reasons that made him obliged to vindicate the arrest of the members made him now object to their release. The real ground why those gentlemen and many others was arrested was because they were trying to carry out their views—their unwritten law as they called it—by working the ruin and the injury of the Queen's subjects by instructions of one kind or another,and that that was carried out to such a degree that no Government could have let it continue without hicoining a Government merely in name and a sham. If the member for Cork had not been placed in Kil mainhain he would soon have become what he was called by many of his friends—" the un- crowned King of Ireland." He would have considered their release if they had given a public undertaking not to set up their law against the law of, the land, or if Ireland had been quiet, or if there had been an acquisition of fresh powers on the part of the Government ; but none of these conditions existed. What he wanted was an avowal of change of purpose. Instead of that, there was a promise that if the Government did something they would cease to oppose the Government. He entreated the House and his late colleagues not to rely on these appear- ances, and above all not to act on them. Lot them not try to buy obedience to the law by concessions to those who disobeyed the law. He believed that no co.ncessions were necessary, and that the Government should not be weakened by any surrender. He thought there were signs of very comiderable improvement in Ireland; the Land League had been defeated, rents were being paid, "boycotting" had been checked, and there was not so much intimidation as theca had been. But the battle against lawlessness was not yet won, and he feared the price they were about to pay would have the effect of weakening the power of .the Government. The right hon, gentleman, in conclusion, said: It 1124 been very p sinful to me; it is painful to leave the Cabinet and the proud position of one of the leaders of that great party to which all My life I have belonged, although in my own mind I am not forsaking one of its principles—(Liberal cheers)—and most assuredly I remain a faithful soldier of its standard. (Renewed cheers.) It is painful to leave one's colleagues and intimate friends at a time of difficulty; and, above all, it is more painful, more painful, indee3, than words can express, to leave the service of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. There never was a chief who won more affection, love, respect, and reverence than he. (Ministerial cheers.) I have only two more things to say. This step is now taken. I hope it may succeed. I can only state that anything which I can do without dishonour to my conscientious con- yiction will bo to 14.00 th the dinloaties of my auccemr,
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
Urgent petitions from the Cypriotes are being forwarded to the Home Government in favour of reforms in the law courts.
MISCELLANEOUS.

With the exception of the ravage caused by the recent storms, the crop reports up to the commencement of May are mainly favourable.. The British Government has asked for the extradition of the three Englishmen who are implicated in the robbery of jewels from the Hatton Garden Post-office. A Ballot was on Tii;,;t;,y mvi a: third t:MG iiTtd passed in the Manx House of Keys. It is modelled on the act which is in force in Great Britain and Ireland. _ _

- A serious explosion has taken place at a gunpowder manu- factory near Bilbao. Three persons were killed outright and several injured. An explosion has occurred.on board the steamer Marion, on the Wateree River, in South Carolina, by which nine persons were killed and several injured. A telegram from Hong Kong states that after a bombard- ment of two hours' duration the French have taken possession of Hanoi, the capital of Tonking. The Russo-Turkish War Indemnity question is still un- settled, and promises to remain so, the demands of the Rus- sian Ambassador being opposed by a powerful minority in the Turkish Cabinet.
At Ormskirk, a young woman, a dressmaker, has died ap- parently ftom the effects of a fright sustained by suddenly hearing the loud yelp of a dog as she was walking through the street.

The Press Association is authorised by the Home Secre- tary to state that G. H. Lamson, before his execution, con- fessed his guilt to the chaplain of the gaol, and acknowledged the justice of his sentence. The Norwich magistrates on Saturday, committed Wm. George Abigail, aged 19, for trial at the Ipswich assizes on the charge of murdering Jane Plunkett, 23, at Catton, Nor- wich, on the previous Taesday, by twice shooting her with a revolver.

A mine has been found under the Spirovo station, on the Moscow Railway. It was most carefully constructed, and was furnished with conducting wires. It is reported that a mine has also been found under the Imperial pavilion at the exhibition intended shortly to be held at Moscow. Strange rumours are current as to the relations between Germany and France. One story says that a treaty is being negotiated by which Germany will guarantee France in her possessions, and in return France will pledge herself to a reduction of the army and not to form an alliance with any other foreign Power. An extraordinary attempt to assassinate Mr. Vanderbilt and Mr. Cyrus Field by infernal machines sent through the post has just been discovered through one of the machines exploding in a mail bag, fortunately without doing much harm. The cause of the attempt is not stated, but it may be supposed to be connected with the financial operations of the two gentlemen. We have intelligence from Paris of a desperate engage- ment between a detachment of the French Foreign Legion escorting a topographical expedition and a large body of natives near Tigri. The Foreign Legiou are reported to have defended themselves heroically, and to have remained masters of the field, after having killed several hundreds of their opponents, but with a loss on their own side of 37 killed and 30 wounded. On Tuesday, an authoritative statement was made that Mr. Willoughby was not murdered on a French railway, as at first believed, but that he fell out of the door against which he leaned on rising suddenly from a long sleep. During the official investigation in France, it was proved that the guard had not fastened the door, and to screen himself that officer had made false statements.

The Riga Ga:ette published an account of an agrarian outrage committed on the 28th ult. near Hosenfoth, Cour- laud. The victim was a landowner, named Baron Nolchen Apprichon, who was fired at from behind some bushes near the road. One shot destroyed the sight of one of his eyes, and the remainder of the charge entered his arm and shoulder. Some 'weeks ago an incendiary fire occurred on Baron Nolchen's estate.

News of a desperate attack upon two companies of French troops in Algeria has come to hand. They were escorting an exploring expedition on the Moorish border at the time, and were attacked by 2,000 horsemen—but according to another report by 6,000 natives on foot and 1,800 horsemen —under Bon Amena, who is said to have been killed along with hundreds of his followers. The French loss is given at forty soldiers and two officers killed, and the baggage had to be abandoned. TEE LARGEST Dock IN TEE WORLD.—The Newfoundland House of Commons has passed a bill authorising the build- ing of a graving dock at St. John's. The builders are to get 30,000 dollars annual subsidy, and also the Government en- dorsement for 600,000 dollar bonds. The proposed dock is to be the largest dock in the world, capable of accommoda- ting the largest steamers. It will be 600 feet long, 100 feet wide at the coping, 83 feet at the bottom, 30 feet in depth, and 66 feet in witdth at the entrance. The deck is pro- jected for the benefit of Anglo-American Transatlantic com- merce.

A GENTEEL CHEAT.—The little town of Pau has recently been edified by the trial of one of its leading medical men for cheating at cards. It was Dr. Gaye, a man of good family, municipal councillor, awl a Knight of the Legion of Honour, who, for deceiving his fellow-townsmen at the bac- carat table, found himself brought before the local magis- trate. The doctor's method of "improving fortune" was threefold. On taking up good cards he would surreptitiously increase his original stake by adding money concealed in the palm of his hand, or he would place a louis under a silver five-franc piece, and only uncover the former when he won. Finally, he bad a habit of withdrawing part of his stake when luck went in favour of the bank. When these pranks were first noticed the doctor's friends were unwilling to believe that be could be guilty of such conduct, and accordingly a watch was set on his play. Hts systematic swindling was quickly discovered. He was expelled from the club and struck off the lists of the Legion of Honour. Here the affair would have stopped but for the Public Prosecutor, who summoned the doctor for swindling, an offence for which he has been sentenced to two months' im- prisonment and a fine of LS. TURKEY. We learn from Constantinople that Alxlurrahman Pasha, formerly Governor of Bagdad, has keen appointed Premier in the place of Said Pasha, who has been dismissed. The new Premier is described as a Minister of high repute as an able and conscientious administrator. THE RISING IN AUSTRIA.

There has been a fierce encounter in Herzegovina between two battalions of Austrian troops and a " band " of insur- gents. The latter were of caurse "dispersed," but the Austrians admit Unit on their side one rifleman was "slightly wounded," whether by bullet, sabre, or fist is not stated. There, however, he is on the return, to attest the fury and duration of tbe combat, in which one side at least appears to have been armed with the long bow. • FIGHTING IN NEW CALABAR.

It is understood that her Majesty has, at Mr. Gladstone's request, made the baronetcy of Mr. Bass to pass with re- mainder to his brother, Mr. Hamar Bass, M.P. for Tamwortb. This is very unusual in the gift of a baronetcy. Sir Arthur Bass bas two daughters and no son. _ . . . .

The West Coast mail brings an account of a "great battle" between the natives of New Calabar and the fol- lowers of Oko Jumbo. It is estimated that 1,000 men on each side were killed. Oko Jumbo's men had the upper band at the time of the latest reports, but it was thought the people of New Calabar would be reinforced by the adherents of Ja Jo, and "nothing short of carnage" was in prospect. British subjects were very uneasy, and were hoping for the appearance of one or two English gunboats.

It is stated thaY a prize fight took place at Bromley, on Monday, between two men named Ross and Watson, for stakes amounting to £2O. Twelve rounds, lasting 35 min., were•fought, when Watson gave in. Both men were badly punished, and no interruption occurred from the police. Lady Thomson, widow of Sir Wyville Thomson, who filled the chair of natural histcry in the Edinburgh Univer- sity, will receive a grant of £4OO from the Royal Bounty Fund. Mrs. Burton, widow of Mr. John Hill Burton, the historian, will receive a pension of £BO a year. On Sunday intelligence was received of the death of Princess Marie of Wurtemburg, sister to the Duatess of Albany. The Prince and Princess of Waldeck-Pytmont, their family, and suite left London at once for Germany. The Princess Marie, who was only 24 years of age, was married in 1877 to Prince William of Wurtemburg. RUINED BY HORSE RACING.—At the Birmingham Police Court, on Tuesday, George William Long, the local manager for Messrs. Wait and Co., merchants, Gloucester, Bristol, and Birmingham, was sentenced to 18 months' imprison- ment for embezzling over £2,500, the moneys of his employers. The prisoner, who had occupied a position of responsibility. for 14 years, attributed his ruin to horse racing, saying that he had lost nearly £2OO on a race in one day. On Saturday, a deputation from the Educational Institute of Scotland had an interview with Mr. Mundella to urge his support to a bill giving better security of tenure to principal teachers in board schools in Scotland. Mr. Mundella said the Government would oppose the bill because they believed it to be derogatory to local authority altogether, but he agreed that there should be some safeguards against arbi- trary dismissal. A high compliment has been paid to the new borough of Hyde by Mr. Terry, CE., of the Local Government Board. In closing an enquiry iuto the merits of an application for a ',loan for improvement purposes, he said it was very satis- factory to find a town so well satisfied with its Council as to leave matters entirely in its hands. Mr. Terry also expressed the opinion that London might take a lesson from some of the provincial towns in respect to scavenging. ' Sir Henry Parkes, Premier of New South Wales, accom- panied by his daughter, visited Bedford, on Monday morn- ing, as the guests of Mr. James Howard, M.P., and on arrival proceeded to the Britannia Iron Works, and saw the manu- facture of agricultural implements, many of them destined for the Australian colonies. After luncheon Sir Henry and Miss Parkes inspected the Britannia farms and also visited Elstow. _ _

MR. SPURGEON.-Mr. Spurgeon has again been taken seriously ill. He was unable to preach at his Tabernacle on Sunday, but it is hoped that his recovery may be speedy, and that he may be sufficiently restored to resume his ministerial duties on Sunday next. It is, however, impera- tive that Mr. Spurgeon's friends should insist on prolonged rest, and see that his valuable life is not further hazarded by spending another winter in our uncertain climate. Mr. Montagu Williams says in a letter that no suggestion of Lamson's insanity was ever made to himself or any of the counsel engaged in the case. The prisoner altogether denied the commission of the crime. His brief contained the names of two scientific gentlemen who decliqed to go into the witness box and two witnesses as to character whom he did not think it would serve the prisoner to put forward. The letter of the Rev. Mr. Lamson, Mr. Williams adds, appears to render:this explanation necessary. A report which has been circulated respecting a "narrow escape of Mr. Chamberlain," was an exaggeration of .a very trifling incident which occurred nearly a fortnight ago at Birmingham. In mistake for quinine mixture, Mr. Chamberlain picked up a bottle containing a weak solution of carbolic acid and drank a small quantity. He was dres- sing for dinner at the time, and the inconvenience occa- sioned was so slight that it did not prevent him joining his friends at the table. No emetic was taken or required. The Bishop of Manchester preaching at Bolton, on Sim- day evening, took a desponding view of the condition of society—especially in regard to the family tie, which was, he said, in danger of falling to pieces. His Lordship said the question was whether we were doing right in letting the religious element slip almost entirely out of our modern system of education, and he made an earnest appeal to Churchmen not to let their day schools pass out of their hands.

REPRIMANDING A MAOISTRATE.—Mr. Walter Smith, a Southport magistrate, has been severely reprimanded while sitting on the bench by the Town clerk of that Borough, be- cause he told a police-officer he was neglecting his duty in not apprehending children who were constantly " tossing " in a certain street. The Town clerk strongly objected to Mr. Smith " lecturing " the officer in court, and told him that he should confine himself to his duty, which was to administer justice. If he had a complaint to make against the officer, he should, as a member of the Corporation, com- plain to the Watch Committee, and not make such "uncalled- for and extraordinary remarks" on the bench. The magis- trate appears to have taken his correction very meekly, and "was sorry if he had made a mistake." MELANCHOLY OCCURRENCE AT LEEDS.—On Sunday afternoon, as Charles, Daniel, and Francis Maloney, aged twelve, five, and two years respectively, brothers, and the sons of Peter Maloney, labourer, of Cross Green-lane, the Bank, Leeds, were playing on the bank of the river Aire at Knostrop, near Leeds, Daniel and Francis, the two younger boys, slipped into the water. Charles, the eldest, stripped, jumped into the water, and rescued Francis, dragging him to the side. He then dived in again and tried to reach Daniel, who caught hold of him. Charlesstruggled bravely for a short time, but eventually both he and the lad he was trying to save were overpowered by the strong current swollen by the rains, and both were carried down the river and drowned. Neither of the bodies had been recovered last night. The youngest child was Laken home by the police and was quickly restored. GREAT FIRE IN ABERDEEN.—On Saturday night a fare broke out in a basketmaker's shop, in the New Market Buildings Aberdeen, and it spread with such extreme rapidity that by about a quarter to nine o'clock the whole buildings were thoroughly gutted. The buildings were about the largest of the kind in Scotland. The total damage is estimated at £40,000. The Press Association Aberdeen correspondsut telegraphed on Sunday night as follows:— "This morning a dead body was recovered from Market Buildings, Aberdeen, and was identified as that of Crichton, a street porter. The body, which was found in one' of the side galleries, was very much charred. The damage is esti- mated at quite £50,000. It is believed that no other lives have been lost. The building is completely gutted."—A later telegram states that no other bodies were found up to ten o'clock, but two men were reported to be missing.

THE ROYAL ACADEMY BANQUET.—The Royal Academy banquet on Saturday night was attended by the King of the Netherlands and an unusually brilliant assemblage. After the customary pleasant speeches in connection with the loyal and patriotic toasts, the President of the Academy (Sir F. Leighton) proposed Her Majesty's Ministers, regretting the absence of Mr. Gladstone, who, it was explained, had been persuaded to husband his strength. Earl Granville, in replying to the toast, remarked that art did not depend upon Government departments, but it looked to the encourage- ment of the great public. The President in the course of the evening referred to the loss during the year of two note- worthy artists, John Linnell and Dante Gabriel Rossetti; and also to the removal by death of Sir Henry Cole, to whom the world of art owed a deep and lasting debt. Re- ferring to the exhibition, the President thought there was evidence of great vitality in the work of the year. SHOCKING SUICIDE 07 A MANCHESTER YARN AGENT.— About half-past nine, the other morning, Mr. Llewellyn Hanmer, head of the firm of L. Hanmer and Sons, yarn agents, commercial-buildings, Cross-street, Manchester, en- gaged a four-wheeled cab, and told the man to drive up Rochdale-road until he was told to stop. The driver pro- cee 'ed in that direction. When at Barnes Green, the driver heard in the cab a sharp crack, and on looking through the window saw Mr. Hanmer sinking in a heap to the bottom of the vehicle, his right hand grasping a revolver. He at once stopped the cab, and called some labourers who were near. On being searched, the pockets were found to contain a pocket book, in which were a large number of business docu- ments, including a bill of exchange for £2,500 drawn on a firm of merchants in Glasgow. This document would be- come due on the Ist instant, but had not been met. He was about 63 years of age. It is stated that the deceased was very highly respected on 'Change, where he was well known.

THE IRISH SECRETARY AND HIS CONSTITIJENTS.—MT. Forster, in reply to a resolution of the Bradford Liberal Four Hundred expressing renewed confilence in the Govern- ment, has written as follows :—lrish Office, April 28th.— Dear Sir,—l am sincerely sorry that I was unable by return of post to acknowledge receipt of the resolution passed at the annual meeting of the Committee of the Four Hundred of the Bradford Liberal Electoral Association, and through you to thank them not merely for their continued support to Mr. Gladstone and his Government, but most especially for the kind expressions of sympathy and confidence in my- self. It may be true that few servants of their Queen and country have had of late more difficulties to contend with than I have had, or have had their motives and actions more misconstrued and misrepresented ; but, however this may be, this much is certain, that no Minister in a responsible posi- tion was ever more generously supported by his constituents, and especially by the leaders and members of the great Liberal party to whom I owe my return to Parliament. In concluding, I hope that I may soon be able to tell my con- stituents how sincerely I thank them.—l remain, dtc., W. E. FousTEE.

During a thunderstorm on Tuesday, Wolviston Parish Church, situated between Stockton and West Hartlepool,was struck by lightning and considerably damaged. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone entertained the Prince and Princess of Wales and a number of distinguished guests at dinner on Wednesday evening, Mrs. Gladstone afterwards holding a reception. At the Old Bailey, on Tuesday, John Fereday, charged with the murder of Henry Sands, at Colney Hatch Lunatic Asviuu,-,7,t5 acquitted by the jury on the ground of insanity and ordered to be detained. The Pope is reported to have beeq seized with a fit after administering the Eucharist to several persons II: the throne room of the Vatican on Sunday. It is, however, declared to to have been only a passing affection, and not of great moment. _ _ _ .

The draft report agreed to by the Commons' Select Com- mittee on the Artisans' Dwellings Act recommends the abolition of all places injurious to the health and welfare of the people. Small towns shall, it is proposed, be excluded from the operation of the Act. The Macclesfield Town Council on Wednesday, un- animously adopted a resolution condemning the Attorney- General's bill proposing to disfranchise the borough. The resolution declared that all the demands of justice would be fully met by placing Macclesfield on the same schedule as Oxford, Chester, and Boston. Mr. Brocklehurst, one of the unseated Libiral members, was present, and said Maccles- field had no champion in Parliament. The Venerable Sir Lovelace Stamer, archdeacon of Stoke- on-Treet, is not quite sure as to what opinion he should form about the Salvation Army, but on one or two points he seems to have made up his mind. Having regard to the fact that they claim 4iLhave 13,393 efficient speakers, he remarks that these ma not be qualified to suit the taste of refined and educated audiences, but they had moved the hearts and rescued from sinful habits thousands whom the Church had failed to reach. This is a very self-condemna- tory confession for a pillar of the National Church to have to make. The Australian " team " of cricketers have arrived in this country. Some of the Englishmen who have been playing in Australia have returned to their homes, where they were informed that in their absence reports had been published attributing to them a " plot " to " sell " a match at Melbourne. The men who are impeached intead to take steps to vindicate their characters from the slanderous asper- sion. The proceedings will be watched with interest by all who are concerned for the honour of the national game. THE LEIGH SMITH EXPLORING EXPEDITION.—Sir Allan Young has chartered the steamer Hope, of Peterhead, for the expedition to be sent in search of Mr. Leigh Smith's exploring party, whose vessel, the Eira, is supposed to be beset amongst the ice about Franz Josef Land or Nova Zambia. The Hope is 300 tons register, with engines of 70 horse power. She will at once proceed to London to be eqaipped, and the expedition, it is expected, will be com- manded by Captain Markham. THE YKLDING MunDEß.—The trial of Esther Pay for the murder of Georgina Moore was concluded on Saturday at Lewes Assizes. Baron Pollock, in summing up, pointed out that the various statements made by the prisoner about collateral matters must not be too strictly construed. As ' regarded Moore, the deceased's father, wicked as he was, dissolute, sensual, of utter dishonesty of purpose, ana cruelty of mind to those women who trusted him it did not follow that he would take the life of his own child.—The jury, after 20 minutes' deliberation, acquitted the prisoner, who audiby expressed her thanks to the jury. The annual meeting of the Council of the Liberation Society was held in London on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. H. R. Ellington, who presided, said they had worked hard and made satisfactory progress. Mr. Illingsworth, M.P., bad written stating his conviction that the dissatisfaction within the Church was the forerunner of Liberation. The treasurer's report showed that the balance of receipts over expenditure for the year was £765. Resolutions were adopted approving Mr. Richard's bill relating to cemetries and burial fees, and Mr. Peddie's bill relating to Scotch dis- establishment.

ATTEMPT TO WRECK THE IRISH MAIL.—The signalman on duty at a railway siding near Rugby, reports a diabolical attempt to wreck the Irish mail. He states that at about 4-40 a.m. lie perceived a large object lying across the metals about 280 yards from his box. Knowing the Irish mail was due, he ran to the spot, and found a large, heavy sleeper lying across the metals over which the Irish mail would have proceeded seven minutes later. He states that the sleeper was firmly secured to the rails by means of a stout piece of iron, and, moreover, fastened in such a manner to one of the iron chains, that had the train passed over a ter- rible accident must have resulted. He removed the obstruc- tion and returned to his box. VroLENT ASSAULT ON A YOUNG LADY.—At the Stafford Assizes, on Wednesday, Baron Huddlestone sentenced John Thomas Smith. 28, to twenty-five years' penal servitude for violently assaulting a young lady named Ellen Birbeck, at Kimberton, and stealing from her pocket a few shillings. The learned Judge said that throughout all his experience both at the bar and on the bench he had never known such a disgraceful and hideous outrage. Not satisfied with robbing the young lady, the prisoner had afterwards thrown Jeer over a gate and committed the assault complained of. His Lordship added that he had hesitated about having the indictment altered so as to include highway robbery, in order to supplement the penal servitude by the cat-o'-nine- tails.

"150 RENT" IN THE ISLE OF MAN.—An old lady named Annie Bradley, who was committed for trial at the Deem- ster's Court, Douglas, on Tuesday, has, it appears, been Carrying out the "on rent" theory systematically for years. Recently she has occupied a furnished house in the Isle of Man, the rent of which was 100 a year, which, however, she did not pay, and her daughter said that she acted similarly at Bowden and at Tranmere, and had left each place in debt. Another of her weaknesses was to pledge watches which had not been paid for, and at Tranmere she pledged the plate, and was sentenced to three month's im- prisonment. On Tuesday she sought to avoid this fate by pleading age and infirmity, but was committed for trial.

_ BRANDING A PAIIPER.—ACthe County Sessions, at Maid- stone, on Monday, Charles J. Moss, the master of the Maid- stone Union at Coaheath, was summoned by Alfred Giles, one of the inmates, for having, on the .6th April, assaulted him and burnt his hand with a hot iron. The allegation was that because Giles refused to leave a certain ward the defendant fetched a hot iron, and with it burnt his arm and left wrist, in order to make him leave go of the gate. The suggestion for the defence was that the complainant was a refractory pauper, that force was necessary to be used, that the iron was used merely to push open the gate to which Giles clung, and the man in trying to knock it away in- flicted the injuries which were-very slight, himself. The Mr.bench held that ir. Moss ought not to have had the iron in his band, and ordered him to pay a fine of £1 and 13s. costs.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT LINACRE GASWORKS. Two MEN KILLED.—On Tuesday an accident occurred at the gasworks, Linacre, by which two men lost their lives. John Dixon, of Laburnum-place, Bootle, and William Leroyd, of Orrell Village, were engaged cleaning the inner side of the tank which surrounds one of the gasometers. For this pur- pose the gasometer was sunk to its lowest level, and the men were working on a suspended platform, the sides of which were guarded by rails. They had finished one sec- tion of the work, and, alighting on the roof of the gasome- ter, shifted their dage or platform, and resuming their places on it gave the signal for it to be again raised. This was done, but when the platform had been lifted about 20ft. above the top of the gasometer, ons of the bolts underneath it gave way. The two men were jerked off, and fell on the edge of the gasometer. They then rolled into the water of the tank. They were quickly got out, but were both dead. From the condition of the skulls, death must have been in- stantaneous from the fall.

Mrs. Turner, widow of the late Mr. Charles Turner, who for some years represented South and South-West Lanca- shire in Parliament, is about to found in Liverpool a home for incurables. The building will cost aboat £40,000, and Mrs. Turner will make provisicn for the maintenance of thti hospital. More than 100 towns have appointed delegates to attcnd the national dcmonstration to be held in London on the lOtk of May in support of Mr. Bradlaugh's claim. The whole executive of the Liberal and Radical Union of Northampton will attend the Trafalgar-square meeting; and the London Trades Council have appealed to the various trade organisav tions to take part. A petition for liquidation has been presented at the London Bankrupicy Court on behalf of Messrs. Bannel and. Hunter, wine merchants, St. Puristan's Hill. The liabilities are stated at £300,000. The assets are expected to be 4011. siderable, and include contracts amounting to £BOO,OOO. . Thomas Olivett, the signalman who reported the finding of a sleeper laid across the rails near Rugby, it was believed with the intention of upsetting the Irish mail, on Monday, has confessed that the story is a fabrication. He has bees suspended from duty. It is believed his object was to obtain promotion. At Accrington, on Thursday, Thomas Cullen, a miner, osc remand, was committed for trial for attempting to do-grie- vous bodily harm by administering rat poison in some tea to Shepherd „Holding, a sub-underlooker at Broadfield Coalpit, Oswaldtwistle. The prisoner came out of gaol in December, having served six months for threatening to shoot the over- looker. The prosecutor gave evidence against him at his trial, and the prisoner threatened to " do " for him. An inquest was held at Dudley, on Thursday, respecting the death of Henry Westwood, 14, who was drowned whilst bathing in the politic swimming baths. The deceased and a number of other boys commenced playing at hide and i seek in the baths, and suddenly deceased was missed. Owing, t is said, to the water not being very clear, the snectators could not see the bottom of the bath, but upon a drag being used the deceased's lifeless body was found. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

On Thursday morning the police had reported to them the swindling of a Giskurne farmer, named Aden Tebay, of £32 at Bury fair, on Wednesday, by the confidence trick. Two men, one dressed like a local preacher, persuaded Tebay that there was a large sum of money to distribute in charity by anyone who could show he had £2O, and Tebay entrusted one ma u with his money and was to receive £5O to dis- ribute.

On Thursday morning, as the steamer Afghan was leaving Hull, coal laden, for eronstadt, she was run into by the steamer White Sea, of Dundee, which was coming up the Humber. She was struck amidships and nearly cut in two, sinking in about five minutes. The captain, his wife, and fourteen of the crew and a passenger were rescued by small boats, but another passenger named O'Neal, a Halifax weaver, was drowned through becoming entangled in the rigging. The captain and crew lost everything. A Central News telegram from Skye says the trial of the five Skye crofters takes place at Inverness on Wednesday next. The Kinistle tenants on Major Fraser's estate were about to accept a bonus to leave, but are now standing out for a reduction of rent. Mr. Macpherson Macleod, pro- prietor of part of Glandale, accompanied by his uncle. Pro- fessor Macpherson, has gone to confer with the disafTectet I tenants.

A Lloyd's telegram states that the steamer Aberfoyle arrived at Hull on Thursday, and landed the second officer and five men, part of the crew of ths barque Mallard, 600 tons register, bound from Pensitcola to Falmouth for orders 3 which vessel was abandoned water-logged and on her beam ends, 43 miles off the Lizard, having encountered the late hurricane. Ihe master died before the rescue was made, and the remaining men, some eleven in number, were washed overboard and lost.

DROWNING A SWEETIMART.—At the Stafford Assizes, on Wednesday, William Fryer, aged 31, metal roller, of Tipton, Staffordshire, was indicted for the wilful murder of his sweetheart, Susannah Jones, on the 21st January. It was alleged that the accused was walking along the canal side OIL the night in question, with Ifis arm round the woman's waist, and that he suddenly pushed her into the canal, where she was drowned. For the defence it was not denied that the prisoner caused the death of his sweetheart, and a plea of insanity was set up. Several witnesses testified to the pri- soner being of unsound mind, and Mr. Charles Henry Greaves, the surgeon at the jail, stated that he was suffering from a diseased mind, and had an impulsive mania. Evidence was given that the mother of the prisoner was considered insane at the time of her death, and that his sister was at present in an asylum. The learned judge summed up strongly in favour of the plea set up for the defence, and the jury returned a verdict of not guilty upon the ground of insanity, and he was ordered to be -detained during Her Majesty's pleasure. WESLEYAN MISSIONARY SOCIETY.—The annual rneetieg of this society was held at Exeter Hall on Monday morning' under the presidency of Mr. H. J. Atkinson, J.P. The large hall was crowded. The report stated that, apart from the continued depression and straightened means, the mission work had seldom presented so many encmrazing Moms of advancement as those which bad marked the history of the past year. During the year the Mission Home donations amounted to £4,100 115.'61. ; the home districts to £81,36W 13s. 2d.; the Christmas offerings to £7,433 193. ; the juvenile associations to £0,772 ISs. 7d.; and, with other donations, the total home receipst amounted to .£117,767 23. 94. That, with foreign receipts and extraordinary re- ceipts, made a total income of £151,797 149. 7d. The gec. eral expenditure was £145, 454 Hs.; on account of special missions, &c., £1,209 3s. ld. ; and after deducing the ordi- nary receipts for the year, there was a deiicientcv of £5,021 23. 61 To this amount must be added the debt of 1880, £38,310 7s. 51, and that, with the less amount received from the Thanksgiving Fund, left a total deficiency of £33,266 13s. 11d.

• MEETING OF THE REFORM CLUB.—Earl Granville pre- sided at a meeting of the members of the Reform Club on Thursday. The Marquis of Hartington moved a resolution declaring the desirability that members of the Reform Club should be elected by a committee, instead of by a ballot of the whole club. The preparation of a detailed scheme for carrying out the change he referred to the general commit- tee, who should report to an adjourned general meeting. Lord Hartington said the Reform Club had higher functione than the mere social form, and did not exist for the mere convenience of its members. He mentioned that up to Manta of the present year there had been thirty-six candi- dates blackballed.—Mr. John Fright supported the pro- posed alteration, and said the systematic blackballing of candidates tended to destroy the political character of the club.—Mr. P. H. Muntz, M.P., moved an amendment of which he had given notice, that a candidate who should have been blackballed may, with the consent of the commit- tee, on a memorial signed by not less than fifty members, including the proposer and seconder of the candidate, be again put up for election at the next ballot.—The resolution was carried and a poll demanded, which will take place in a fortnight. CURIOUS BREACH OF PROMISE.—A singular breach of promise case has been heard in Dublin. rue p'a hi if was a simple-hearted youth of about 30--he is said to have "looked" only 20—and the derend.;nt a well-preserved widow, who was born a few years after the battle of Water- loo. The widow had a fortune, and the suitor, Mr. Robert Morris, of Ballycanew, in Wexford, conceived the happy idea that be could administer the lady's estate to her satis- faction—and his own. lie sought her society, and various tender passages occurred between them. The courtship tc. came mixed up in quite a pathetic way with the life sad fortunes of a pig, which the suitor had bought with the widow's moneys. In a moment of weakness, she agreed to marry Mr. Morris on the day on which the pig should be pronounced to be fit for slaughter. With this inducement before his eyEs, it may be presumed that Morris bestowed much of his time upon the pig, and superintended its diet with zealous care. Fattening food was at a premium. But whilst the pig was growing, a rival suitor appeared on the scene, and ultimately, to his grief and consternation, Morris found himself jilted, and the fair proprietress of the pig be- came -.Mrs. Cranwell. The match was arranged by a local auctioneer, notwithstanding the fact that be had received from Morris an" I 0 " for £5OO conditional on his mar- riage to the widow. In the witness box Morris was candid enOugh to own that he had never " cared" for the widow. His sole object was to obtain the command of her money, and for his disappointment in this respect he was allowed, by the scandalous state of the law, to seek a.substantial solatiunt. The jury awarded him Gd., and he will have his own costs to pay. Of the fate of the pig nothing was (Hs. closed at the trial.

ANOTHER FEILA.LE IMPOSTOR: DISCOVERY OF EXTEN- SIVE FECAUDS.—A woman, who carries on business in Ply- mouth as a fruiterer, has lf.,een discovered in and confessed to the perpetration of serious frauds. Some months since she waited on a blind gentleman in Plymouth, and entered into negotiations for the purchase from him of Buckfast Abbey, a well-known mansion in Devon. She represented that she was acting for an elderly lady, who desired the mansion*for her nephew; and, as the negotiations proceeded, she arranged an interview between the owner and the lady in question. The gentleman, being blind, had no suspicion that in this interview he was being imposed on, but he has since discovered that the female who first came to him per- sonated the old lady in two interviews, and she managed matters so adroitly that she induced him to advance her money in order to relieve her of temporary financial diffi- culties. As security for the purchase money of the Abbey she deposited with him supposed deeds, which afterwards turned out to be mere waste paper ; and further inquiries , show that extensive frauds have been perpetrated on other people, amounting in all to £6OO or £7OO. THREATENING THE QUEEN.—The magistrate at Bow- street Police Court was engaged on Saturday afternoon in hearing a charge against a lad of 17 of sending a threatening letter to the Queen. The prisoner is Arthur Young, a rail- way telegraeh clerk at Sprotborough, near Doncaster. The letter purported to come from an Irish Roman Catholic priest, and it demanded a sum n of £2,000 for the purpose of shipping abroad 50 evicted farmers who had " banded them- selves together" for Her Majesty's "destruction." It spoke of attempts on the lives of tile Queen and her sons and daughters, and specifically named Prince Leopold, who was asked bow he would like to have a bullet put through him on his wedding day. The money wos to be sent to the writer through the agency of his "dupe," whose address was given as "A. Y., M. S. and L. Offices, Doncaster." Inquiry lei to the arrest of the prisoner, who is said to have been ad- dicted to the reading of sensational fiction, and the letter was now coufigently declared by his superior officer to be Young's writing. The prisoner was remanded. PLAN FOR DEFENDING THE CHANNEL TUNNEL. The Press Association learns that Dr. Siemens has, by request, presented to the military committee on the subject of the channel tunnel a novel and ingenious plan for defending the tunnel, if constructed, from hostile invasion. He proposes that immediately above the lateral drainage tunnel there should be a driftway or tuba terminating on the tunnel side in a double arch, with numerous perforations, and on the land side in several chambers of wrought iron sunk into the ground. Those chambers would be filled with common chalk, and connected with a large cistern charged with diluted muriatic acid, and on opening the communication the acid would flow into the upper portion of one of the chambers, , from whence it would be distributed by perforated pipes over the entire area. The result would be a powerful chemical reaction, giving rise to a generation of carbonic acid which would for half a mile or more form an impassable barrier to the passage of human beings. Dr. Siemens recommends this plan as being cheap and easy of adoption, whilst leaving the tunnel intact.

div.head: TORTURE OF TWO ITALIANS AT MONTEVIDEO.
div.p: THE TORTURE OF TWO ITALIANS AT MONTEVIDEO.

A Reuter's telegram from Buenos Ayres states that advices from Montevideo report excitement at that place owing to the arrest of the ex-War Minister and of the Chief of Police as responsible for the torture of two Italian sub- jects falsely accused of murder. It is added that some Brazilian subjects having met with similar treatment the Brazilian Government was concentrating troops on the frontier' and had de.patched an envoy to Montevideo to demand redress. The Uruguayan Government was reported to be mobilising 3,500 men for ,the service of the frontier, and taking measures to fortify Montevideo. Arms were also being provided for 25 000 men. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION. An official statement of the result of the, court-martial on Circassian officers and others who were implicated in the recently-discovered plot at Cairo has been published by Ourabi Pasha, the person most immediately concerned. Forty-three prisoners havebeen convicted, and their punish- ment will be exile. The rest of the accased, being civilian., are to be banded over to the civil authorities. Ourabi denied that the prisoners had been tortured. He said that the questions had been put to them in writing, and that written answers were given. The prisoners, when confronted with each other before the Court, stated that the object of the con- spiracy was to take Ourabi Pasha's life, dethrone the Khe- dive, and bring back Ismail Pasha, aad was instigated by the latter and Retib Pasha.

A later telegram says :—The Khedive having refused to confirm the sentence of the court-martial upon the Circas- sian officers and other implicated in the plot against the Ourabi Pasha until the minutes of the proceedings are sub- mitted to him, the Ministers accordingly attended at the Abdin Palace in order to comply with his Highness's re- quest. It is considered doubtful whether the Khedive will confirm the sentence. A Daily 2lretcs Berlin telegram says :—Germany has de- clared, in respect to the Egyptian question, that if any intervention becomes necessary, it can only be made on con- dition that all the Great Powers are consulted. It is not believed here that there will be any necessity to interfere for some time to come. It is reported that England is will- ing, under certain conditions, that the Sultan should even- tually be entrusted with the settlement of the Egyptian question; but, further, that this proposition meets with strong opposition on the part of France. . A Constantinople telegraktf says that the Turkish Ambas- sador in Berlin was recently instructed to ascertain Prince Bismarck's views as to a possible military occupation of Egypt by Turkey. The Chancellor's reply, it is stated, was to the effect that such an occupation would simply compli- cate the political situation in Egypt, and that Austria and Italy, if addressed on the subject, would probably make a similar reply. _ _

, A late telegram states that fellowin, the advice of the French diplomatic agent, the Egyptian Cabinet, after much deliberation, has resolved to modify the finding of the court martial upon those implicated in the plot against Arabi Pasha.
DISCONTENT IN THE TRANSVAAL AND ZULULAisID.

A Durban correspondent- telegraphs that Governor has refused to receive the Zulu chiefs who came to Pietermaritz- burg without the permission of the Resident, to lay before him their grievances and desires, which include, it is said, the restoration of Cetewayo to the throne. Food is scarce in Zululand, and much suffering and discontent are said to prevail. The correspondent adds that troubles are antici- pated in the Transvaal, war between two chiefs being con- sidered to be imminent.

A Mar itzburg telegram states: Careful inquiry into the causes of the Zulu deputation connects it with the com- plaints of Cotewayo's relatives on which Sir Evelyn Wood adjudicated in August last. Having neglected to carry out the terms of the award, these chiefs, hearing of Sir H. Bul- wer's arrival, wished to lay their complaints before him without waiting for a pass from the Resident, who had pro- mised to recommend Sir H. Bulwer to see them. They en- tered Natal, being joined on the way by numerous other chiefs, who had no authorisation to leave Zululand. There is the best authority for stating that nothing was said about a request for Cetewayo's return until the deputation was in Natal. The incident shows the activity of Cetewayo's party, from the intrigues of which danger is much to be Apprehended. The unsettled state of Zululand gives this party ,great power. A correspondent at Durban referring to the Zulu deputa- tion, states that Bishop Colenso repudiates any sort of con- nection with the movement, the origion of which is ascribed to sinister intrigues of serious significance.

div.head: RELEASE OF THE INIPRINONED MEMBERS.
div.p: THE RELEASE OF THE INIPRINONED MEMBERS.

The Press Association's Dublin correspondent telegraphed on Thursday morning :—Throughout the country generally the release of the suspects was enthusiastically celebrated by illuminations, processions, and bonfires—north and south, east and west. It may be safely said that Mr. Parnell is more popular throughout Ireland than ha has yet been. The following telegram from Mr. O'Donnell to one of his con- stituents, sent off immediately after Mr. Gladstone's state- ment in the House of Commons on Tuesday afternoon, is made public:—"From F. H. O'Donnell, House of Com- mons, to Mr. Maurice Flynn, ex-suspect, Dungarvan, county Waterford. Complete ,surrender of Government. Parnell, Dillon, and O'Kelly released. Forster resigned. Remedial legislation promised. Davitt not yet liberated, but hoped for soon." It is generally believed here that the change of front on the part of the Government will materially con- tribute to enlarge Mr. Parnell's parliamentary following at the next general election, that is if he should succeed in re- taining all the advantages now in his favour. •

div.head: ARRIVAL IN LONDON.
div.p: ARRIVAL IN LONDON.

Messrs. Parnell, Dillon, and O'Kelly, arrived at Easton Station on Thursday morning from Dublin. They tr avelled by the train from Holyhead which meets the north mail boat, and it was not until nine o'clock that they reached Lon- don. Their arrival being unexpected, only few persons were in waiting at the station. Mr. Parnell looked much better than he did when he arrived in London recently on his way to Paris on parole. Since then he has shaved, and he seems but little altered in appearance from his imprisonment. Mr. O'Kelly is stouter than when ho was last in London, but does not appear to bo in anything like as good health as formerly. With Mr. Dillon the case is entirely different from that of his colleagues. He is evidently in a very feeble condition, and is even thinner and looks more like an invalid than ever. Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Kelly expressed themselves to a repre- sentative of the Central News as both gratified and surprised at the turn of events. Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Kelly entered a cab together and drove to the Westminster Palace Hotel, where they intended to reside. Mr. Parnell drove to his private apartments.

div.head: INTERVIEW WITH MR. PARNELL.
div.p: INTERVIEW WITH MR. PARNELL.

Mr. Parnell in an interview on Thursday with a special representacive of the Central News corn municated the fol- lowing particulars respecting the release and the course the Irish party will probably adopt. Mr. Parnell said: The news of the change in the Government's Irish policy was a sur- prise to us. The first intimation I had of anything unusual in the political situation, was a telegram on Tuesday after- noon, which I received in Kilmainham Gaol, stating that Mr. Forster had resigned. We could scarcely credit it at first. Later on in the day we had further confirmation of the news, and at 8-30 that evening the governor of the gaol an- nounced that I was discharged, and that my colleagues Messrs. Dillon and O'Kelly had also been set free. The governor further added that so far as he had ascertained from opening his letters, four or five other suspects had been ordered to be released. The news respecting the latter had come by post, but the order for our liberation came by special messenger from the castle. The governor added that, judging from the passing of the communication he had received from the castle, it was desired that we should leave the prison at once, and then the governor pointed out that the word " immediately " WAS emphasised. Mr. Dillon, how- ever, not feeling well, was anxious to stop until morning but after some conversation we agreed to drive to Kingstown. This we did and put up at the hotel there as we failed to catch , the '(roods train for Avondale. On Wednesday we went bade to Dublin and had interviews with our friends and subse- quently with several members of the Executive of the Ladies' Land League. As to what the Irish parliamentary will do it is difficult to say until after the Government's new line of policy for Ireland has been disclosed. At present everything is so much a matter of speculation that it nil! be better to wait developments. It is necessary before we decide to wait and see what the Government are going to do with the land question. That is the pressing issue just now. We are disposed to hear what they have to say upon that and other matters. With regard to Michael Davitt, his release is of the most vital importance in order to secure the tranquility of the country. Much, of course, will depend on who the new Irish Secretary is to be, for none but a thoroughly capable man will suit. No one of our party could, of course, take the office, even if it was offered him, for it is impossible that the Government would concede terms which would be asked before one of our party would ally himself with the administration. I have to thank scores of friends for telegrams and messages of congratulation on my release. Among those messages I received the following from the Archbishop of Cashel, at Thutles :—" Archbishop of Cashel heartily congratulates Mr. Parnell, Mr. Dillon, and Mr. , O'Kelly on their release. He congratulates the country, ' through them, on the general situation, though the triumph cannot be considered complete until Michael Davitt is free, and far from it if Shaw be appointed Chief Secretary." Mr. Parnell sorted out this message from a large roll of similar telegrams.

MONEY ON EASY TERMS.—NO FEES. NO SURE- TIES REQUIRED.—Having a large and bona fide capital placed at my command, I am prepared to ADVANCE same in sums from £lO to £5,000 to all respectable persons (male or female). Farmers, Dairymen, Lodging-home Keepers, Cab Proprietors, Tradesmen, and others who may be in want of cash accommodation, on their own security and NOTE OF HAND ALONE; also on Deeds, Dock Bonds, Ac., from 5 per cent. interest. No sureties or bondsmen are required, and the repayment can be arranged so as to suit the convenience of the borrower. All communications received in the strictest confi- dence. Applications can be made either personally or by letter stating amount required ; or, if the applicant desire it, a gentle- man will be sent direct from the office to arrange terms.
