div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 6, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 6, 1882.

to consider the matter; and it was resolved that a request for a special election be forwarded to the Local Government Board. Mr. Hazlehurst attended, and wisely suggested that it would be well if some means could be provided of pre- venting the recurrence of such an unfortunate state of things. It was decided that in future the overseers should be requested to include the nomiration of guardians in the business to be dealt with at the annual township meeting, which seems a prudent course, to which none can fairly object, as if any one is dissatisfied with the names of the gentlemen adopted at such gathering, his right to nominate others will not be affected. A rather amusing incident occurred at the meeting of the Runcorn School Board on Wednesday. The candidates for the position of schoolmistress at Mill Brow appeared before the Board in order to be examined as to their qualifications. Amongst them was Miss Wilton, of Greenway-road, who was ultimately unanimously selected for the post. The facts were elicited that Miss Wilton formerly occupied a position as teacher under the Widnes School Board, and the percentage of "passes" in the case of her children had dur- ing several years been abnormally-high, but shortly before she left they fell off to a comparatively low figure. She was asked by Mr. John Simpson, the vice-chairman, who pre- sided in the absence of the Rev. Canon Barclay, if she could give any explanation of this matter. The lady replied that she was not able to account for it in any satisfactory manner, but she was inclined to think that it arose from the fact that during the year in question the gentleman who occupied the position of Her Majesty's Inspector had not previously examined the scholars, and "she thought they were not able to catch his patrician tone." Mr. Simpson, unfortunately, suffers from deafness, and he asked Mr. Thomas Norman, who had during the previous part of the proceedings been acting as "interpreter," what was the lady's answer. Mr. Norman, after a moment's hesitation, said, "She says that the Inspector talked too fast!" FLACCUS.

PRESBYTERIANISM AT RIINCORN.—On Sunday the Revs. F. B. Caldwell, 8.A., oi Liverpool, and J. T. Maxwell, of Over, 'preached at St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, on behalf of the trust funds. The oollections realised upwards of £9.

- - --- RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.—At this court, on Tues- day, before the juJge, Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, and the registrar, Mr. E. J. Nicholson, there were heard 88 plaints, one adjourned plaint, and 25 judgment summonses. The sitting only occupied about one hour, "ZEAL WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE IS NOT GOOD."—At the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, on Monday, a note was passed round the table which caused no little perplexity and fun. It read as follows :—" Gentlemen,— If you alow the back doar open to beerhouse at the top of the fair ground this whison i shall right Magor Oried !" Who, after the receipt of this by the Commissioners, will say that the Free Library has been started one day too soon? We wonder how the gallant Major will feel when he reads in The Examiner this attempt to spell his name. And vet itlis about forty years since Lord Brougham said the school- master was abroad. _ _

FOUND DROWNED AT RUNCORN.—On Thursday an inquest was held at the Cemetery offices, Runcorn, by Mr. Wersley, on the body of Joseph Benny, of Fowey, Cornwall, seaman on board the schooner Restless, who was drowned at Runcorn, on the 18th ult.—Mr. E. Marwood represented the owners and captain of the vessel. From the evidence of E. Osborne,seaman on' board the schooner Fame, and Mr. E. Marwood, it appeared that the Restless was lying in the Alfred dock on the night in question, and it was supposed that he rose in the dark and fell overboard. The body was not recovered sooner owing to the depth of the mud in which it lay. The jury returned an open ver- dict; and the jurymen each gave his fee to the mother of the deceased, who is a poor widow. RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY CODLETETEE. On Thursday, a meeting of this committee was held in the Com- missioners' Board-room, and there were present Dr. Mc Dougall (vice-chairman), who presided, Messrs. Simpson, Steele, Handley, Riley, Hazlehurst, Rhodes, and Brookes (secretary). The draft rules and regulations presented by the sub-committee were considered and revised up to clause 5. The consideration of the remaining clauses were left over to the next meeting. The estimates committee pre- sented their estimate of the expenditure required during the current year (exclusive of any addition of books to the library) amounting to .£73 10s. The estimates were ap- prove-el and adopted on the motion of Dr. Steele, seconded by Mr. Hazlehurst.—Mr. Hazlehurst proposed and Mr. Simpson seconded the following resolution, which was car- ried unanimously, "That the committee desire to express their obligation to the commissioners for permission to use the Board-room on two evenings in the week, and inform them that they have chosen Tuesday and Saturday evenings from 7to 10 o'clock. They also request that the commis- missioners will permit the room to be opened on Saturday afternoon at 2 instead of 7 o'clock." A resolution that the monthly meetings of the committee be held on the third Thursday in the month concluded the business. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDILNEL—This Board held their usual fortnightly meeting on Tuesday afternoon, at the Board-room, Dutton Workhouse. Mr. Robert Ashton was voted to the chair, and there were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood,lMessrs. Darbyshirr, Lowe, Midwood, Percival, Smith, Weir, Knowles, Highfield, Norman, Challorer, Wallington, Rigby, Jackson, Hazle- burst, and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—Mr. Rigby said he saw an account had been handed him by the clerk for £2O, being his expenses as returning officer. He wished to know how it was that the authority was to be put to such an expense, seeing there had been no election.—The Chair- man believed it was the sum regularly allowed.—The Clerk said that in case of a contest the expense was charged upon the townships concerned.— Mr. Rigby asked what work had been done for the .£2O now charged.—The Clerk: There is a lot of work in connection with the matter.—ln reply to another question from Mr. Rigby, the Clerk said that in the case of an election, in addition to the ordinary allowance of £2O, a charge of one halfpenny was made upon every as- sessment. There were 37 townships.—Mr. Hazle- hurst did not think the sum allowed by law in case of an election at all excessive.— The annual report of the Medical Officer, which had been prepared by Mr. J. G. Bride, stated that in the three regis- tration sub-districts of Runcorn, Frodsham, and Budworth during 1881, there had been 301 deaths, as against 325 in 1880. This number represented the very low rater of 15.6 per 1,000 of the population, and 71 of the number, or 3.6 per 1,000, were of children under one year of age, and 102, or 5.3 per 1,000 of persons aged 60 years and upwards. There had been recorded during the year 606 births, as against 613 in 1880. This was equal to an annual rate of 320 per 1,000, showing a decrease of 7. Mr. Bride also showed what action had been taken during the twelve months for pre- venting the spread of disease, and the supervision exercised by him, or on his advice, over places and houses which the Sanitary Authority had power to regulate, together with the action, if any, taken in regard to offensive trades, and a clas- sified list of diseases, ages, and localities. The Board de- cided that the statement required by the Local Government Board, as to the total liabilities connected with the work- house hospital, had been prepared by the Hospital and Building Committee.—Mr. Farrington (inspector) having reported to the authority that repeated complaints had been made about the nuisance arising from the drainage outfall connected with the workhouse, the matter was referred to the Hospital Building Committee.—This concluded the proceedings.

WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.—The members of the Widnes Football Club held their annual dinner at the Central Hotel, on Saturday evening. There was a :large company present. Mr. David Faster pr esided. In proposing the toast, "The Widnes Football Club," Mr. Houseman said he gathered from the report that during the season the club had scored 17 goals, 37 tries, and 74 minor points, as against 3 goals, 7 tries, and 29 minor points for their opponents. He noticed with pleasure that the charity match, in aid of the hospital, had cleared over £l2. When he was speaking to the Widnes football team, he believed he was speaking to one of the best in Lancashire—not the very best, but he believed it could well hold its own; and he wished it every success. He suggested the advisability of organising some charity matches, as had been done in Yorkshire with such good results; and observed that Widnes might propose a challenge cup for the county. In a game like football, accidents, he said, would happen; and he advised the club to join an accident insurance company. The cost would, perhaps, be £4O a year, but the advantages in any accident or fatality would be great. He coupled with the toast the name of the captain, Mr. Ireland.—ln responding, Mr. Ire- land announced that the club was offering £5 to be competed for in sports by the Athletic Club.—Mr. E. M. Davies pro- posed, in a few appropriate remarks, the toast of " The President and Vice-Presidents of the Club."—Mr. David Forster, in replying, expressed his regret that Mr. H. W. Deacon, their president, was not present; and spoke of the interest which he took in their club, to which he wished present success and future prosperity.—Mr. Mcllwaine, one of the vice-prtsidents, also responded. He thought great credit was due to their retiring trreasurer, Mr. E. M. Davies, for the manner in which he had manipulated their finances. As Englishmen, they liked to see their club just as they liked to see a private individual, with a balance at the bankers' and he considered their best thanks were due to Mr. Davies for bringing this about. He thought the sug- gestion as to joining an accident assurance company a valuable one, and commended it to the consideration of the club. He thought less than £4O a year would be required.— Mr. Kendrick proposed "The health of the honorary mem- bers," which was acknowledged by Mr. Simcock.—" The Widnes Athletic Club" was then given by Mr. J. Burgess, who considered the amalgamation scheme, whereby it was proposed to have one ground in common for the Cricket Club, the Football Club, and the Athletic Club," would prove a great saving of expense to all if carried out, and he hoped it would be successfully accomplished.—Mr. Mcllwaine responded, and deplored that in consequence of several unsuccessful engagements, the Athletic Club had only at present some £5O in hand instead of the usual £2OO, and hcped they would soon regain their old balance. The amalgamation scheme would have, in his opinion, a beneficial influence.—The toast, "The health of the officers of the club," was proposed by Mr. G. Brown, and responded to by Mr. Ireland, Mr. C. M. Davies, and Mr. Burgess. Other toasts followed, and the meeting terminated.

RUNCORN BRUNSWIORMUTUAL lI(MOVEMENT SOCIETY. —Mr. Timothy Simister, the president, occupied the chair at the weekly meeting of this society on Wednesday even- ing, and Mr. John Simpson, of Frodsham, delivered his lecture on the past compared with the present, to a deeply interested audiene. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Simpson, on the motion of Mr. Kniveton, seconded by Mr. Fred, Norman. RuNcoits. ScnooL BoAup.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, at the offices, Bridge-water-street. Mr. John Simpson, vice-chairmah, presided in the absence of the Rev. Canon Barclay, (who is in the south of England), and there were also present the Rev. Father Fennelly, and Messrs. Lea, Briscoe, Norman, Rigby (clerk.) The only business of public interest was the appointment of a school- mistress for Mill Brow School. There were several ap- plicants, but only three attended for the purpose of seeing the Board. Their names were as follows:—Miss Houghton of Walton, Liverpool; Miss A. B. Tyre, Trinity School ; and Miss M. E. Wilton, of Greenway-road, formerly teacher under the Widnes School Board. The three can- didates having been carefully examined, Mr. Norman pro- posed that Miss Wilton be appointed. He referred to the fact that she had been very successful in securing a yery large percentage of passes at the Widnes school, with the exception of one particular year, and reminded the Board that herself and father were bothßuncornians.—Mr. Briscoe said that after taking all things into consideration, he had determined to second the motion.—The Chairman said that, supposing all other things were equal, he thought it would be de,sireable to appoint Miss Wilton.—Mr. Lea was strongly in favour of Miss Tyre being elected, but he bad no personal objectons to Miss Wilton. Miss Tyre, was "as sharp as a needle." and it would do any of them good to see the way in which she taught a class.—The Chairman said there was certainly no doubt that Miss Tyre would never be fast for something to say; aid he had great confidence in her. Still they must remember that Miss Wilton was disengaged, and the others were in situations.—The resolution in favour of Miss Wilton being appointed was carried unanimously. The salary is £6O yearly, with.one third of the Government grant.

VISIT OF LIVERPOOL STUDENTS TO WIDNES.—On Saturday afternoon, the students attending the course on the "Alkali manufactuTe " at the College of Chemistry, Duke- street, Liverpool, held in connection with the City and Guilds of London Institute, and conducted by Mr. Granville H. Sharpe, paid a visit to the extensive chemical works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., at Widnes, and, notwith- standing the unpropitious weather, there was a very fair attendance. They were met at the works by Dr. Hurter, who first drew attention to the pyrites burners, and then proceeded to explain the working of the sulphuric acid chambers. The Glover and Gay-Lussac towers were then ascended, and their respective functions fully pointed out. The next move that was made was in connection with the soda department, the structural arrangements of the saltcake pots and roasters claiming attention first. Following up the Leblanc soda process, the revolving black ash furnaces were inspected, two of which were on the point of discharging their glowing contents. Whilst witnessing the withdrawal of the charges, the " candles" being seen to perfection, all present were impressed with the many advantages of the modern mechanical black ash furnace over the now almost defunct hand-worked one. After visiting the lixiviating tanks, the process was minutely followed out to the produc- tion of soda ash, caustic soda, bicarbonate of soda, and washing soda, out of which latter some magnificent crystal- lographic specimens were remarked. The party next pro- ceeded to the bleaching powder section of the works, the chlorine stills, chambers, and plant belonging to the Weldon recovery process being in turn carefully studied. Particular attention was paid to, and great interest manifested in, Deacon's chlorine process, the working of which was criti- cally examined. By the courtesy of Dr. Hurter, the students collected several samples of the raw and manufactured products to be found in the works, and having thanked him for his kindness returned to Liverpool during the evening.

SERXONS AT SUTTON AND TREETOP. - The annual charity sermons will be preached at St. Ann's Retreat, Sutton, on Sunday, by the Rev. Father Dubberley, SI., and the May sermons will also be preached, on Sunday, at the Church of our Lady Portico, by the Rev. Jas. Conway, S.J.

In its criticism of the exhibition of the Royal Society of Painters in Water Colours, the Illustrated London News has the following on Mr. E. F. Brewtnall's painting, "The visit to the witch," (158) :—" Rather stagey, perhaps, but not a little artistic in colour."

LANCASHIRE BANKRUPTS. - (From Tuesday night's Gazette):—Bankrupts: H. Worsley, Golborne, near Wigan, surgeon ; and C. Sayer, Harrington-street, Liverpool, quarry proprietor and forwarding agent.—Liquidations by Arrangement: J. E. Lee, St. Mary's Gate, Manchester, and Boond-street, Greengate, Salford, ironworker; R. Bennett and J. Bennett, Great Ducie-street, Strangeways, Manchester, watchmakers; J. F. Higham, Stretford Road, Hulme, musical instrument dealer; H. Wickham, Brunswick Road, Liverpool, linen draper ; C. Ayre, Fairfield, Liverpool, plumber and painter; and T. Thompson, Morecambe, boot and shoe maker.

TIM HIGH SUBMIT OF LANCASHIRE.—On Wednes- day evening, the High Sheriff (Colonel M'Corquodale), entertained at dinner, at the North-western Hotel, the mem- bers of the grand jury at the Liverpool Assizes and other guests, the party numbering about GO. The High Sheriff was supported on the right by his Worship the Mayor (Mr J. Hughes) and on the lefp by Colonel A. H. Brown, M.P., foreman of the grand jury. The usual toasts were proposed and duly bonoured. The musical selections were given by the Childwall Glee Union.

EMMANUEL REFORMED CUURCII.—The largest congre- g aim that has ever attended the services of this church, which are conducted in the Warrington Public Hall, as- sembled on Sunday evening last, when the building was filled in all parts except the centre gallery. The reason for the extraordinary attendance is that the persons who put in an appearance at the service were thus enabled to obtain seats and retain them for the service of the Blue Ribbon Army. which commenced at the conclusion of that of Em- manuel Church. The Rev. Mr. Palmer, of Tunbridge Wells, officiated, and preached a suitable sermon from Mat- thew x. 38 v. Throughout the service the large congrega- tion conducted themselves in a becoming manner, and the offertory amounted to about £4 10s.

WAUNINGTON COUNTY COURT.—Mr. W. Wynne Ffonlkes, judge, held a sitting of this court on Thursday, but the cases heard were void of public interest. A rather extraordinary case was, however, heard before the Registrar (Mr. E. J. Nicholson). It appeared that the defendant had been previously sued for 4s. 9d., and towards that sum he had paid 3s. The plaintiff now asked for an order for the balance, is. 9d., but the Registrar pointed out that if he did so there would be 3s. costs added to the amount, and he ap- pealed to the plaintiff whether she had better not trust to the defendant paying the amount. Did plaintiff not think if she withdrew the case defendant would pay her? Plain- tiff said she did not, and, as she was inexorable, the Regis- trar made the order, and remarked that it seemed a very dreadful thing a man should have to pay 3s. or 4s. costs for is. 9d.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST MISSION, LATCHFORD. —On Wednesday evening a service of song entitled "The basket of flowers, or the triumph of truth over falsehood," was given in the Mission-room, Knutsford-road, Latchford, by the choir of the Runcorn Primitive Methodist Chapel. The author of the music, Mr. Elijah Billingsley, of Runcorn, conducted the choir, which was assisted by several members of the local choir. There was a large audience, and the music was apparently much enjoyed. The connective read- ings were given by Mr. Robert Naylor. Alderman Davies, who occupied the chair, expressed his sympathy with the object of the gathering, and said he was pleased that the mission was doing such a much needed work—viz., the enlightenment of the ignorance of the masses, who seemed to go through this life without any regard to the life that was to come, and, as he took it, to try and get them to attend that or another place of worship. Although he did not attend the mission, he was greatly pleased at its success. The usual votes of thanks concluded the entertainment.

LOCAL ARTISTS AT THE ROYAL ACIDEXY.—III the sacond gallery, says the Manchester Guardian, in a notice of the exhibition of the Royal Academy, bangs a small study of Venetian life (182) that will be sure to attract attention from the fact that it is painted by an artist whose recent elevation to the dignity of associateship has caused considerable discussion in artistic circles. By accident, or perhaps designedly, the Hanging Committee have placed close beside it a smaller but more perfect work by Van Haanen, from whose example Mr. Woods has largely Profited. "Bargaining for an Old Master" (182) proves that the young English painter has not yet acquired the art of composing a picture. The canvas is crowded with detail, much of which is very skilfully rendered, but there is a painful absence of the qualities of selection and con- centration needed to give effect to a subject of this kind. Mr. Woods shows mere mastery in imitating the tone and texture of the things of still life than in reproducing the subtler realities of human character, and the consequence is that the principal group in his picture is somewhat over- weighted by its accessories.—The Venice of to-day, the Standard remarks, in all that it offers of comedy and character is Mr. Wpods' ground, as well as Mr. Van Haa- nen's and he treats it the most piquantly in "Bargaining for an Old Master" (No. 182). The "old master "—now, alas, not a little discredited—lies out upon the pavement for closest and most critical inspection—its vis-a-vis a col- lection of pots and pans, marvellously well painted—the local colour of the place caught not less well than in last year's "Gondolier's Courtship." The same journal also states that such work as "Nina," Mr. Fildes (No. 268), would lose infinitely in engraving. It is not addressed to the engraver at all. It is a colourist's work—a rich and complete study of one Venetian type. Venice, which in English art alone, from Turner to James Holland, has given ' a thousand subjects to the painter of architecture and to the painter of the sea and sky, has come now to be a chosen resort of painters of the figure and of human story—of painters who mind paint modern life, but who demand a modern life that shall be rich, vivid, unfamiliar. picturesque.

SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVER- sARy.—On Sunday last the Rev. F. Luke Wiseman, of Didsbury College, preached two sermons to large congrega- tions. The collections amounting to £8 Is. Bd.

WARRINGTON BICYCLE CLI373.—TIIe opening run of the above club took place, on Tuesday evening last, to Hollins Green. The members present were :—T. Craddock (sub captain), Edward Caldwell, W. Skelton, J. Tinsley, T. Atherton, J. Unswortb, Calvert, N. B. Powlson, and R. lent.

BILLIARD MATCH: WARRINGTON v. BEDFORD LEIGH.— This match was played on Saturday last at Bedford Leigh, and reeulted in a victory for the home team by 118 points. The previous match was played some few weeks since at the Conservative Club, Warrington, when the Warringtonians were the victors by 112 points. In the aggregate the Bed- ford Leigh team are, therefore, the winners by six points. After the match the teams adjourned to a commodious room at the club, where an "excellent spread" was provided by the victors, after which speeches, songs, and toasts were the order of the evening, and an enjoyable time was spent.

WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.—At the meeting of this committee, as recently constituted, held yesterday, there were present Messrs. Rylands, Darbyshire, Cartwright, Cooper, Garnett, Blackhurst, Appleton, Balharry, Swinton, Gibson Kilsball, Houghton, Greening, Sutton (clerk), and Owen (valuer). On the proposition of Mr. Blaekhurst, Mr. Rylands was re-elected chairman for the ensuing year, and on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Darby- shire, Colonel McCorquodale was re-appoinied vice-chairman. After some discussion it was decided that 11-45 a.m. be the time of meeting.

PRESENTATION.—Mrs. Tonge, of Sankey Bridges, on Wednesday received a very handsome present at the hands of the teachers of the Wesleyan Sunday School there, on the occasion of her recent marriage. She had been a teacher of the second Bible class from the commencement of the school, about five years ago. On Wednesday night the teachers invited her and Mr. Tonge to a meeting at the Chapel, presided over by the superintendent of the Sunday School (Mr. Summersgill). The presentations consisted of a handsome writing desk" in walnut, and " gipsy table." After devotional exercises, Mr. Brough sang an appropriate solo, "Blest be the tie that binds," accompanied by Mr. Tomkinson on the harmonium. The chairman then read the 133rd Psalm,' and the narrative given in the second chapter of St. John's Gospel of the marriage in Cana of Galilee, giving some suitable and practical comments. A hymn was then sung, "Gathering one by one," after which Mr. J. Lewis George, assistant superintendent, made the pre- sentation, followed by a few well chosen remarks to the bride. The bridegrooin responded on behalf of his bride. Mr. Savage, one of the teachers, said a few words which concluded this interesting meeting. DEATH OF A WARRINGTON MAN IN RAINHILL ASYLUM. —An inquest was held at the County Lunatic Asylum, Rainhill, by Mr. T. W. Barker, deputy county coroner, on Friday afternoon week, touching the death of John Mannion, aged 44 years. Deceased was formerly a baker by trade, and lived in Elizabeth-street, Warrington. He was admitted to the institution on the 3rd of March, being imbecile and paralytic. On Wednesday night he was partaking of boiled bread and milk for supper, when a portion of the food got into his windpipe. In his weakly condition he had not power to throw it off, and artificial respiration was tried by the assistant medical attendant, but deceased expired shortly afterwards. The jury returned a verdict that death was the result of suffocation by choking.

Mr. HENRY WOODS, A.R.A.—Among the portraits of celebrities in the last number of The Graphic is one of our townsman, Mr. H. Woods, and under the heading of" Our illustrations" are the following remarks :—Mr. Henry Woods, the new associate of the Royal Academy, was born at Warrington, in 1846, and educated at the Grammar School there. He first studied art in the Warrington School of Art, nailer its present master, Mr. J.Christmas Thompson, and afterwards at South Kensington, and was engaged for some time upon illustrations for books and periodicals, having been a member of the artistic staff of The Graphic from its commencement. He first exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1869. His first picture of any importance was exhibited in 1873," Going home," a Thames subject. Since then he has exhibited "Haymakers," "A nosegay," " Con- valescents at Highgate,"" A Venetian ferry,"" Street trading in Venice," "The ducal courtyard," "The gondolier's court- ship," and "The foot of the Rialto." The current number of the Illustrated London News also contains a portrait of Mr. Woods, and in an article on "New associates at the Royal Academy" has the following :—Mr. Henry Woods, A.R.A., painter of figure in combination with landscape and architecture, was born in 1846 at Warrington, and was educated at the Grammar School there. He also commenced his art studies at the school of art of his native town, under Mr. J. Christmas Thompson—who is still master of the 'school. In 1864 young Woods came to London, and studied at South Kensington for some years. Like several other painters who have won distinction, he has drawn largely for the wood enoraver in illustration of books and periodicals. He first exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1869, but his more important works date from 1873. Among the earlier of these are "Going home," " Haymakers," "Convalescents at Highgate," "Good-bye," and "A good bargain." For the last few years he has painted at Vienna, and there he has worked, we believe, occasionally with his brother-in- law, Mr. Fildes, A.R.A., and the Dutch painter Van Haanen, whose " Pearl stringer" obtained a deserved success at our Royal Academy two years ago. We were among the first to note the merit of Mr. Wood's Venetian pictures, among which are "A Venetian ferry," " Sunshine," " Street trading in Venice," The ducal courtyard," "The foot of the Rialto," and "The gondolier's courtship.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—At the fortnightly meeting on Wednesday, Mr. Blackhurst presiding, there were present the Rev. John Yonge, Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Cartwright, Woolfall, Burn, Marsh, Brown, Walling- ton, Derbyshire, Longshaw, Houghton, Greenall, Taylor, Bonnell, Cooper, Balharry, Caldwell, Hall, Kilshall, Gibson, Owen, Appleton, and J. C. Sutton (clerk.)—Mr. Brown moved that the school fees as recommended by the com- mittee in 50 cases be allowed. Mr. Wool fall seconded.— Major Cartwright asked a question on a subject which cropped up on Monday, thraugh Mr. Riley summoning a number of people who did not send their children to school regularly. The case was an extraordinary one. It was that of Michael Birmingham, who had school fees from the School Committee for one or two children who never at- tended school, and yet the committee according to the statement which was made, continued to pay Oa fees. He wished to know whether the C )mmittee granted fees knowing that the children did not attend school. —Mr. Derbyshire said the committee had no option whatever in granting fees if the people could show that their condition was such that they could not pay the fees themselves. They had notbing to do with the atten- dance of the children at school; there was a school attendance officer to look after them. (Hear, hear.) When school attendance cases came before the magistrates he thought they ought to deal more severely with those per- sons who had school fees allowed than with those persons who paid the fees themselves.—Major Cartwright had no doubt the magistrates did their duty. —The Chairman thought it a proper case to bring before the Board so that enquiry might be made, which he had no doubt would check that sort of thing.—lt was reported that there were 512 inmates as against 472 in the corresponding week of last year, showing an increase of 40.—The minutes of the School Building Committee stated that Mr. Darbyshire had been appointed chairman for the ensuing year, and that it was resolved that Messrs. Derbyshire and Hough- ton be appointed Garden and Grounds Committee. The architects submitted tracing of school site showing proposed straigtening of the west boundary fence, and purchase Of a triangular plot of front land as per arrangement with the representatives of the late Mrs. Martinscroft, such purchase being subject to the approval of the Local Government Board. The minutes were confirmed.—The Clerk read a certificate stating that £3OO was due to Mr. Napier' the builder of the new schools at Padgate, and Major Cartwright asked when Mr. Napier was going to clear out.—Mr. Pierpoint (architect): In three or four weeks if he puts extra men on the ground. I, as architect am more anxious than the Committee to get rid of him.—Major Cartwright: I have no doubt that the Board is anxious to get quit of the pair of you. (Laughter.)—The Chairman: We have to pay the Clerk of Works.—Major Cartwright: What for—smok- ing his pipe ?—Mr. Brown: I think the penalty ought to be enforced.—Mr Cooper: If you remember he took this coa- tract at a price greatly below that of the Warrington buil- ders; but it seems it is costing after all as much as if we had let it to the Warrington builders. There is no doubt about it.—Mr. Derbyshire, as chairman of the Committee, remarked that if the Board thought it would be right to terminate the agreement with the Clerk of Works, the Committee would agree to it.—lt was decided to terminate the agreement with Mr. Siddeley at the end of the month,—Mr. Pierpoint asked upon what grounds the Board wanted to get rid of the architect. Gentlemen should be a little more guarded in their expressions.—Major Cartwright said the remark was not a personal one, but his opinion was that they had been too long on the job. (Hear, hear.)—The School Committee's minutes stated that the Rev. J. Yonge had been appointed chairman, and that the doctor reporka the health of the children was good,—indeed the condition of the children all through the ,time of the epidemic had been excellent. The schools were now full, and no more children could be admitted until vacancies occurred.— Major Cartwright gave notice of his intention to move that steps be taken to memorialise the Local Government Board in favour of triennial elections.—This was all the business. div.head: RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMIS- SIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Monday. There were present Messrs. Norman, McDougall, Williams, Hazlehurst, Fisher, J. J. Speakman, P. Speakman, Timmis, Lake, Shaw, Handley, Briscoe, Whittaker, Rhodes, Meadowcroft, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secretary), Barker (surveyor), and Mouritz (medical officer). Mr. Norman was voted to the chair in the absence of Dr. Steele, at Buxton.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.-EXTINCTION OF TIIE SMALL..
PDX EPIDEMIC.

The report of the Medical Officer stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn for the month of April was 26; and there had also been one death in Halton-in-Runcorn, and two inquests, making the total of deaths 29. Of these five were due to zymotic diseases, one measles, scarlatina 2, typhoid fever 1, diseases of the respiratory system 5, of the circulatory system 4, of the nervous system 6, and of the digestive organs 7. Five deaths had occurred under one year, ten under four; and of the remainder, ten averaged 64 years each. The mortality was 21 per thousand per annum.

The CHAIRMAN said it must be very satisfactory to the members to know that all the smallpox cases had been stamped out. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN said he thought this happy result had been brought about by the prompt action of Mr. Handley, chairman of the Hospital Committee. He had pleasure in moving a vote of thanks to that gentleman. Mr. BRISCOE seconded the resolution, which was passed unanimously.

Mr. HANDLEY, in reply, observed that he had only done what was his duty in the matter. It was, however, very satisfactory to know that they had been successful in arrest- ing and stamping out the smallpox epidemic.
EIGHVirAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.-THE RAILWAY BRIDGE SLOPE.

The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee were passed on the motion of Mr. BRISCOE, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMS. It appeared from them that Messrs. Nor- mal, Fisher, and Briscoe had been appointed to inspect the footway in Canal-street, in order to consider the best means of improving it. A correspondence had taken place between the solicitor to the Loudon and North-Western Railway Company and the Law Clerk, as to proceeding with the rail- way bridge slope, pending the preparation of the draft con- veyance. Mr. Linaker had written saying that the Com- missioners would offer no objection to the company pro- ceeding with the work. A resolution had been passed adjourning the consideration of a plan of proposed stables at the top of Nelson-street for Messrs. Hazlehurst and Sons, and instructing (be Law Cleik to write Major Orred's agent with reference to the alteration of windows looking on the fair ground. It was recommended that notices be served on the executors of Mr. W. Rigby and Mr. P. Speakman to provide a proper supply of water to property in Bridge- water-street, Pool-lane, and Grindrod-square. It was recom- mended that Messrs. Brundrit and Co.'s tender to supply macadam at Stone Croft at 108 3d per ton in respect of Ash- ridge-street, and Messrs. Kershaw, Lupton and Co.'s tender to supply macadam on their wharf, near the Bridgewater offices, at Os per ton, in respect of Percival-lane be accepted, subject to the price named including the wharf- age charges. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN moved, and Mr. WHITTAKER seconded, a proposal in favour of the London and North-Western Railway Company being asked to submit a plan of the work they intended to carry out at the bridge slope; but Mr. McDoucata.,.the chairman, and Mr. SHAW made some re- marks to the effect that such a proposal would be likely to cause further delay. The resolution was then withdrawn.

div.head: HOSPITAL
div.p: THE HOSPITAL

The minutes of the Hospital Committee recommended that the terrhs offered by the Runcorn Board of Guardians for infectious c,tses coining from the Workhouse be accepted. The committee had received a letter from the Local Govern- ment Board to the Effect that they were not prepared to give their sanction under sec. 133 of the Public Health Act, 1875, to the Commissioners providing a supply of medicine, drc., to the poorer inhabitants, but stating that the Runcorn Board had power under section 131 to provide medicine and medical assistance for persons in hospital, without the sanction of the Local Government Board being required. It was recommended that the expenses in connection with the recent case of smallpox treated in the hospital, which amounted to £l3 13s. 5d., be paid, under the powers con- ferred by section 131 of the Public Health Act. Recom- mended that the tenders for the erection of the hospital premises should "exclude" one ward and the kitchen and scullery of the administrative department. Mr. HANDLEY moved the adoption of the minutes, and said that the result of the treatment of the recent case ef smallpox showed the great value of isolation. In fact, all the-cases which had occurred had sprung, more or less, from one source. The minutes would have shown the members that the committee were in favour of only such part of the hospital plans being proceeded with at present as were con- sidered necessary; and that the rest be carried out as it was found requisite. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion, which was agreed to.

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES.
div.p: GENERAL PURPOSES.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Mr, J. J. SPEAKMAN moved the passing of the Finance Committee's minutes, which showed the treasurer's balance on the 25th ult. to be as follows :—General fund, £290 19s. Bd.; district fund, £lO 2s. 10d.; sinking fund, £O5O 2s. ; loan (unspent), £2,264 103. 3d. Mr. BRISCOE seconded the resolution,which was agreed:to.
MR. MURPHY, THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY ADVOCATE, AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday and yesterday evening Mr. E. Murphy, who has become so well known in the district as one of the most successful advocates of the Blue Ribbon Army, paid a visit to Runcorn, and was accompanied by his brother, Mr. F. R. M. Murphy, and Mr. and Mrs. Clark Willson, the noted singers. At the commencement of the proceedings on Thurs- day evening there was a very poor attendance, but this was very considerably increased as the evening wore on. In the course of some introductory remarks Mr. E. MURPHY said that he regretted that a misunderstanding had occurred in regard to the price of admission. It was settled that there should be a few reserved seats, as at Warrington and other places, and the body of the hall should be open to the public; but their good friends did not understand that. He was very sorry, and quite willing to bear his part of the blame. :They could not expect a large audience when one shilling was charged for admisson—(hear, hear) —but they hoped that next day they would have an over- flow meeting. . _ . . .

During tire course of the evening the following duets were given by Mr. and Mrs. Clark Willson :—" David and Go- liath," "Are your windows open," "Sooner in the morning," "Glad tidings," "Bring me the bowl," " I've been re- deemed," "Ring those charming bells," "I shall be satisfied," "The ninety and nine," "Go down, Moses." Mrs. Willson sang two solos, "If Papa were only ready," and "In sight of the crystal sea." Mrs. Willson possesses a voice of distinguished by 'splendid compass and purity of tone; and she was enthusiastically rebeived. Mr. MURPHY, in commencing his address, said he bad come to Runcorn to introduce the gospel of temperance, this Blue Ribbon Army movement. While he was at Warrington, where they had enlisted something like 10,000 people in the Blue Ribbon Army, certain friends came to him from Runcorn, and at last he had consented to comply with their wishes. He was there that night to talk to them on the subject of reform. (Applause.) He believed in the first place that in this nineteenth century men were ruled more by intellect than brute force, and they could catch more flies with molasses than with vinegar. (Laughter and cheers.) If they wanted to close the public-houses they must close the demand for them, and they would see how quickly the publican would close his house and walk out. (Applause.) They had public-houses in Runcorn. Why? Because they had a certain number of people who would drink. If they got these men to sign the pledge the public-houses would soon close. (Applause.) Speaking of great reformers who had struggled against misdeeds at the first but had:triumphed in the end, be referred to William Tell, the hero of Switzerland. Then there was the great religious reformation. There was a time of religious darkness. But God moves in a mysterious way Ills wonders to perform; He plants His footsteps on the sea, And rides upon the storm. And in good time He raised up a mighty reformer. His influence spread over France, it crossed the English Chan- nel, and passed into this good old country. And now we all thanked God for Luther. There had been a great reforma- tion in his own land too. He referred to the great civil war, when North and South fought together. Every possible peaceful measure and measure of compromise was tried in vain, and finally a bitter war broke out; but they succeeded in shaking the shackles off more than 41 millions of God's downtrodden people—(applause)— and now, wherever the stars and stripes waved, they were known as the emblem of liberty. There was an analogy between these reformations and the reformation of temper- ance. In the beginuing they might be in a minority; but he asked—Were minorities always wrong? He believed that temperance principles were gaining ground every day. Just lately, Sir William Harcourt. the Home Secretary, had declared that he was a teetotaller. Earl Cairns wore the blue ribbon. Load Mount-Temple was on their side. He also alluded to the efforts of that intrepid reformer, Sir Wilfrid Lawson. (Applause.) This reform was necessary for phy- sical and intellectual liberty, for the man who was a slave to drink possessed neither. (Applause.) He condemned moderate drinking. People thought it right to drink a little, and said that moderation was the cure for intemper- ance. But moderate drinking was the cause of intemper- ance, and no man would expect to cure a thing by doing what was the cause of it. (Applause.) He called upon people of influence and position to join in the movement. Some might not care to don the blue ribbon, and hesitated to do se because thee said it was the sign of a reformed drunkard. It would just be as reasonable to say that a man born in a stable must nncessarily be a horse. (Laughter.) It made a great deal of difference whether a man was sober or not, and whether he thought more of his home than the public-house. He spoke of his own home which drink fora time darkened, but from which he was glad to say the curse was afterwards removed, and in conclusion urged them all to join in the good work. At the conclusion of Mr. Murphy's speech, there was a, rush to the table where the pledge books were; and we under- stand that the pledge was then and there taken by about 150 people.

div.head: NEGLIGENT MEMBERS.
div.p: NEGLIGENT MEMBERS.

Mr. LAKE said he wished that the members of the Bye Laws Revision Committee would attend the committee meet- ings a little better. Even since the number upon the com- mittee had been increased there had been meetings at which no business could be transacted, owing to the absence of a quorum.

-41.1POBTANT PROPOSAL AS TO THE BOARD'S PROPERTIES. The Properties Committee recommended "that the Sur- veyor be instructed to review bis valuation of Waterloo House, the Commissioners' present offices, the Market Cot- tages, and the Town's-yard, and that advertisements be in- serted in the following newspapers, viz., Runcorn Examiner, Runcorn Guardian, Liverpool Daily Post, and Manchester Guardian, inviting tenders for the several properties, the Commissioners not being bound to accept the highest tender."

Mr. LIKE, in moving the adoption of the report, said the committee thought it was highly desirable that the various premises belonging to the Board should be more cancen- trated—including the Free Library. Owing to the position of Waterloo House, it was not even the best building for the purpose. If the premises sold for a reasonable sum, they would probably bring £5,000; and it would be evident to any one that for such an amount they could easily put up buildings which would be much more ornamental, and answer the purposes required much better than even Waterloo House and the present offices would. The committee how- ever, did not recommend that any forced sale should take place.

Mr. Hazt,Enunsr seconded the motion on the ground that if the recommendation led to nothing else they would, at any rate, know the actual price which any one was wil- ling to give for the properties of the Board. It must be evident to anyone that if the Free Library were to have its hoiue in that building the days of the commissioners' resi- dence in it were numbered. It seemed quite ridiculous to him to suppose that having the library open only two evenings a week would justify the expenditure of £l6O a year--[Mr. SHAW : Hear, hear.l—or, indeed, any expendi- ture whatsoever.

Mr. HANDLEY wished to ask if the business which had been brought forward was considered extraordinary or not. If so, he should also like to know if the 43rd section of the Commiss;oners' Clauses Act had been complied with. The section read as follows:—" Where any business other than ordinary business is required, or intended to be transacted at any monthly meeting, the clerk shall give notice thereof to each of the commissioners, and no such extraordinary business, nor any new rules or regulations shall be adopted at the monthly meetings unless due notice thereof had been given at a previous meeting, and sent to each commis- sioner in the manner required for special meetings." Mr. LAKE: The Board appointed this committee for a certain purpose. We were asked to make a repott ; and we have made it. Ido not think the business is of such a nature as would make it come under the meaning of the word "extraordinary," as mentioned in the section. Mr. HANDLEY : it is certainly an extraordinary proposal. The CHAIRMAN said he should like to hear the opinion of Mr. Linaker upon the question. The Ls.w CLERK said he was of opinion that the business was of such a character as that contemplated by the section quoted by Mr. Handley. Some discussion of a conversational nature followed,after which Dr. MCDOUGALL said: Are we to abide by the La, Clerk's ruling. Ho rules that the section applies in this case; and, therefore, it seems to me that it is not competent for us to deal with the question. The Lem CLERK said, amidst cries of dissent from one or two of the members, that the committee had travelled "out of their functions."
At the end of the meeting Mr. LAKI gave the necessary notice in regard to bringing the matter forward at the next assembly of the Board.
NEW RATE.

On the proposition of -J7J--.-Snoarmex, seconded by Mr. P. SPEARMAN, it was resolved that the seal of the Board be aflixeel to a general district rate of Is. 101. in the pound. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN remarked that during the last year the rateable property of the Board had increased £1,207. This terminated the business on the agenda paper.

LIBERAL Prone TO FRODSIIM—The members of the Liberal Club Tea Party Committee with their wives and friends, to the number of about 40, had an enjoyable pic-nic to Frodsham on Tuesday afternoon. Soon after one o'clock the party left the club in Bewsey-street, in four waggonettes, and for an hour and a half had a pleasant drive through the country resplendent with the beauties of spring. At the Ring o' Bells, Overton, the company alighted, and proceeded to the hills, over which they spent some time in rambling. The invigorating atmosphere gave the visitors rare appetites for the excellent tea provided for them by Mr. Rigby, at Belle Monte, and the tempting edibles were disposed of with great relish. Afterwards the party found enjoyment in the various amusements furnished by Belle Monte, and about eight o'clock a start was made for Warrington, where they arrived about half-past nine, the afternoon's pleasure having been increased by the fine weather.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this authority was held on Tues- day afternoon. In the absence of the Rev. Canon Barclay, Mr. Robert Ashton was voted to the chair. There were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, John Lockwood, Messrs. J. Knowles, J. Weir, J. Darbyshire, T. Andrews, J. Mid wood, C. Rigby, H. Lowe, W. Jackson, J. Challoner, J. Highfield, E. A. Wallington, and W. H. div.head: CLAIM BY THE LATE MR. DUTTON'S EXECUTORS.
div.p: THE CLAIM BY THE LATE MR. DUTTON'S EXECUTORS.

A communication was read from Messrs. Robert Davies, and Co., informing the Board that the executors of the late Mr. James Dutton would meet the deputation from the authority, on the 3rd inst., in regard to the Frodsham Lord- ship sewer. Mr. CHALLOSER said that he and Mr. Andrews had arranged to attend. Mr. Ashtcn, though recovering, was yet too ill to form one of the deputation.

div.head: QUESTION OF WAYLEAVE.
div.p: THE QUESTION OF WAYLEAVE.

A number of letters were read by the Clerk in reply to the enquiries of the Board as to what sums had been paid by other authorities for wayleave and such like matters. That from the Notthwich Union said the guardians there had paid wayleave at the rate of one shilling per lineal yard. In one case—Marston and Wincham—the owner of the land produced a plan showing the land laid out for building pur- poscs, and claimed additional compensation on that ground. The case proceeded to arbitration, and the award was the usual allowance of one shilling per lineal yard—in all £ll is. 6d.; and the Costs amounted to about £l3O. (Loud laughter.)

div.head: SCARLETINA IN FRODSTIANI DISTRICT.
div.p: SCARLETINA IN FRODSTIANI DISTRICT.

The action which had been taken in reply to the request of the Board, that the day and Sunday schools in Frodsham, Overton, and Kingsley, shoold be closed, in order to prevent the spread of scarletina, came up for consideration. The Rev. S. Hague, vicar of Kingsley, wrote to the effect that had he received the letter three months ago, he would at once have concurred in the recommendation, as fever at that time was spreading rapidly through the parish. To close the schools now, would, the vicar thought, cause need- less consternation, and be productive of more harm than good.—Mr. T. Overton (Kingsley) forwarded a letter pretty nearly to the same effect.—Mr. R. H. Turner, (Crosbie House school, Frodsham), observed that he was quite willing to comply with the request of the authority in closing his day school for a month.—On behalf of the Trinity Wesleyan Sunday School Committee, Mr. Turner wrote that they were prepared to act in accordance with the suggestion of the Authority, provided the schools in the town acted in liar- mony.—Mr. W. B. Gibson, of Overton, stated that the com- mittee of the Five Crosses Sunaay school had closed the school for a month. The committee could not, however, understand what benefit would arise from that course. The children would be certain to meet in the lanes, and come in contact with those who might have the complaint in their houses. The Authority would be doing more good if they would see to the repairing and cleaning of the cottages, and making them fit for the people to live in. (Laughter.)—Mr. R. Trotter (Methodist Free Church Sunday school), said that the committee of the school had decided to close for a month.—The Rev. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham, replied that the recommendation of the Authority for the closing of both day and Sunday school should be carried out.—The Rev. R. P. Borwick wrote stating that without a precept he was most willing to do anything reasonable or for the benefit .of the public. Every morning after the assembling of his pupils, he took a plate with carbolic acid, and a red-hot iron, and fumigated the school and children. All his boarders were in excellent health, with one exception; but he promised to have a further consultation with Dr. Robinson. The CHAIR3fAN asked what course they ought to adopt as to the Kingsley schools. Mr. CuALLONTER did not think they could do anything, with the exception of offering recommendations. The CHAIRMAN: There has not been a single case of scarletina at Kingsley for a long time.

div.head: FRODSHAM SEWERAGE SCHEME.
div.p: THE FRODSHAM SEWERAGE SCHEME.
MC CLERK reported that Mr. Henry Bancroft, engineer had forwarded a bill for £220.

In reply to Mr. Midwood, Mr. LINAKER said the account was not one for commission. Mr. RIGBY : Is this the finishing up? (Laughter.) The CLERK: I think there is a balance to come yet. This account is one altogether outside the question of Mr. Ban- croft's commission. It is merely his costs for the arbitration. Mr. LOWE : Mr. Midwood must not say, too much, for I believe he is one of the arbitrators, and that he has a big bill to bring in. The CLERK: There is the bill from Messrs. Newton and Vawser, of Manchester, for £22 is., so that the two bills pretty nearly agree. Then there is an acconntof £9B 18s. 10,1. for legal expenses. Mr. RIGBY : To whom are those due? The CLERK: To myself. The account has been taxed by the Clerk of the Peace; and it includes £37 money out of pocket. Mr. LOWE: What do the entire expenses of the arbitra- tion amount to, with what you have paid for compensation? Mr. RIGBY : Aye, out with it. (Laughter.) The CLERK: About £4OO. Mr. CHALLONER : You are wrong, Mr. Linaker. The CLERK said that in addition to the items be had al- ready mentioned he might say that, as far as he could see, Mr. Wright's costs would be taxed under £100; and then there were the umpires, £95. The CHAIRMAN: £5OO in round numbers. The claims by the executors of the late Mr. Dutton and Mr. Ashton's haye yet to be considered. I 111 T. CHALLONER: Say £548. ' The CLERK: Mr. Wright claimed £440, and he said be

would not settle the mati.er unless we paid him that amount. Mr. CHALLONER: It hat: only cost us £7O more, and I • Iwould rather pay that than give it Wright, as the money goes into so many hands. Mr. LOWE: SO would I.

Mr. MIDWOOD said that whilst they were upon this question, he should like to know what ti:e orginal cost of the sewer was. The CLERK: £2,879. Mr. MIDWOOD: Are there any extras upon that, and what are they? The CHAIRMAN: There are some extras. Mr. MmwooD: We were given to understand that he had sent his bill in some weeks ago. The CLERK: Yes, his bill on the contract. Mr. Minwoon: Has the bill for the extras come in, Mr. Chairman ?
The CLERK: No, it has not. It will go to the enginw first. Then there is the cost of the land for tho outfall works —£2l9 15s.
Mr. Mmwoon: And what is Mr. Dutton's affair? The CLERK: He claims £BO, and you have offered him £6O.
Mr. MIDwOOD: Then it appears the original cost was to be £2,879; and the bill has now reached £3,672 ss. 41. with- out the extras.
The CLERK: The actual sewerage works were to cost £2,879.

Mr. RIGBY (looking at the Clerk's bill for legal expenses, which bad been handed to him for perusal): May I be allowed to ask Mr. Linaker what this item means—' To perusing same, very lengthy, one sovereign." (Laughter.) Mr. WiLLINGTON (humourously) : It perhaps took him a long time. Lawyers cannot go through a thing in half-an- hour. (Laughter.) Perhaps Mr. Linaker will explain it to you. Mr. LOWE : I don't think he will, for he will want 6s. Sd. if be does. (Laughter.) Mr. RIGBY : He seems very shy about it. The CLERK: Mr. Rigby, the next bill I have taxed,l will ask you to go to Chester with me; and we will go through it item by item. (Laughter.) Mr. RIGBY: Perhaps it will cost me more, then! The CLERK: It depends upon how you behave yourself. Mr. RIGBY (still perusing the bill): This is a" raver up, this is." (Laughter.) Mr. CHALLONER :Itis no use bothering about it. We have to pay it, and the sooner we do so, and the quicker we shall have done with it. It is no use waiting until the next bill comes in. [Mr. Rigby (rather satirically) : Capital !] I move that it be paid, and then we shall have done with it. Mr. RIGBY said he did not find any large items in the clerk's bill. The resolution was seconded by Mr. WEIR and carried unanimously. • Mr. LOWE : There is plenty of money at Frodsham THE PUBLIC HEALTH IN FRODSHAM DISTRICT. Mr. FARRINGTON, nuisance inspector, presented his re- port, and brought under the notice of the Authority, a letter which had appeared in the Manchester Guardian, in which the scarletina in Frodsham and the adjoining district was described in grossly exaggerated terms. Several members very strongly condemned the letter; and it was resolved that the inspector should write to the journal referred to, giving the statements an unqualified contradiction. This concluded the business of public interest.

WIDNES PARISH CHURCH BRANCH OF THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, On Saturday, the first annual meeting of the Widnes branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, took place. At about four o'clock, the members assembled at the school-room in Waterloo-road, and headed by the Star of Temperance Brass Band, marched to the Parish Church, where a special preacher, the Rev. F. B. Tyrer, M.A. vicar of All Saiets, Liverpool, delivered an appropriate dis- course. At half-past five, about 300 people assembled in the school-room for tea, which had been prepared by the wives of the members of the society, who likewise pre- sided.

At the public meeting which was afterwards held, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, the president, ifccupled the chair, and there were also present the Rev. F. B. Tyrer, W. 11. Duggan, and Messrs. W. Roberts, Kilcross, Chadwick (secretary), Farrant (assistant secretary), Bruce, Starkey, and others.

The CHAIRMAN in his opening observations referred to temperance generally and the three-fold object of their society, viz. ;—the promotion of temperance, the reformation of the intemperate, and the removal of the causes leading to intemperance, and this they endeavoured to do by means of their association, and by individual effort. (Hear, hear.) By their association they endeavoured to promote measures such as the one for Sunday closing, in which he might tell them the society had long taken a deep interest; also in the matter of grocers' licences and the payment of wages in public-houses, and other things offering facilities for in- temperance. (Hear, hear.) Nor was individual effort to be lost sight of, but formed an important factor in the work of temperance reformation, and might tend to check•drinking practices at funerals, christenings, and similar gatherings. (Applause.) The society was only a small part of a great whole of a band of earnest workers known as the Church of England Temperance Society, with the Queen as its patron and themselves in Widnes as its humble supporters and followers. (Applause.) The previous day (April 28th) had been the anniversary of their establishment. Its origin was very small; but owing to the energetic work of the lay members they were now in a flourishing condition. They now numbered 350 members, of whom 180 were not totally pledged and 170 were entire abstainers. In connec- tion with the society they had their monthly lectures, which had been largely patronized and thoroughly appreciated by the public. The chairman now referred to what took place last week in London in connection with the Church Tem- perance Society, and proceeded to state that the amount spent' as shown in the Budget, by the nation on intoxicating I i , drink was n 1868 23 millions, in 1875 31 millions, but in 1881 it had fallen to 28L- millions. Nor did he believe that this was solely owing to bad times, for while in 1873 the savings bank returns showed that £2.293,000 were therein deposited, in 1871 the deposits were £3,189,000. (Applause.) He concluded by an earnest appeal to others to join their ranks, whether under the red ribbon or the blue. (Ap- plause.) Mr. W. Chadwick read the report, which showed a balance in favour of the society. Mr. R. F. B. Tyrer stated that during last year one second rate firm in Liverpool took £3O a week less in drink than they formerly did. The proceedings terminated with the usual vote of thanks.

div.head: PRESS ON MR, PORSTEM,S DEFENCE,
div.p: THE PRESS ON MR, PORSTEM,S DEFENCE,

The Times in a leader, observes :—" The Prime Minister's reply to the fate Chief Secretary was marked by an unac- customed embarrassment of manner and by occasional movements of irritability. He had to deal with the warning of Mr. Forster that nothing is more perilous than an attempt to keep the peace by enlisting the aid of the organisers of lawlessness. He bad at tbe same time to avoid any statement at which the susceptibilities of the liberated members might take alarm. The task was difficult, and Mr. Gladstone's mastery of the intricacies of diction and dialectics was all needed to carry him successfully through the trial. It is unnecessary for others to follow him through this labyrinth of language. The fact that there is substan- tially an arrangement between the Government and the Land League party is no secret to anybody. If no such arrangement exists the main reasons in justification of the change of policy disappear; but Mr. Gladstone, in alluding mysteriously to information' respecting the views of the released suspects, laid bare the reality of the compact against which Mr. Forster had entered a protest." .4 Daily Yews leader says :—" In any case Mr. Forster's main argument seems to us to b 3 thin and poor. He would only have released the suspects, it seems, on one of three conditions—either their public promise to abstain from their evil courses, or the fact that Ireland had been restored to actual tranquility, or the fact that the Government had obtained new, different, and sufficient powers for the en- forcement of the law in Ireland. M. Gladstone most effectually disposed of the first condition. There was dig- nity as well as good feeling in his manner of dealing with it. It is absurd to suppose that Mr. Parnell and Mr. Dillon would make public confession that they had done wrong and promise to amend their behaviour for the future. Mr. Forster himself, whet he testified to his belief in Mr. Parnell's personal honour and dwelt with an emphasis which would have delighted Thackeray in his cynical mood on the fact that Mr. Parnell is a gentleman by station,' cannot surely have supposed that this man of honour and 'gentle- man by station' has been doing wrong believing himself to be doing wrong. Mr. Parnell we must sesame, believes that he has been acting rightly, and can hardly be expected to apologise for it. To keep him in prison until he repcn:a might suit an Ottoman or Russian system, but would hardly suit an English Government or an English public opinion." A Standard leader holds that "the time has at length been reached when there should be an inquiry into the Irish policy of Ministers. The Government must be placed on its trial at the bar of public opinion more directly than has yet been done. It is only by set Parliamentary debates that the constituencies can be properly enlightened. On such ques- tions as these Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues, it is clear, will say as little as they can. The OpposTon is charged with the responsibility of compelling them to say as much 'as they ought. The Conservative party will expose itself to the charge of neglecting a grave national, as well as political duty if its leaders do not without a moment's unnecessary delay arraign Her Majesty's Ministers for the course they have taken in regard to Ireland. There are times when a vote of censure is the weak expedient of aggressive faction, but there are also times when it is a plain and imperative obligation, and such we hold it to be at the present crisis cit our national affairs." Tan can truly deny that theTphoelipcyaildyisTcuelscsgerderopnh l'night s a totally new de- parture, resting for its justification on consequences which ahYusr's—d al:rye i ()lacy, startling and none can foresee. A revolution an p novel, could not fail to plunge the House into a warm debate which set aside the cloture rules fixed for Thursday night. , Perhaps the House and the more thoughtful portion of the country will agree with the late Chief Secretary, that Ire- land should take precedence of all other subjects not abse- ' lutely essential to financial requirements, it for no other reason than that the Irish imbroglio itmolves the most far-reaching and perilous issues alike F.locial and political in a fashion and under conditions "unprecedented in our history.
