div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The quarterly meeting of the Council was held on Tues- day evening, under the presidency of his Worship the Mayor (Alderman Pickrnere). There were also present : Aldermen Davies, Harrison, Holmes, and Burgess; Councillors Platt, Pierpoint, Woolfall, Taylor, Francomb, Wallington, Brown, Greening, Fairclough, Barker, Ridgway, Litton, Caldwell, Ashton, Burgess, Dixon, and Monks; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), :and T. Longdin (borough surveyor). THE RECENT ATTACK ON THE QUEEN'S LIFE. The MAYOR: I have received a letter from Whitehall, acknowledging the memorial sent by this Corporation on the occasion of the attempt on her Majesty's life. It is as follows :—" Whitehall, 3rd April, 1882.—Sir,-1 have had the honour to lay before the Queen the loyal and dutiftel address of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the • Borough of Warrington, in Council assembled, on the subject of the recent attempt upon the life of Her Majesty. And I have it in command to assure you that Her Majesty a is deeply sensible of the loyalty and affection of her faithful • subjects.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, W. V. IlanoonnT. —The Town Clerk of Warrington." 4910.6 g. RESIGNATION OF A COUNCILLOR. • T -The Mearon said he had to announse, with exceedingly • great regret, that he had received a letter from Mr. J. P. Williams, a Courcillor of the Corporation resigning his seat. He was sure they could all only feel as one in reference to the matter, and that they would all feel they had lost a very good man, who was not only useful, but always attended most reaularly to his duties in this Council and at the committees. He was sure the Council would regret the cause of Mr. Williams' resignation, which was ill- health. The letter was as follows : Chatterton Rouse, Seaforth, 25th April, IBB2.—Dear Sir,— The Mayor of Warrinatnn is respectfully asked to excuse the further attendance ot J. P. Williams, councillor, and to ask the members of the Council to allows inembr who has been stricken down by sickness, to retire from duties which he is no longer able to fulfil. With many, very many, thanks for the kindness, on all occasions, and at all times, received, I remain, your very humble and obedient servant, J. P. WILLIAMS. In conclusion, the Mayor moved—" That this Council accept with regret the resignation of Josiah Pemberton Williams, Esq., as councillor for the South-West Ward, without pay- ment by him of the fine of £2.5 imposed by the bye-law of the Council, dated 14th June, 1847, made under the 51st sec. of the Act 5 and 6 Wm. IV., cap. 76." Alderman Keaer seconded the motion, and remarked he was sure, as the Mayor had said, the Council were all one in regret at the cause which had brought about the resigna- tion. He trusted that Mr. Williams' health would speedily be restored. The motion was unanimously carried. THE COUNCIL AND ELECTRIC LIGHTING. The Mayon said he had to announce that he had received a communication from the Mayor of Manchester in reference to electric lighting. He called a meeting on Saturday last, and he (the Mayor) attended with the Town Clerk at the con- ference of municipal authorities held in the Mayor's Parlour in the Town Hall, Manchester, to take into consideration the course of action which should be adopted with refelence to the Bills now before Parliament relating to electric lighting. At that meeting it was explained that the whole of the Bills relating to this subject bad been referred to one Select Committee, and that the Board of Trade had Issued a memorandum inviting the promoters of, and peti- tioners against, the various schemes before the committee, tn consult together fcr the purpose of grouping themselves, and to select persons to represent their various interests before the committee. There were present at the meeting, representatives from the following towns :—Leicester, Blackburn, Bolton, Buxton, Longton, Belfast, Warrington, Southport, Salfora, Keighley, Oldham, Wigan, Hindley, Dewsbury, Carlisle, Bury, Hinckley, Birkenhead, Halifax, Manchester, and Birmingham. He explained that he was not in a position to assent to the combined action at that meeting, neither did ha dissent therefrom, but arranged to bring the matter before the Council. It would be observed that it was proposed to divide the cost amongst the whole of the local authorities according to their municipal rateable value. Whatever expense Was gone to would be divided pro rata according to the rateable VBl Pe of the various boroughs. Costs of deputations, and these other incidental expenses of that nature being borne by the authorities incur- ing them. According to this principle, he thought the amount of costs which the borough would have to contribute would not at the utmost exceed £3O or £4O. It was clearly very desirable that the interests of corporations, when the creation of monopolies affecting such interests was older discussion, should be carefully watched and jealously guarded, and he thought it was without doubt their duty to give their support to the general combined action which was to be taken. That action was not with any object of prejudicing or defeating the introduction of the electric light, but it was to facilitate its introduc- tion on terms most advantageous to the local authorities. He begged to move the following resolution: "'hat this Corporation approves of the resolutions passed at a conference of municipal authorities, held in the Mayer's parlour in the Town Hall, at Manchester, on the 29th day of April, 1882, with reference to the Government Electric Lighting Bill, and agrees to concur with the combined action therein referred to." Alderman DAVIES seconded the resolution. Councillor WALLINGTON thought the arrangement was an excellent one, and he had great pleasure in cordially sup, porting it. Alderman HARRISON: I suppose, Mr. Mayor, we may calculate that, at all events, the cost will be under £5O. The MAYOR: Well, I expect so: considerably less than 150. The resolution was carried. INTERNATIONAL FISHERIES' EXHIBITION. The MAYOR also announced that he had received a com- munication from the Lord Mayor of London in reference to a great International Fisheries' Exhibition to be held in London next year, under the patronage of the Queen and the Prince of Wales, and stating they would be very glad if the Corporation sent anything from the local museum to assist them. Alderman HARRISON: You might send a deputation. Alderman BCRGESS : Could you not send something out of the river? The MAYOR remarked that they were asked to fill tht3 forms of subscriptions, and he added when he got the forms he would lay them before the members of the Council. (Laughter.) THE POLICE INSPECTOR'S REPORT. The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Watch Committee containing the letter from the Homo Secretary in reference to the cost of the police clothing, which was given in our last issue. Alderman HARRISON seconded. Alderman KEAN thought these members who felt agerieved about the contract for the police clothing going out of the town should carefully read the minutes. It was a singular letter to receive in so trifling a matter. Councillor WALLINGTON asked if the prices quoted were those of the last contract. Alderman KEAN said they were the prices of the contract entered into 12 months ago. Councillor Peocter thought the ratepayers generally ought to know that before the letter was received the Watch Com- mittee had taken steps to remedy the matter complained

of. Alderman HOLMES had read the last report of the inspec- tor and a grat many other reports, and he had come to the conclusion that the inspection of the police did very little good. Captain Legge came here and spent a great deal of time in examining the books, seeing if the clothes fitted, and if the shoes were properly brushed, and all the rest of it. He thought that was perfectly useless, because if Cap- tain Legge went through the town with Mr. Hunt he would see part of a wall taken away, and would ask what steps were they taking to prevent a repetition; and possibly he might go in some other street and see the whole of the win- dows of some factory smashed. Very likely if he visited the town in this way, Captain Legge would offer some sug- gestions to Mr. Hunt as to the proper management of the police and the watching of the town. He considered a re- port of that sort would be far more important to the rate- payers of Warrington than troubling them about the police coats. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BURGESS really did not think the police did their duties so badly as that. He must say that he never saw the windows of a factory broken. Councillor PlERponrr could show them a street in War- rington where there were houses with not a single pane of glass left in the window frames. The MAYOR. said the Committee were unanimously of opinion that the police did their duty in the borough as far as they could. Of course it was not possible for the police to be everywhere at the same time, and very often children took the opportunity when the police were off that particu- lar part of their beat to do damage. Respecting the state- ment of Alderman Holmes, he said if they wanted more protection to property they must have more police. He was glad to Bee the Council had proceeded in one t direction, and that was of giving extra light in the street. That was as good as three extra policemen. They had not as many policemen as they ought to have according to the population, and if they had more there would be less damage. Councillor CALDtvELE said if he remembered rightly the Home Secretary would not sanction an increase of the force unless the Council showed just cause. The MAYOR pointed out that after the chairman of a corn- ntittee had replied no member could speak on the subject. Councillor CALDWELL : I beg pardon. The minutes were passed. THE lATCHFORD SEWEUADE SCIrEME. The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee recom- mended the following plans for approval :—Alteration to house 17, Fonndry-streetNsr ,Ifeosrlisl. wr. iinosseer ndpahScouo.th; alterations to at Bank Quay for to houses in Lltch ford for S. Reynolds, Esq.; workshops in Froghall-lane for Mr. Hubert Pierpoint ; three houses in Hopwood-street for Mr. Joseph Monks; seven houses in Bes- wick-street for Mr. William Bostock ; houses off Manches- ter-road for Mr. William Porter; two cottages in Dannett- street for Mr. Richard Hewitt ; four houses in Bittersby- lane for Messrs. E. and J. Jameson ; streets proposed to be laid out between Museum-street and Thynne-street. They also recommended that the tenders of Messrs. Grant, Coburn, and Co., of Newry, for the supply of 500 tons of granite cubes; of Messrs. Butterworth and Brooks for the supply of Curbs; be accepted.—The report of the deputation appointed to visit the exhibition at E tstbourne of Shone's system of sewerage was approved, and ordered to be printed and sub- mitted to the Coutell.—At a meeting of the committee, on the let inst., the apportionment of the cost of paving Hind street, as follows, was approved :—Executors of the late T. rorter, £199 13s. 11d.; Rylands Bros., Limited, £2l is. lid.

—£22o 15s. 101—Recommendation, that the• tender of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited, for an air receiver required in connection with Latchford sewerage, and of Mr. Isaac Shone, of Wrexham, for an air compressor and two ejectors, be accepted. Alderman KEAN, in order that the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee recorded at a meeting held on the previous night, might be passed, moved the suspension of standing order 8. His reason for this course was because the committee wished to at once commence to deal with the sewerage of Latchford. It was now May, but the reason they had delayed the matter was because they wished to see bow the machinery at Eastbourne worked. As they would know it was a complete success, and the committee were confirmed in the view they held before, that it was the only method to remedy the existing-, state of things at Litchford. Councillor WALLINGTON seconded the motion, which was

carried. Alderman KEAN then moved the confirmation of the minutes of the committee, remarking on the satisfactory natuxe of the deputation to Eastbourne. Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the motion. Aldetman WEBS-TER remarked that unfortunately he was absent from the Council when this sewerage scheme for Latchford was proposed. Had he been present he should have strenuously opposed it; and he could not let this opportunity pass without entering his protest against the method adopted, more espec'ally with regard to the outfall, which was p'.aced within a very short distance of Warring- ton Bridge, and 'would soon he in the centre of the town. How such a scheme could have been sanctioned by the Council in face of the poster placed on the walls within the last few days warning people against set.ding refuse in the river he really could not understand. He was satisfied the Government Inspector would seriously objct to the outfall, as he believed it would be detrimental to the health of the town. If the ejectors were capable of performing what they were stated to do, he could see no reason why they should not carry the sewage to the present outfall at Bank Quay. It would be a better plan, and more satisfactory to the inhabitants of the borough. Alderman DAVIES said it was true the sewage was to be discharged below Warrington Bridge, but it was discharged at that point now, so that the Committee were not, as far as the outfall was concerned, making any alteration from that which already existed. No doubt the time would come and Warrington was looking forward to it more than any other town, when they would not be permitted to discharge sewage into the river at all. (Hear, hear.) The present scheme was only part of a general scheme, and when the Corporation were prevented from discharging at the point proposed, they would discharge it into the main sewer which went to Bank Quay. He hoped the time would soon come when depositing tanks would have to be placed at Bank Quay, and all the sewage have to be purified before it was sent into the river The MAYOR observed that the ej,ctor system of disposing of sewage was the most perfect he bad ever seen, and it had occurred to him that at a slight cost the sewage could be

ejected into the main sewer. Alderman BURGESS, referring to Alderman Davies' re- marks, said he thought the scheme should be carried out in its entirety now. The future spoken of might be more dis- tant than they contemplated. If this system were so per- fect as it was represented to be, which he gravely doubted, he thought they should have the entire benefit now, more especially as the outlay, as the Mayor had remarked, would be so small. The MAYOR said it was his opinion that the sewage of Latchford was at present so small and contained so much water, that the deposit in the river would be infinitesinal. He thought the scheme ought to be tried, and if it was worked satisfactorily, they could easily carry it forward. Councillor FnArTcomn explained that the proposed sewer at Black Bear Bridge was much lower than the present sewer at Latchford; so that an ejector would have to raise the sewage into the existing sewer. They would therefore want a much greater outlay because they would require a sewer which wculd take it from the level from Warrington Bridge to Bank Quay. The MAyon: Oh, no. Councillor FRANCOMB: We could not use the present sewer. Councillor PLATT could see no objection to this scheme being carried out at present, for no portion would be un- necessary Or useless. Councillor WALLINGTON wished to remind the dounC;:l that another ejector costing £250, would be required to carry the sewage over the river if the scheme propounded by Aid. Webster were adopted. Alderman WEBSTER said when they did come to deal with it they would require other ejectors. Councillor BARKER complimented the committee on the system they lead adopted, which was the most perfect they could have chosen, and upon ascertaining what the machinery could practically perform before they ordered it. Councillor FIERPOINT remarked that he had no doubt of the usefulness of the scheme if properly carried out. Were there the slightest nuisance from discharging the sewage at the point contemplated, he would suggest that it be done where it would not be detrimental to the inhabitants. He was glad to bear Alderman Burgess remark that they should be careful as to the working powers of the new machinery. He thought that advice om a gentleman like Alderman Burgess, after what they had witnessed in several parts, of work carried on by the corporation, should be taken very carefully so that they might be put to no extraordinary ex- pense in any new fangled system which they expected would come to a good issue at last. A!derMan BURGESB 5i he was unconscious of having made any such remark. The MAYOR thought Mr. Pierpoint only wished to appear witty. (Loud laughter.) When he saw the machinery at work at Eastbourne there was not the slightest nuisance, nor the slightest smell that he could discern. Alderman KEAN said this scheme above all others was the best, and was more calculated to enable the corporation to deal with the sewage of Warrington than any other could be. It would not be advisable at present to convey the sewage into the main sewer, because the outlet was not prepared for its reception. When the Government prohibited the pollu- tion of the stream they could do so and make one proper outlet. There was no nuisance from the ejectors. When the scheme was completed at Latchford, the velocity with which the sewage would be passed through the sewers from the ejectors Would be such that it would not smell. He thought the committee had acted wisely in recommending this scheme, and they felt sure that after it had been at work 12 months, the inhabitants of Latchford would be satisfied was the right one. The minutes were passed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.

Meetings of the School Attendance Committee were held on the 6th and 20th April, when orders for payment of ac- counts amounting to £42 13s. sd. were passed. The INSPECTOR reported that 48 cases bad been enquired into by the Board of Guardians and school fees allowed in 36 cases for 73 children, also that 34 cases were taken before the magistrates and a fine inflicted in each case. The average attendance of Children in schools under inspection for March, 1882, was 5,946.—Forty-two cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. Alderman WEBSTER, in moving the confirmation of the proceedings, said his attention had been called two or three timeaof late by members of the Council, and by others, to a paragraph which had been going the rounds of the news- pairrs as to the attendance and the number of children on the books of the schools in the borough of Heywood, which he believed rejoiced in a school board. It was said, on what authority he did not know, that the Education Department would be perfectly satisfied if 16 per cent. of the population were on the books of the schools of the borough, and it was also said that in Heywood, 20 per cent. of the population of the borough was on the books of the schools. Several parties had called his attention to the matter, and he had been asked how Heywood occupied such a prominent position. He had replied he did not know, but that he would look into the matter. Since then he had gone into the questicn, and he found that in Warrington, the number of children on the books amounted to 20.12- per cent., there- fore there were really more on the books here than at Heywood, and this was only in the elementary schools. If they took into consideration the attendance at the various private schools the attendance would be very much higher. Then with regard to the average attendance, which was a most important thing, there was very nearly 16 per cent, of the scholars in average attendance. (Hear, hear.) There- fore he thought the honour claimed by Heywood would be shared by Warrington, because here they had a higher relative number of children on the books in regard to the population as compared with Heywood, and also a higher relative number in attendance. Whatever, consequently, had been said regarding Heywood had no foundation in fact so far as Warrington was concerned. Councillor Dncoar seconded the adoption of the minutes. He believed that the attendance throughout the Borough of Warrington would compare favourably with that of many other towns, especially when they took into consideration the standard of Warrington people. He felt sure they ought to be ahead, and therefore when he saw the report respecting the attendance at Heywood he thought it only right the chairman's attention should be called to it. He (Mr. Dixon) was consequently very glad to see they were ahead in the matter of attendance, though there was still room for improvement. Councillor FAIRCLOUGIT, alluding to the report of the inspector, said that a number oc cases were inquired into in court on Monday, and he took the trouble to ask the school inspector certain questions about some of them. Ho was surprised to find that parents applied to the Board of Guardians for the fees of their children to be paid, and that these had in some cases been granted for something like 18 months or two years, though the children had not gone a quarter of the time to schoel. As an instance, he said that suppose John Smith applied to the Board of Guardians for the school fees of his children, the case was inquired into, after which the order was made that the school fees be allowed for three months. The parents were next asked about what school the child would go to, and whatever school was decided upon the fees were paid to the school by the Board, whether the children went to the school or not. In two cases which came before the bench on Monday, it was found that though the fees had been paid for a consider- able time, the children had not gone to school at least half the time. He wished to know whether the School At- tendance Committee had any power to look into these cases. He thought that if the parents did not send their children to school the fees ought not to be paid. Alderman HARRISON said it was no duty of the School Attendance Committee to make inquiries of that kind. He neomsrttaiinordnceeolaf t bathe Cl edoe kuwne ci tn thetl tt ohe aasetchhei ofr wla 00 cunl adi l ixoWan' ecdnt at yt ht df SeCceihi. do onll of ta fngoyor again that week the school fee would certainly be due to the teacher. The children must go some portion of the week, otherwise the teacher could not exact the fee, "because,"

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY, 1882.

said the worthy alderman, "if we, that is the Guardians— (laughter)—found that the child had not gone to school any portion of the week they would not pay the fees." It was no duty of the Guardians to ascertain whether the child went to school at all, but it would appear to him to be the duty of the teacher to make a report if the children did not attend school. It was one of those difficult things which one really did not know how to deal with. To say the Guardians paid the school fees in any one particular week without the child not going to school was not a fact. Councillor Feaßceonein : Well, I have been wrongly in- formed. Alderman KEAN was understood to say that when the Guardians agreed to pay a child's fee, the teacher booked the child until further orders, and exacted the money. Alderman HARRISON said that, supposing the Guardians agreed to pay the school fees of a child for three months, the Guardians would not pay for any of the weeks the child was absent; but if the child went only a portion of a week the fee of 3d. would have to be paid. The MAYOR observed that it was the duty of the Attend- ance Committee, through theirofficer, Mr. Riley, to summon the parents for not sending their children regularly to school, and they would be fined for not complying, although the fees were paid. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH : But what is the use of paying these fees if the children do not go to school? Mr. KEAN: To get punished for it. Councillor WALLINGTON: Were fines inflicted in the cases to which you refer? Councillor FAIRCLOUGH : Oh, certainly. Councillor WALLINGToN : And they were paid? Conncillor FAIRCLOUGH: A few paid. Councillor WALLINGTON: And these fines come to more than the fees? Councillor Fairclougle answered in the affirmative. Councillor WALLINGTON then observed that they ought to call upon the Guardians, who paid the fees, to see that the children went to school. Alderman HARRISON It is no part of their duty. Alderman KEAN: I think the action of the magistrates will teach these people better things some day. Alderman WEasTER, in replying, observed that parents were summoned again and again, and they were always quite willing to pay the fines though they did :not pay the fees. He thought himself the poor-law officers might exer- cise some judgment in the matter, still it would all come to the same thing in the end. The MAYOR thought it was astonishing the number of parents brought before the magistrates and the amount of money paid in fines. One person had been summoned for the fourth time, and still the parent would not send the child to school. The minutes were afterwards confirmed. PRESENTATIONS TO THE LIBRARY AND MUSEUM. THE DEATH OF DR. KENDRICK. At a meeting of the Museum, Library and Arts Commit- tee on the 14th of April, accounts were passed amounting to £2O lie. 103. The thanks of the Committee were ordered to be tendered to the undermentioned gentlemen for the fol- lowing gifts :—Mr. Gittens, fossil in slab of limestone; Mr. J. Cave Whittle, seven fossils from coal measures, Sze.; Mr. J. P. Rylands, De Witt's "Lady of Latham ;" Mr. Alderman Davies, his paper on Richard 111. and Hamlet, and Raper's "Practice of Navigation ." Mr. John Peers, Tillotson's " Works " and 6 other books and 3 broadsides; Mr. S. Buck- man, his paper on" Ammonites from the Inferior Oolite ;" Mr. E. Massey, three Old Playbills; Mr. Sherratt, a broad- side on the "Ten Hours Bill." Councillor GREENING moved, and Councillor BURGESS seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of the Commit- tee. Alderman WEBSTER remarked that the committee had lost a valuable friend in the death of Dr. Kendrick, who as the letter said was "the long and unceasing friend of War- rington, and to whom the Museum and Library owe a debt of gratitude for the care which he took to advance their in- terests and for the treasures with which his bounty has enriched their collections." The very last conversation he had with the deceased was with reference to the best means to be adopted for the purpose of making more accessible to the public some seals and other objects he had deposited in the Museum as he contemplated making the collection still , larger. He was sure they would all sympathise with Mrs. I Kendrick and the family in tkeir bereavement. The minutes were confirmed. THE " MORALS OF MORTALITY " : A" GRAVE RECKONING." At a meeting of the Cemetery Committee on the 3rd April, an order for payment of accounts amounting to £29 2e. was passed. The Registrar reported that the inter- ' ments for the past four weeks were adults 27, minors 44, and still-born 10, and for the corresponding period of last year, adults 27, minors 30, and stillborn 9. The receipts for the past four weeks were £62 14s: 101, and for the correspond- ing period of last year £56 lie. Alderman DAVIES called attention to the Cemetery Regis- trar's annual reporc which showed that the receipts for the year bad been £7lB 9s. 11d. Commenting on a table in the report, the worthy alderman said it presented a lesson in what he called the morals of mortality. (A laugh.) It was a very grave reckoning. t Laughter.)—[Alderman KEAN: It is a dead letter, perhaps. (Renewed laughter.)]—The reason why be was calling the attention of the Council to the report, as he had done before, was because of the remark- able number of still-born children buried at the cemetery. It might surprise them, he thought, when be told them that the number of still-born children buried in the cemetery was equal to 15 per cent. of the whole of the people dying in Warrington. He should be able to tell them, if the table contained the information, what per centage it was as to the minors, that was what per centage it was as to the burying of children generally, but he could not do so be- Cane the table did not give the number of adults, minors, and still-born children. However, ho found that the ntun- ber of burials of still-born children at the cemetery was equal to 23 per cent. of the burials of children generally. The burials during the past four weeks were—adults 27, minors 44, still-born 10, that 10 being in proportion with the 44 equal to 23 per cent. He did not know how far that compared with other towns, but he thought it was worth the while of the committee to inquire what was the condition of things in other towns. Alderman HARRISON said that was a question which had arisen before; he believed statistics from other towns had been procured, and they were found to be pretty well con- sistent with each other. In consequence of the facilities for the burial of still-born children there was a theory that sometimes foul play` was used, but that was such a very grave assertion one almost shrunk from making the sugges- tion. However, they were no worse off than other towns in reference to this particular question. Councillor BROWN had no doubt that Warrington would bear favourable comparison with any other town in the matter of its still-born children as well as it would do with any other borough in regard to the education of its children. The average of still-born childreif.was not more than for many years past. The minutes were then confirmed. THE TOWN HALL AND PARK. At meetings of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Commit- tee, on the 6th and 12th April, accounts amounting to £4O 10s. 2d. were passed. The bath keeper reported that the income from the baths for the past four weeks was £lO 12s. 23., and for the corresponding period last year £22 7s. Bd. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor CALDWELL seconded the confirmation of the proceedings of the Town Hall Com- mittee, and they were agreed to. THE MARKETS. Captain Ltrroel moved the confirmation of the proceed- ings of the Markets Committee, which contained no itemsof interest, and this having been seconded by Councillor WAL- LINGTON, was carried. THE SANITARY COMMITTEE DISCHARGES ITS MORAL OBLIGATION. The proceedings of the Sanitary Committee comprised recommendations that Mr. Clement George be appointed clerk in the office of the inspector of nuisances at the wages of 18s. per week ; that an allowance of £lO be voted to Owen P. Warner, the engineer at Longford depot, for over- time workedby him up to the end of December, 1881; and that the sum of £5O be voted to Hamblett Guest, as and by way'of compensition for the in jurie ssustained by him at the Longford wmks, on the 27th Jane last. This sum to be paid without prejudice to the Corporation, and on the distinct understanding that no liability is admitted in respect thereof. The minutes also stated that the report of the Medical ! Officer for the year, 1881, was read and adopted, and I ordered to be printed. Alderman BURGEi'S, in moving the adoption of the minutes, adverted to the last recommendation, and remarked that he believed it was quite true there was 110 liability attaching to the Corporation in the matter. But he believed it was quite true that the unfortunate man sustained severe injury, and injury, he was afraid of a permanent character, and while there was legally no liability attaching to the Corporation there was that moral obligation which he hoped the Corporation would never attempt to escape under any circumstances. (Hear. hear.) The committee thought that the sum o; £5O which it was recommended should be given to the man Guest was not an excessive sum, but it was his duty to tell the Council that that amount would not be the whole amount the man who had sustained serious, and very likely permanent injury, would receive. For a great many weeks after the accident the man's wages was paid as though he were at work,—[Alderman KEAN: Very properly so.)—and it was only since Guest had attempted to work and found that he was not equal to the duties that he formerly discharged that he had made an application which the committee had entertained, and which he hoped the Council would confirm. The report of the medical officer was in the hands of the Council, and he thought it was an able report-s--(hear, be tr)—and he asked the Council to consider the various details set forth in the report. Councillor Mcienes seconded. Councillor DIXON asked if the man Guest had made an application for compensation for the injuries he had re- ceived. Alderman Kw n: That was stated by the Chairman. Councillor DIXON drew attention to the nuisance at the top of Arpley-street, and said he would be very glad if the chairman would take the matter in hand. Alderman KEAN thought the recommendation of the com- mittee in regard to the m In who had sustained injuries was a very proper one. (Hear, hear.) No one could have read the account of the accident without shuddering and wonder- inc how it was possible the man could recover. It was one of the most alarming accidents that he ever read of, and he thought the committee had acted very wisely in making an acknowledgment to the man in the shape of a grant of £5O. He hoped the Council would not object to it. Councillor PLATT thought the Sanitary Committee had acted generously to the man who was injured whilst in their employ. They had done what any reasonable employer in the town would have done' and he did not think any mem- ber of the Corporation would object to it. Adverting to the nuisance complained of by Councillor Dixon, he said he
thought it was the duty et those who derived a profit from the attendance of persons at places of amusement to provide

convenience for those persons. Councillor LITTON remarked that the injured man sent a most grateful letter to the Infirmary, acknowledging the attention he had received there. The MAYOR had no doubt the committee had acted most wisely, and that by their action they would command better servants than they otherwise would do. Alderman BURGESS stated in reply that there was an ap- plication made by Guest to• the committee, and he repeated that there was no liability attaching to the Corporation. Alludiog to the treatment the man had received at the Infirmary, he said it was of the most skilful character—(hear, hear,)—and they all thought a debt of gratitude was owing to Dr. Richmond and the other gentlemen connected with the institution for the way in which he was treated. It was one of the evidences of the great value of such an institution as that in their midst.

ZHear, hear.) As to the nuisance at Arpley-street, he main- tained that where there was a public performance there was an obligation on the promoters and proprietors to pro- vide the necessary accommodation for the large number of persons they brought together. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were confirmed.

PRO2OSED RXDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF OAS. The Gas Committee's minutes contained 'a recommeada- that the tender of Messrs. Newton, Chambers, and Co. for the supply of 220 yards of 18inch pipes 9ft.long, and 210 yards of 16in. pipes 9ft. long, and 800 yards of fin, pipes Oft. long, and irregular castings, be accepted; also a recommendation that an accident fund be established in connection with the works for the relief and assistance of the workmen in case of accident, and that the sum of £5 be subscribed toward the fund, each .man employed to contribute one penny per week. Alderman HOLMES proposed the adoption of the minutes. He said at the last meeting of the committee the accounts for the past year were presented, and it was shown to them that there had been a very large consumption of gas during the past year, and that there was also a very fair increase in the profits of the gasworks. The committee had considered the question—although they had not absolutely decided upon it—of recommending the Council at the next meeting to make a reduction in the price of gas. (Hear, hear.) The committee had not yet arrived at the precise figure which they would recommend, but still he thought they might take it that at the next meeting the committee would bring for- ward a motion for a reduction in the price of gas, which he hoped would meet with the approval of Councillor Dixon. Councillor PLATT said everybody found they had con- sumed a much larger quantity of gas during the last year than before, and they found they had to pay a considerable amount of money extra, which no doubt accounted for the increase of profit Alderman Holmes had spoken about. It behoved the Corporation to inquire whether for that increase of profit the consumers had derived a corresponding benefit. He had heard a great many persons say if they had burned more gas it must have been in consequence of the inferior quality of gas suppiied. He asked if the quality of the gas had anything to do with the gas bills increasing so enorm- ously as in some cases. Councillor WaLLINGTorT had heard it said that the pro- fits made by the Gas Committee went towards paying the debt and interest upon the works. If there was a reduction of gas would there still remain a profit to pay that interest on the debt ?—(cries of " Certainly.")—because, as he under- stood it, if there was not sufficient profit they came upon the improvement rate, and if they came upon the improvement rate they fell upon the property owners—(laughter)—and they were a feeling people. (Laughter.) Alderman KEAN thought they should give the Gas Com- mittee credit for having sufficient wit and judgment to know, when they recommended a reduction in the price of gas, that they had sufficient profit left to pay their liabili- ties. There had been great clamour for a long time for a reduction in the price of gas, and now Councillor Walling- ton wanted to throw cold water upon the reduction by stating that the burden might possibly fall upon the pro- perty owners and ratepayers. He felt quite satisfied that would not be the case. In regard to Councillor Platt's re- marks about the consumption of gas, he said if they con- sumed too much they should reduce the pressure at the meter. Alderman Haratisox" said that being a member of the Gas Committee he ought to be the last to complain, but be was bound to say the complaint was very general, and he could bear testimony to the fact himself that his gas bill had very considerably increased, and he was not aware that there had been a great increase in the consumption of gas. Councillor Dixon' asked the chairman to give the Coun- cil the number of feet of gas that had been manufactured,

and also the quantity sold. Alderman BURGESS thought there was a great deal to be said in regard to the est-a charges. His own bill certainly astonished him; he could not for the life of him understand it. There was something which required explanation. He was quite satisfied whatever abatement the chairman of the Gas Committee might make in the price of gas it would nothing like cover the extra charge imposed upon him this half year;—(Hear, hear.)—and if they were going to in- crease the charges at the ratio his had been increased, the sooner they decreased the price of gas two-thirds the better. • Alderman Dams said be thought the chairman of the Gas Committee if he had not announced any reduction would have been more cordially received. (Laughter.) He also thought the chairman had got very little encourage- ment to make any further reduction. He asked Councillor Dixon what the increase in his bill was. Councillor DIXON: 15 to 20 per cent. Alderman DAVIES remarked that 7.'as pretty strong evi- dence that Councillor Dixon had been staying out rather /ate In the evening. (Laughter.) He thought the Council Ought to have been very pleased indeed to hear there wee some prospect of the Gas Committee being able to reduce the price of gas. Alderman WEBSTER said if people would examine their meters from time to time and see that they had a proper check on the influx of gas into them, he was bound to say there would not be such complaints of extraordinary quantities of gas being burned. He made a point of attend- ing to his meter, and during the last seven months which embraced many dark days there was only a slight increase amounting to SOO feet—a mere bagatelle. Alderman HARRISON: The meters are placed in such beastly places there is .no getting at them. (Laughter.) ALDERMAN HOLMES, replying to Councillor Platt, observed that the Committee bad always determined to keep up the quality of gas throughout the year. The Act of Parliament only required them to produce gas of 16 candles but it had been nearly 19. The explanation which was given to him of the increased consumption of gas was that there was a greater pressure in the mains than formerly and consequently there was a greater anveunt of gas flaring through the burners than there was before. If people who had gas in their houses would take the trouble to turn it off at the meter there would not be the amount of gas consumed as at present. Councillor Wallington asked whether the Council had a profit commensurate with the reduction suggested. He should have hoped a question of that sort was not one to put to a member of the Gas Committee. They would certainly con- sider whether they had money to pay before they made the proposition—(hear, hear),—and he thought Councillor Wal- lington might trust the Committee that before they brought a recommendation forward they would consider whether they had the means with which to pay it. He thought surely for once they could please Mr. Dixon, but it seemed almost impossible. In conclusion, he pointed out that meters were tested at the gas works, and if they registered wronely the cost of testing was borne by the Corporation. The minutes were then agreed to. RIVERS COMMITTEE.

On the motion of Alderman Davies the minutes of the Rivers Committee were passed, comprising the report of a deputation appointed to represent the Corporation at an interview with Mr. Dodson on the Rivers Conservancy and Floods Prevention Bill.
NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

The few horses that were seen decorated on May Day looked very well, but the day was chilly and the thing looked premature. The Newton Gun Club held its first Spring Meeting on Saturday. The shooting began shortly after noon, when, also, the rain began to fall, and was continued till about six; the poor pigeons being literally tempest tost, and it rained piteously for ten hours. This is but poor sport, we fancy, for gentlemen. The annual sermons were preached in St. John's Baptist Church, on Sunday, by Rev. Mr. Carson, to large audiences, and the choir was assisted by Mr. McClure, of St. Paul's, Wigan, and collections were made. Mr. McClure, 8.A., of Wigan, otfi- elated for Rev. J. Allatt, at Crow-lane Church; and at the Primitive Methodist Chapel Rev. F. Shimmin preached the annual sermons, when a collection was made. At the Wesleyan Chapel, Rev. Mr. Wamsley, the superintendent of the circuit, preached, and collections were made. It has been decided to hold a Demonstration and Athletic Festival in Knowsley Park, on Whit Monday, under the auspices of the Liberal Clubs of the city of Liverpool; and it has been suggested that the neighbouring clubs might co- operate in making it a very great success. The matter had only to be named to be approved of here. Various members of Parliament will be asked to attend, and it is believed that such an event will be extremely useful in stirring up the Liberals.

BLUE RIBBON ARMY AT EABLESTOWN.—The Blue Ribbon Movement was inaugurated in Earl estown last week, when a meeting was held in the mission Tent, Legh-street, on Mon- day evening. A large number of pledges were taken and blue ribbons distributed. A united Committee has been formed

to carry on the movement. The Rev. T. It. Matthews, vicar of St. John the Baptist Church, being elected president, and Mr. Thomas Newman secretary. Meetings are to be held every Saturday evening. The question of a seven or four- teen days continuous mission has been spoken of, and may probably be carried out in a few weeks. The drunken, riotous, behaviour of a number of men in Earlestown last Sunday week, shows the necessity for some active work in . _ _

tbis direction, and it is hoped that the various temperance bodies and Christian churches in the town and neighbour- hood, will unite together for a vigorous, onslaught upon this enemy to the social and religious welfare of the people. CHURCH PARADE OF THE VOLUNTEERS - The annual church parade of the Newton company of Yeomanry Cavalry and the Newton company of the Press Guards took place on Sunday. There were some 50 of the Yeomanry besides the band of the Ashton contingent,—a goodly number to look at—and 75 of the Press Guards, with Major Relf and Cap- tain Wood in command respectively. The band played some very fine sacred music through the street, stopping short at the church gates on the principle that you may take a horse to the water but cannot make him drink. Re-

turning to the Pied Bull to wait the the time of dismissal of the church, where the Bev. Herbert Monk, the incumhent, preached an excellent sermon, having special reference to the calling and profession of arms in the Christian warfare. The men individually and collectively looked very well, and behaved very decorously. These military parades are a time honoured institution, and bring vast crowds of sight- seers together. On this occasion, however, there were fewer females in the crowd than usual, although there were still a good many, the rear and vanguard of this crowd being something formidable. Unfortunately St. Peters was not roomy enough to contain the whole of this populace, or -they habitually shun the precincts of church or chapel, for much of thissoncourse of people remained outside with the band and were drenched to the skin by the heavy rain which fell just after church "took in," making them fly for shelter or take the consequences of their indiscretion in not providing umbrellas after all the storm warnings. Fortu- nately the volunteers escaped the rain then and on their return, thus showing the practical benefit of going to church. 1.0.G.T., HOPE OF EATMESTOWN Loncax.7—The quarterly

meeting of the above lodge was held in the Lodge Room, Bridge street, Earlestown, on Monday evening last, when there was a fair attendance of membels. After the usual routine business had been transac_ed, the reports of tho various officers were tendered and adopted. That of the W. Secretary, Bro. E. Newman, showed a fairly successful quarter Just past, and that a good work had been done. About eight public meetings had ben held, with good attendances, two degree meetings had also been held; and the lodge, it was stated, was in the midst of arrangements for the visit of the District Lodge on May 20th, when it is intended to hold an out-door and in-door public meeting. It is hoped the mem- bers will all unite together and do their utmost to make these meetings successful. There is every probability of this at present, and Brother Newman urged all the mem- bers to give in their hearty ea-operation and assistance. There was an increase of three members on the quarter. Not having completed returns, Brother. Newman said he could not give the report of the Juvenile Temple, of which he was superintendent until, the following week. Brother John Little, W. F., secretary, gave in the financial report, which was laid over for a week, not being quite complete. The report of the W. Marshall brother Allison was also ten- dered showing the state of the lodge furniture and other pro- perty. After the adoption of the various reports, the officers for the ensuing quarter were duly installed by Brother John Warburton, lodge deputy e—W. C. T. Bro. John Taylor; W.V.T. Sister J. E. Warburton; W. Secretary Brother E. Newman; W.F. Secretary Bro. John Little; W. Treasurer Brother George Warburton, senior, &c. The sick, ab- sentee, visiting, and finance committee were then apppointed, and other details for the Sunday closing meeting to be held. arranged, after which the Lodge was closed in usual form I by the W. C. T.

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.
div.p: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

The Ilavott moved and do-u-n-cilior Fairclough seconde3 the adoption of this Committee that the Town Clerk be instructed to apply to the Waterworks Company for the terms upon which the company will grant a •supply of water to the Corporation for street watering and other pur- poses, with a view to coming to an agreement on the sui4ject. The motion was paved and the Council rose.

div.head: WARRINGTON PE rTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDA.Y.—Before Mr. _George Artinptall and Mr. P.
div.p: WARRINGTON PE rTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDA.Y.—Before Mr. _George Artinptall and Mr. P.
Stubs.:

John Byrom, Henry Hanhinson, George Perrin, and John Pickle' for behaving in a disorderly manner at the Bowling Green Inn, Rixton, on the 26th April, were bound over in two sureties of £5 each, and themselves in £lO, to keep the peace for six months. Peter Hatton, landlord of the Bowling Green Inn, Rixton, for permitting the riotous conduct of the four last-men- tioned defendants, was fined ZI and costs, and cautioned that if he came before the bench again he would be fined £lO and his licence would be endorsed. For riding a cart withoet reins, Henry Hankinson,Rixton, was fined 2s, 6d. and .costs. John Smith, summoned for obstructing the highway by allowing his cattle to stray in Favourite-lane, near Padgate, was dismissed. Matthew Raybald was fined 103. 61. for keeping a dog without having a licence for the same. THErr or A WATCH.—TWO sisters, named Margaret and Louisa Scott, were charged with stealing a watch, value £2, he property of Colour-Sergeant Hopkins, of the 2nd Royal Lancashire Militia, stationed at Orford Barracks.—The father of the prisoners was connected with the militia, but he died recently. His wife and two daughters (the prisoners) have not yet, however, left the barracks, and it seems that the quarters they occupy are underneath those of the prose- cutor. The watch was missed on the 28th April, and on the 2nd May Louisa Scott had offered it in pawn. .13,-)th prisoners had been seen in the qearters of Hopkins, who stated he did not wish to press the case against them. On Louisa Scott being apprehended she said she got the watch' from her sister, who had obtained it in Liverpool. It sub- sequently transpired that Margaret had taken the watch and given it to her sister.—The prisoners were only ordered to be confined until six o'clock this afternoon. ASSAULTING TUE POLICE.—Lexi Ball, dataller, of Hay- dock, for being drunk and disorderly, at if aydock. on Tues- day, and for having at the same time assaulted P.C. Hodg- kinson, was fined 403. and costs, with the alternative of one month's irnprisonment.with hard labour.
The annual dinner of the Cob:len Club is fixed for Satur- day, the Ist of July ; the Earl of Derby in the chair. It will be held this year at Willis's-rooms.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

What might have been a serious accident was prevented by a seeming chance on Sunday afternoon. A gentleman in walking swiftly past the end of the passage leading from Hay- dock-street to Back Market-street heard a loud scream of a little child, and on looking saw a gigantic game cock stand- ing at the attack with his attention fixed on the child's eyes. He instantly run forward and drove the fowl away,and found that the bird had actually pecked the child on the thigh, and would certainly have done more injury had he not been nigh. There is a Scotch proverb which says "To seize an opportunity is to jump like a cock at a groset (groseille) or gooseberry;" showing the that bird has actually that pro- pensity as we have ourselves witnessed. True enough, as we take our walk to and from church or chapel on Sunday morning, at noon, or night, we see our industrial youth beguiling the time like Mr. Thdtnas Idle with that favourite pastime of pitch penny, or pitch and toss, and on gentiy remonstrating with them on the enormity receive a very civil reply and a promise to desist, only to find the same group or others at it on our return. " The Mains" is now a favourite place, and near the first railway arch, for there the ground has been "poached" up by the race horses in training, and although the ground has been sown with hay seed it is still suitable for their purpose, and there they play with impunity, whether they know it or not, for there is no bye-law to forbid them, and the police know it, and the sooner the local authorities make bye-laws the better for the decencies of tke Christian Sabbath. But the wrong doe'rs are not to imagine that therefore they arc ex- empt from danger of the law; there is the law of trespass, a much more formidable weapon to use against them, and the regulation as to public paths and footpaths. The police are not übiquitous, but when they receive definine instructions they may be depended upon to carry them out both in spirit and to the letter. And as Mr. Legh has this year amended his qualificl.tion as a voter by substituting "The Mains" in- stead of his whilom residence opposite the Market-place, which, by the bye, is under repair for the approaching races, it should not be difficult to find authority; and yet it does seem anomalous to legalise one playground and not another. But then, our complaint is about the desecration of the Sabbath, including "Race Sunday."

div.head: NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room, Town Hall, on Monday; Mr. Gooch presiding. Present, Messrs. Stone, Pardey, Faircloug,,h, Emmett, Gil- lespie, Worley (clerk), and Brierley (surveyor).

WORE IN CO3IILITTEB. T-he meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sani- tary Committee was held on the 17th ult. Mr. Brierley reported 28 cases of scarlet fever, five having occurred during the week; one case, Walter Lambert, Crow-lane, had been removed from Mr. Peace's premises to the Infec- tious Hospital at Warrington, on the 13th inst. Plans for two cottages in Market-street, for Mr. B. Higgins, seven cottages in Peel-street, for Mr. Ed. W. Davies, and a house in Park-road for Mr. W. Urquhart were submitted and ap- proved. A cheque of £25 was ordered to be paid to Mr. J, Unsworth.—At a meeting of the Gas and Water Commit- tee, the Surveyor reported that Dak tons of fuel were used at the gas works for the past month; gas made 1,993,001 feet, averaging 10,002 feet per ton. It was ordered that the Burping revenue on gas acceunt be applied during the current year in increasing the illuminating quality of the gas to 20 candles. Mr. Brierley was instructed to ascertain terms for telephonic communication between the Town Hall and the gas works, and the chairman of the commit- tee (Mr. Glover)- was . requested to examine the ac- counts kept at the gas works to ascertain the desirability or otherwise of the same being kept at the Town Hall. It was decided that the water main to be laid under the railway in Chemical-street be deferred until the timber crossing the rails could be permanently removed.—The Finance Com- mittee recommended that Mr. Houghton, the collector, be requested to attend, one day in eich week (Tuesday) at a place to be arranged for at Earlestown to enable persons to pay their rates, gas or water accounts, and so avoid the necessity for coming to the Town Hall, and that Mr. Brier- ley be instructed to arrange for a convenient room for that purpose.—The School Attendance Officer (Mr. Ball) re- ported to the committee, on the 17th ult., that the number of scholars on the books for quarter ending March were 2,231, average attendance, 1,520, as compared with Decem- ber, 1881, on books 2,174, average attendance 1,415. The committee ordered legal proceedings to be taken against J. Willcox and P. Collins for the irregular attendance of their children at school.—The minutes were passedb

div.head: PROPOSED CEMETERY.
div.p: THE PROPOSED CEMETERY.

The CLERK sail, as requested,' he had written to the Local Government Board and asked them to forward for the use of the Board any circulars they might have relating to cemeteries; and he had received one containing a large amount of information as to the requirements for burial grounds, suitability of sites. He had also received a report of the medical officer, Dr. Parsons, which contained some valuable information. The papers, be believed, would be of great use to Mr. Brierley in forming his plans. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—TIIE FEVER EPIDEMIC. Dr. WATKINS, the medical officer, read his quarterly re- port as follows :—I have the honour to present my report

for the first quarter of the year. There were registered— Births, males 57, females 58, total 115; deaths, nl3.lcS 27, females 27, total 54; excess of births, 61. The birth-rate was 42.23, and the death-rate 1970 per 1,000 of the popula- tion estimated to the middle of the year. The following is a table of deaths classified according to diseases and ages for each of the last three months :
Scarlet fever DiarrhceA Puerperal fever Phthisis
Under 5 years. 5 years & upwards. Total. 2 ••• 3 ... 5

div.head: Bronchit!s & Pneumonia Heart disease
div.p: Bronchit!s & Pneumonia Heart disease
Injuries Other diseases

24 30 54 The deaths in January. were only 12, but the comparatively high death-rate of the quarter was caused by 22 deaths in February and 20 in March. The five deaths from scarlet fever were all of quite young children. The two deaths from diarrhom of a non-zymotic character. There were no less than four deaths from puerperal' fever. The first three cases occurred in rapid succession, and were clearly traceable to infection communicated by the same midwife. She sus- pended her work and went from home, but returned in too short a time and without any sanction commenced her at- tendance on labour with the immediate result of a fourth fatal case of puerperal fever. Immediate and prolonged sus- pension from her work was ordered, and no case had occurred since. Of the 14 deaths from pulmonary diseases 13 took place in February and March. The other deaths recorded call for no particular comment. It is, however, gratifying to observe that just over 20 per cent. of all the persons who died in the quarter had attained the age of 60 and upwards. Scarlet fever still prevails in epidemic form. In the first fire weeks of the year 41 cases were reported. The age and sex of these patients were not recorded. In the remaining eight weeks of the quarter 56 cases were reported. Of these 29 were males and 27 females; 19 were below five years of age, and 37 of that age or upwards, but with very few exceptions the disease was confined to children Three cases were sent to the special hospital in Warrington. On the last day of last year there were 39 cases of scarlet fever under official inspection; these added to the 97 new cases make a total of 136 cases known to us in the quarter. I did not for a moment suppose these were all the cases, for here is a very prevalent disposition, from mistaken motives, to conceal the existence of the disease in families. There have been then at the least 136 cases of the fever, and but five deaths from it in the quarter. This is convincing proof of the generally mild type of the epidemic, but it is at the same time, I grieve to state, a snare to those who are with- out experience of the insidious nature of the disease. No cases of scarlet fever, floe ever slight, should be treated as of trivial importance; first in the interest of the patient himself, for the utmost dangerous and fatal sequelce of the disease are often observed in those cases that from their very mildness have been overlooked, treated as unimportant, or altogether left to chance, or in other words neglected; secondly, in the interest of the public, for the infection re- ceived from the mildest conceiveable case may become developed in another individual into the most malignant form of the disease. Another fact to be impressed upon the attention of the public is that scarlet fever may exist without any rash being visible. I have seen several such cases lately. Many of the most rapidly fatal cases have run their course with- out rash. Sixty-two houses have been fumigated; 5 of them have required to be done twice. This necessity probably has arisen from some article of infected clothing not having been submitted to the process of disinfection. In my last annual report, I strongly urged the use of a special disinfecting apparatus for clothing, but apparently the recommendations in that report, as in others, had been "taken as read," and then forgotten as a dream. The SURVEYOR stated there were at present only 13 or 14 cases of fever in the district, and a conversation took place as to the advisablility of retaining the services of the special sanitary officer, Mr. Johnson. Ultimately the matter was cl,ferred until the meeting of the Sanitary Com- mittee. This concluded the business.
LYMM.
LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board Room on Thursday evening. The Chairman, Mr. Cameron, presided, and there were also present Messrs. Rogers, Dcwhurst, Foster, Gibbon, Callender, Taylor, Ridgway (clerk), Mullard (deputy clerk), and Dr. Fox (medical officer).
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The MEDICAL OFFICER read his quarterly report as fol- lows :—During the quarter which ended on the 31st March, 1882, there were registered 26 deaths at all ages and from all causes in the urban district. This is equivalent to an annual death rats of 222 per thousand. The number of births in the SAM 3 period was 42, yielding an annual birth rate of 36. Out of the total number of deaths three only- -11.6 per cent.—had attained the age of 60 years and up- wards: whereas seven—or 270 per cent.—failed to complete the first year. The complaints which are grouped under the zymotic order were fatal only in one instance, a case of diphtheria, the origin of which was due to conditions entirely confined to the dwelling in which the death occurred. In answer to Mr. Dewhurst, Dr. Fox said the death rate was greater than in the corresponding quarter last year, but it was the same in several other districts in Cheshire.
TRH BOARD AND WARRINGTON INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.

Mr. Richard Dutton, as chairman of the School Attend- ance Committee, wrote to call the attention of the Board to the fact that cases of infectious disease (scarlet fever and whooping cough) were reported to the committee by Mr. Toft on Tuesday last. He also, as a resident in Lymm, took the opportunity to ask whether the Board had made any recent attempt to isolate cases by conveying non-paupers to Warrington hospital. He was glad to know that Lymm still contributed £5O a year to that institution, for he thought no more economical arrangement could be made consistently with efficiency. He would respectfully enquire through the Chairman whether the village was getting all the advantage possible from the arrangement with the Warrington Cor- poration. ' The CLERIC said the arrangement with the Warrington Corporation would expire on the 3rd June, and up to that time they, of course, had all the privileges. The CHAIRMAN remarked that the attendance at school bad not been so good of late, as the officer did not feel it would be well to compel them, seeing there was infectious disease about. Mr. TAYLOR said the arrangement with the Corporation might be extended to the end of the year. Mr. RoGEus thought it would be exceedingly unwise for the Board to be without any means of isolating infectious disease,-and he gave notice of his intention to move a reso- lution on the subject at the next meeting of the Board. The discussion then ceased. A SMOKE NUISANCE.

The CHAIRMAN read the following letter from Mr. Alfred Bickley, dated the 4th inst.:—" As a resident in your dis- trict, South View, Statham, I have to lay a complaint of a great nuisance arising from the furnace put down by Mr. Newborn in the yard adjoining our garden. lhick volumes of black smoke are emitted for over an hour every morning, and for shorter periods incessantly during the day. When- ' ever the wind is in a southerly direction the fruit trees and garden generally becomes smothered. This is a serious matter to me, having taken the house, principally for the sake of the garden, for five years. Believing that the Local Board have power to cause this nuisance to be discontinued , I respectfully ask your assistance." The CLERK said the Board had full power to deal with the matter. The owner of the furnace ought to use the best means to prevent the nuisance. Mr. CALLENDER observed that from the volumes of smoke he had seen issuing from the furnace, he thought there was no smoke consuming apparatus fired. On the motion of Mr. TAYLOR, seconded by Mr. FOSTER, the letter was referred to the Sanitary Committee. OBJECTIONABLE WHARVES. .

Mr. MORT, the Sanitary Inspector, called the attention of the Board in his report to the nuisance caused by the dis- charging of night soil and other offensive manure on those canal wharves in the district which border upon the high- way, or which are in close proximity to dwelling-houses. The manure consisted occasionally of very offensive matter, and was sometimes allowed to remain on th% wharves for an unreas;mable length of time, causing a public nuisance as well as being injurious to the health of the persons liv- ing in the immediate vicinity. He had ascertained that stem were being taken in adjoining districts to have similar nuisances abated, by causing the naanure wharves to be re- moved to more remote and secluded localities, and the Board could also take similar steps. The CLERIK was instructed to communicate with the Bridgewater Navigation Company with reference to the nuisance.

TIIE SCARLET FEVER CASES. The SANITARY INSPECTOR treported that there were still one or two cases of scarlet fever in the district, but so far the disease had been of a very mild type, and the patients in each case had recovered in a short space of time.

IMPROVEMENTS FOR THE GAS WORKS. Mr. ROGERS moved the resolution of which he had given notice, that repairs be made to the gas works at an estimated cost of £65, and improvements, which would require the ex- penditure of £173 Os., making a total of £238 6s. Mr. CALL-ENDER said he thought the resolution a step in the right direction. Before giving his sanction to so impor- tant a matter, he should like to have an abstract of accounts, so that he might know what amount was received from and paid by the gas works. Mr. ROGERS remarked that the Board would understand that the only time in which these repairs and improvements Gould be carried out was in the long summer months, and it was imperative that they should get to work at once. lie believed he could satisfy Mr. Callender as to the ways and means. During the year ending the 25th March last, the gas works paid interest on loans £316, principal £616, and after paying all the working expenses there was a balance of £277 7s. 6d., with which to do the work he proposed. There would then be £3O or £4O left. The repairs and improvements were very necessary, and for the past twelve months he had been working hard to bring about a balance in order that they might be done without borrowing. Mr. CALLI.NDAR then seconded the proposition. The CHAIRMAN observed that he was satisfied the work was required to be done, and the motion was carried without dissent. THE PRICE OF GAS.—MR.
