div.p: _ MAY DAY CELEBRATIONS. RUNCORN. The weather in Runcorn district on this day was of a bleak description and the contrast between the lines of Tenny- son, where he speaks of the month as "the merriest and maddest of all the year" and the sad reality, was not very pleasant. The custom formerly adopted by teamsters of decorating their horses on this day, appears to have nearly died out in Runcorn. VIDNES.

Monday was not a favourable day for any public celebra- tion, as the weather was so cold and showery as to cause many people to keep within doors. The May Day Associa- tion, which was started some three years ago, continues to flourish, and this year offered a number of prizes of fair value, which took the form of orders upon tradesmen. The chairman of the committee is Mr. E. Percy; the treasurer, Mr. James Ilnlme ; the bon. secretary, Mr. J. B. Foulke; and the committee is made up of Messrs. T. Edwardser, Wilbraham Wood, T. D. Matthews, Frederick Simcock, H. Edgley, R. Moore, and H. Mather. The various competitors, with their teams, assembled on the piece of ground near the George Hotel, at about one o'clock ; and some time after the judging commenced. The following was declared to be the result :—Manufacturers' doable teams, draught horses—let prize, Messrs. James Muspratt and Sons; 2nd, Messrs. Hay Gordon and Co. Manufacturers' single teams—let Widnes Alkali Co.; 2nd, Mr. Peter Longton. Manufacturers' single cobs—lst Peter Longton ; 2nd, T. D. Matthews. Con- tractors' and cartowners' double teams—let E. Percy; 2nd, Alice Lightfoot; 3rd, E. Percy. Contractors' and cart- owners' single teams—lst London and North Western Rail- way Co.; 2nd, T. Sadler; 3rd, 11. Mather, Contractors' and cartowners' single cobs—let, James Hulme; 2nd, John Dagnall. Tradesmens' class—let, James Hutme; 2nd, Wm. Palin. Ponies and donkeys—only one entry, and the prize was, therefore, given to James Kennedy. The various teamsters afterwards paraded the principal streets of the town.

KNUTSFORD. It would seem that age cannot wither nor custom stale the interest evoked in the May-day festivities which annually take place on the heath at Knutsford. Since the practice of celebrating the Ist of May at Arley has been abolished, now several years ago, the festival at Knutsford seems to have grown in popularity and completeness, and it is no uncom- mon occurrence for the coronation of the May Queen to be witnessed by ten thousand spectators. Some approximate idea of the attendance on Monday may be gathered from the fact that the 'railway company alone conveyed between six and seven thousand passengers to this old Cheshire town. The surrounding towns of MacClesfield, Warrington, Altrin- dam, and Stockport provided plenty of material for vehicular traffic, and it is computed that the coronation on Monday attracted to the town the average number of visitors. Al- though the event may be looked upon by the visitors as one item in the year's amusement, to the residents of Knutsford it is the great and almost the only recognised holiday of the year. Formerly these festivities were identified with the Church schools' and the most proficient or best-conducted scholar was awarded the place of honour on the first of May. A more liberal spirit now prevails, and the children of any and all the schools in the district are invited to take part in the ceremonial. The choice of the May Queen is now left in the bands of a ladies' committee, and the selection this year fell upon Miss Eva Holmes, a young lady whose scholastic acquirements are being entrusted to Miss Davies, of Knutsford. This year there was an innovation in the form of the representation of the seasons. Four very pretty girls- were charming representatives of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. The procession which paraded the town included the youthful Queen—who appeared to be some three or four years younger than our present Queen was at the time of her coronation—her maids of honour, the Misses S. Norbury, M. Gallimore, M. Toft, G. Warburton, B. Vernon, and A. Grimsditch ; the crown bearer, Harry Williamson; the sceptre bearer, the sword bearer, the fal- coner, pages foresters, Robin Hood, Little John, Will Scarlet, the beefeaters, the morris dancers, and the rest of the royal retinue. The coronation took place on the heath at half-past three, amid a sharp shower, which necessitated the protection of the Queen by the aid of an umbrella. The proceedings were conducted with due solemnity, and the consummation of the important event was signalised by the playing by the band of the National Anthem, in which Her Majesty's liege subjects heartily joined. WARRINGTON. The leaden skies and cold biting winds if the previous months have now given place to the sunny smiles and warmer breezes of what is considered the most beauteous month of the year. The fields are resplendent with flowers springing up in every direction, the trees are in all the glory of efflo- rescence, and the air is resonant with the merry lays of the birds; and there is no wonder that the advent of the month which effects such joyous changes in nature should give oc- casion for much rejoicing. Observances in honour of Flora, the goddess of flowers, have been practised from time imme- morial, and in England the custom of maying varies in different counties. One of the popular modes of celebrating May day, was the May pole wreathed with flowers, round which the people danced in rings; and another the corona- tion of the May Queen, a custom which has of late years been revived in Lancashire and Cheshire—at Worsley and Knutsford. In the towns the incoming of the " merrie month, " the beauties of which the poets have frequently described, is celebrated chiefly by the carters, who parade their horses through the streets covered with floral and other decorations. This is the way in which May Day has been observed in Warrington for many years, and the carters' festival took place as usual on Monday last. In former years, however, the celebration lost msch of its effectiveness through there being no organised procession, the carters for the various firms proceeding through the town with their charges separately and at all hours of the day. Attention has repeatedly been called to the propriety of holding a united demonstration, and this year an attempt has been made in this direction which has proved fairly successful. What was announced as "The first annual May Day show and procession took place on Monday, and was witnessed by hundreds of spectators who lined the principal thoroughfares through which the procession passed. The show was originated by Mr. F. Wall, who offered several prizes for the best and cleanest turn - outs. The competing teams assembled in Parker-street at now, and that street and Sankey-street were well nigh impassable for the crowds of persons who pnt in an appear- ance to see the start. Admiration was generally expressed at the clean and smart aspect of the turn-outs. The horses had been scrupulously groomed, and no little time had been bestowed upon the cleaning and burnishing of the harness, which was adorned with devices of gay flowers and ribbons. The carts, too, were in all the splendour of new paint, and the drivers themselves, attired mostly in their Sunday best, looked a very respectable class of men. Shortly after one o'clock the procession started down Parker-street, 2.11„ proCseded alone.' Wilson Patten-street, past 'Arpley-atation, through Bridge-street, Horeenearket-street, Winwick-street, and Winwick-road, along Folly-lane,Bewsey- road, Scotland-road, Church-street, round the lamp at the Parish Church and back through Buttermarket-street and Sankey-street, to the field behind the Post-office, where the inspection took place. In the procession were a team of powerful bay horses belonging to Messrs. S. Horton ic Co.' and a grey and roan team belonging to Messrs. J. Collin and Son, who also sent sisr other horses. The carting agents and coal merchants were strongly represented. Mr. Robert Heaton, carting agent to the Cheshire Lines Committee, had entered five animals; Messrs. Clare and Ridgway, builders' mer- chants, sent five horses; Messrs. Blundell and Son, coal proprietors, three ; Messrs. Evans and Co., four; Mr. R. W. Francomb, four; Wigan Coal and Iron Co., three; Mr. Peter baker, carter, two; and the following one horse each : Messrs. Henry Allmark and Robert Isherwood, coal dealers; G. and J. Greenall, Great Western Railway, Pierpoint and Bryant, size merchants ; George Lowe, coal dealer; John Buckley, carter; George Holbrook, Jas. Str Inge, baker; S. Davies, baker; Newall and Barker, engineers, &c. So far everything had gone well, but on arrival at the field some delay occurred, and it then transpired that the gentlemen who were to officiate as judges had not turned up. After a time Messrs. James Warburton and John Hedgcock under- took this arduous and invidious task, but owing to the bad, or rather want of, arrangements the work proceeded slowly. • In class 1, for the cleanest, best dressed, and smartest turned out pair of cart horses, shown in cart or lorry, there were only two entries, and the premier prize was secured by Messrs. S. Horton and Co. (James Tatlock, carter), the second being awarded to Messrs. J. Collin and Son. Class 2, for the cleanest, smartest, and best turn- out of single cart horses shown in any vehicle, brought out a host of the competitors, and it was decided to divide the class into two sections, lorry and cart horses, and give extra prizes. In the luny class J. Grimes, carter to the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, carried off the first prize against 18 competitors, the second prize falling to Mr. R. W. Francomb, and the third to Mr. Robert Heaton. J. Briars, carter for Mr. R. W. Francomb, was first in the cart class, Messrs Blandell and Son being second, and Mr. R. Heaton third. For the cleanest, smartest, and best dressed harness horse (class 3) there were five entries, and a youth named Wm. Strange' driver for his father, Mr. Jas. Strange, obtained first place, Messrs. J. and G. Greenall coming second. Class 4, for cleanest, smartest, and best dressed cob also brought out five competitors, and the first prize fell to G. Millar, carter to Messrs. Newell and Barker' Mr. T. Ireland, Latchford, obtaining second, and Mr. S. Lawless, fishmonger, third. In the last class, for cleanest, smartest dressed, and well-cared for donkey, shown in any vehicle, three animals were enthred, and the prizes were awarded as follows :-1, Mr. George Delooze ; 2, Mr. John Longshaw ; 3, Mr. Wm. Hunt. Large numbers of persons visited the field, and seemed to be well pleased with the excellent show of horse flesh. While the carters were preparing for in- spection many of the spectators spent their time in playing at the game of "Whoa Emma," the prize being a cigar, and It was regrettable to see the number of juveniles who 'ob- tained it. Mr. Wall gave a dinner in the evening at the M r. H. Lion Hotel, and it was excellent/sr served. Amongst those present were Councillor Francomb jains Warburton(chairman),e Heaton (vice-chairman), Messrs. F. Wall, John Hedgcock, J. Whittle, W. J. Horton, John Warbur- ton, T. Ireland, J. Whittaker, Joseph Caldwell, W. Bradford, T. Perks, T. Johnson, Marsh, Longshaw, Smith, T. Yates, J. Houghton, Mottram, W. Houghton, T. Houghton, Howard, J. Wilson, W. Allsop, B. Grimshaw, T. Lytbgoe, E. Sankey, J. Mercer, F. Dignum, E. S. Dallow, &c. In proposing the toast of the evening—" the health of our friend Mr. Wall," the Chairman said he had known Mr. Wall for a great number of years, and if he had only as much ballast as he had "go" in him, he would be one of the cleverest and most success- ful veterinary surgeons in the world. As a friend he had always found Mr. Wall thoroughly straightforward and honest—(hear, hear)—and he had never known him do any- thing he should be ashamed of. He had never been misled by taking Mr. Wall's advice, and he had every confidence in

him. Mr. Wall had started that day a new scheme. The masters were always having some sort of enjoyment, but there were very few " stirs ' for the workmen. If a carter got two or three glasses too much they were hard upon him, and if the man ran against a lamp post the masters were inclined to " sack " him, but he thought the masers ought to look at themselves and see if they tried as they ought to elevate the men a little. He had no doubt the efforts put forth by Mr. Wall would have a good effect. He believed the idea originated by Mr. Wall of trying to get the men to take a pride in themselves, a pride in their horses, and a pride in everything about their horses would have a wonderfully good effect. He thought their thanks were due to Mr. %Vail, and that in a few years the thanks of the whole town would be due to Mr. Wall, who would be looked upon as a benefactor to those engaged with horses in the town. Mr. John Hedgcock endorsed the sentiments of the chairman, and remarked that Mr. Wall had started a move- ment which would doubtless be carried on for years. The toast was drunk with enthusiasm, and Mr. Wall, in reply, said whether the object he had in view had been achieved or not he left them to guess. Some might say it had been a failure, but at any rate it had given him encouragement and that was all he wanted. He expressed his regret that the judges had failed to put in an appearance, and urged those present to form a committee to carry on the movement with him as the leading spirit. In conclusion he proposed the health of the judges, Messrs. James Warburton and J. Hedgcock, who from what he had heard had given satisfaction in their awards. Mr. Warburton and Mr. Hedgcock briefly acknow- ledged the toast, and the evening was spent in an enjoyable manner. The carters, with their wives and friends to the number of 130, were also entertained to tea by Mr. Wall at the Workmen's Club, where some of the prizes were afterwards handfel to the winners. Had the movement been properly managed it would have proved an undoubted success and it is to be hoped that Mr. Wall, having discovered that be cannot cope with such an under- taking single handed, will next year secure such assistance as will promote the comfort of competitors and spectators. Many carters did not enter the competition, and among these were the men employed by Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, brewers, who always make an excellent display. This year was no exception to the rule, and the 15 splendid animals belonging to the firm were much admired as they traversed the streets in procession. The carts had received their customary new coat of paint, and the drivers wore new smocks and hats, some of them pro- voking the risibilities of the onlookers by wearing pieces of blue ribbon on their smocks. Messrs. Rylands Brothers' carters also kept aloof, and the five noble horses belonging to this firm proceeded through the town together drawing lorry loads of wire rods. The horses were gaily dressed with flowers and ribbons of almost every hue, and their ap- pearance reflected great credit upon the men whe had charge of them. With the exception of a few showers the day was fine, and the sun shone brilliantly, but a strong cold wind pre- vailed and neutralised the sun's rays. During the day the streets were filled with persons in holiday attire, and the bands of the Blue Coat and Workhouse schools, which turned out according to custom at an early hour, were followed by a large number of persons who seemed to derive great pleasure in listening to the performances of the youthful musicians.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. George Pilkington and John
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. George Pilkington and John
Brock.'
HOMELESS.—Thomas Roberts, a wanderer, was, on the evidence of P.C. Murray, sent to gaol 14 days, with bard labour, for sleeping out on the premises of Messrs. Gaskell

and Deacon. - - A GOOD USE FOR THE BIRCH ROD.—Patrick O'Neil and Patrick Hogan two lads, were charged with stealing 211bs. of brass, value 11.5., the property of Mr. William Niel, Bold Foundry. It appeared from the evidence that on the 14th ult. a copper kettle was missed from the works, wkich it was found on enquiry the prisoners hod been seen carrying. A search was made, and the article discovered in an empty building. Each of the youths was sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod.—James Lynch and Thomas Griffin, two lads, were charged with breaking into the house of Alice Scott, confectioner, and stealing sweets, value is. ed. It appeared that whilst prosecutrix was away on Sun- day last the prisoners forced the back door and stole the sweets. They were, however, heard by a neighbour, and information given to P.C. Pitt, who afterwards took them in custody. Each boy was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch.

WEDNEsDAv.—Before Messrs. Gibbon (chairman), J. Brock, and Holbrook Gaskel I, jun. ALLEGED THEFT FROM A FLAT. Annie Nash, a young girl, and Mary and John Nash her parents' were charged with stealing a quantity of wearing apparel from the flat Garston whilst lying in the Widnes docks on the 13th ult. The two last named prisoners were also charged with steal- ing a quantity of clothing from the flat Carrie. The girl was discovered to be endeavouring to sell some of the stolen property at Runcorn. Police-constable Barker in conse- quence visited the home of the prisoners and found a further quantity concealed The prisoners were remanded for a week on the application of Superintendent Barker. ASSMILT ON THB POLICH-Thomas Fyldes was charged with being drunk and disorderly: and also with assaulting P.C. Barker. On the previous night when that officer was in Earle-street the prisoner went up to to him and asked him why be struck him with his staff the other night. The officer informed him that he must have made a mistake, when the prisoner commenced to use bad language, and struck Barker on the breast.—The Bench imposed a fine of 103. and costs, or, in default 14 days%imprisonment. BREACHES OF THE FEACE.—John Burke, a man about 30 Years of age, and a youth named Peter Noon were summoned for committing a breach of the peace in Waterloo-road on the evening of the 22nd ult.—They were bound over to keep the peace for three months.—A young woman named Margaret Connor was charged with a similar offence com- mitted in Forster-street, Widnes, on the 23rd ult.; and she was ordered to pay costs.—Summonses had been issued against Catherino Power and Robert Sutton on similar charges, but they did not appear and warrants were granted for their apprehension. KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT LICENSE.—Owen Rourke, of Grenfield-street, was summoned for keeping a dog without license.—P.S. Strickland proved the case, and the defendant was fined 10s. and pstg. A STREET AITITOYANCE.—Wm. Ireland and Thomas Smith, boys, were charged with kicking doors of houses in Pleasant-street, on the 23rd ult.—P.C. Pitt, P.S. Strickland, and a woman named Ryan were called, and the defendants were each fined is. and 10s. 3d. costs. AN UNLAWFUL GAME.—A boy named George Bailey was charged with playing" peggy " in Warrington-road, Lugs- dale, on the 22nd nit.—On the evidence of P.C. litt the defendant Wql9rdered to pay S. Qd. COSfs. BREACHES OF THE EDUCATION ACT.—Mr. banby, clerk to the School Board, appeared to prosecute the following per- sons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and a fine of ss. including costs was inflicted in each case :—Thomas Molyneaux, Thomas Welsh, James Carr, James Simposon, John A. Brien, Patrick Quinn, James Hughes, John Keating, Thomas Owens, Bartholomew Lavine, and Francis Garbutt. YESTERDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock.

ANOTHER ALLEGED SAVAGE ASSAULT.—A young man named Michael Donlan was charged with violently assault- ing Frederick Beck.—Complainant, who appeared with his head plastered, stated that he lived at 38, Davis-street, Moss Bank, and was a signalman. On Monday night, about ten o'clock, he heard something thrown at the window shutters of the house where he lodged, and found that a window had been broken at No. 46 and another at No. 48. He saw the prisoner running away, and rushed after him. When Donlan raw that he was nearing him he threw a missile at hith, but it missed him. As soon as he got up to the prisoner a fierce struggle ensued, and Donlan hit him on the head with a piece of glass several times, and held him by the throat until he was exhausted.—David Boast, 48, Davis-street, Moss Bank, and Elizabeth Flynn, wife of Michal Flynn, No. 46 in the same street, gave evidence as to the windows having been broken.—Dr. McLennan stated that there were seven superficial scalp wounds on the left side of the complainant's head. Each of these was from a quarter to half an inch in length, and such as might have been caused by broken glass. He examined Beck on Monday, and found him in such a weak state that he advised him not to go to work.—Sergeant McGregor said he apprehended the prisoner at No. 10, Carlile-street, and asked how he had come by the blood upon his shirt. He replied that he did not know. He also found that Donlan had cut one of the fingers of his right hand.—Mr. W. T. Hnsband defended, and said he considered the circumstances of the case pointed more to a drunken freak than malicious injury. He com- plained that he had not had time to prepare hisrcase by con- sultation with his client; and Mr. Brock agreed to remand the prisoner until Wednesday, as the police did not raise any objection. An application for bail was refused. THE CHARGE OF BREAKING A. MAN'S LEG—Paul Kerley was again brought up, charged with unlawfully wounding Luke Kelly, under circumstances previously reported in The Examiner.—On the application of the Inspector of Police, the prisoner was remanded until Wednesday.—Mr. James Moore, of Warrington, defended. THE SERIOUS CASE OF UNLAWFULLY WOUNDING.—John Fit zharris was again charged with unlawfully wounding William Myers on the 15th inst. Mr. Husband defended.— Prisoner was remanded until Wednesday, as the supposed accomplice in the offence, had not been apprehended.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S MARKETS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL PRODUCE.—No change in prices for sugar. No- thing to report in rum, molasses, or treacle. Coffee and cocoa quiet. Rice firm. Fustic steady. Ashes, 27s 9d. Berries steady. Nitrate of soda, 13s id to 14s. Cutch firm. Lard 56s 9d asked. Tallow strong. Resin, 6s 3d. Oils, seed and others, as last. Turpentine dull. Petroleum 60, LIVERPOOL CoRE.—A moderate trade In wheat, without change in value, Flour steady; a fair inquiry. "Mixed corn neglected at 6s sd. Cargoes of both wheat and maze in little Inquiry.

CLYDE CRUSHED SUGAR.—Market continues steady, with a good business doing, The official report states : Fair business done. Prices very steady. GLASGOW PIG IRON.—A quiet but steady market, and a moderate business done at 47s 3d to 47s 21d. cash, and 47s .51d to 47s 4fd. one month Closing: Buyers, 47s 3d cash, and 47s 40 one month; sellers near. CoRK CORN —Black oats, is 6d.

- - CORK BUTTER. Ordinary: Firsts, 109 s; seconds, 95s thirds, 945; fourths, 85s; fifths, 655. Superfine, 130 s. Fine mild, 118 s. Mild, 113 s. Salt kegs: Firsts, 112 s; seconds, 91s; thirds, 88s; fourths, —s; fifths, —s. Firkins in market, 1,270.

div.head: EXAMINER gATURDAY, MAY 6, 1882
div.p: THE EXAMINER gATURDAY, MAY 6, 1882
RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Sir Richard Brooke, Bart. (chairman) and Messrs. S. B. Chadwick, Wm. Bankes, and R. M. Brooke. THE PUBLIC HALL THEATRICAL LICENSB.—Mr. Arthur Salkeld applied for a renewal of this licence during the en- suing twelve months.—Mr. Johnson said the license had now been renewed for three years; and Superintendent Wil- liamson remarked that the place had been conducted satis- factorily. The ingress and egress were also thoroughly satisfactory.—The license was renewed. TRANSFER DAY.—The following transfers were made:— Clarendon Hotel, Church-street, from George Lee, deceased, to his widow, Elizabeth Lee; the George Inn, Pool-lane, from Thomas Griffiths, deceased, to Martha Griffiths, his widow; the George and Dragon, Egerton-street, from A. Ledgard to Henry Dixon. A WomEN's QUARREL. Elizabeth Lydiate was sum- moned for assaulting Eliza Cook, of Surrev-street.—Com- plainant said that on the 25th ult. she went to the Co-oper- ative Stores for some goods, and upon returning she hap- pened to look through the back window of Lydiate's house, on which she rushed out, seized her by the shoulders, and asked her in a vehement manner if she owed her something, as she thought she must or she would not have looked through the window so earnestly. Defendant then struck her four times in the face with her fist.—Lydiate was fined ss. and 108. 6d. costs. ALLEGED THEFTS BY A WOMAN. Emma Carter wa charged with stealing a chemise, an apron, a pair of trou- sers, pair of stockings, a towel, and brush, belonging to Jno. Albiston ; and also a brush, can, plate, and-other household articles, the property of James Eddie, Cross-street, all on the 27th ult. The latter case was taken first.—Mrs. Eddie said the brush, jug, can, and basin produced were hers, and she last saw them safe on the previous Thursday. between nine and ten o'clock at night. The Ifrush was then in the yard, and the other things in the kitchen She went to bed about ten at night, and on the following morning missed the articles.—Sergeant Walley stated that about a quarter to twelve on Thursday night be was on duty in Church- street, when he met the prisoner, who had a brush and jug in her hand, a can hanging on her arm, and a plate and basin wrapped up in her apron. He asked her where she had obtained the things, and she replied that she had brought them from her son's boat. From what the prisoner's son said to him the following morning he went to Carter's house and told her he wished to know where she had found the goods, as her son stated that she had not been near his boat en the 27th ult. Prisoner said she had taken the things back to the vessel. He then searched the house and found all the things produced concealed in the chimney. Evidence in the second case was given by the sergeant, and was of a similar nature to that in the previous charge. The things belonging to Albiston were included in those found in the chimney.—There was a previous conviction for le- ceiving stolen property against the prisoner, and she was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial on both charges.

THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. Wm. Bankes, ALLEGED Calumet. ASSAULT.—Joseph Taylor, of No. 9, Bridge-street, was charged with having, on the 31st ult. unlawfully and feloniously assaulted Mary A. Brookes.—Com- plainant said she was a widow, and at present living with a boatman named Edward Hillier, with whom she had been connected about 11 years. On the date mentioned, the pri- soner's boat was lying near that of her "husband", at about 5 o'clock, when Taylor came from the direction of the lock- side, and whilst standing by the forecastle said, "Is there anyone aboard?" She answered "Yes, there must be some one [aboard, or I should not be." Prisoner then crossed his own flat and came upon her boat. He pushed her down in the forecastle, and was guilty of considerable violence, amongst other things striking her upon the head four or five times. He also pushed her against a stove in which there was a good fire, and injured her wrist. The prisoner was a stranger to her. He did not succeed in effect- ing his purpose. Her " husband " afterwards went to the prisoner and spoke to him about his conduct. He then coolly replied," Come on, and I will give thee a drink, and we will settle it." Prisoner then went up the locks with his boat. On Monday morning she took out a warrant against the prisoner.—ln cross-examination by Mr. W. H. Linaker, who appeared for the defence, complainant said she had been convicted once in that court for drunkenness.—Dr. McDou- gall gave evidence as to there being certain discolourations upon the complainant.—Edward Cooke, flatman, was also called.—Sergeant McMichael said he apprehended the pri- soner on Sunday, and, in reply to the charge, he said he was not guilty. In a few minutes afterwards he asked to see the complainant for the purpose of asking her to" make it up," and he would pay for the warrant.—Mr. Bankes said he thought there was sufficient evidence to send the prisoner for trial.—Under these circumstances, Mr. Linaker said he did rot think it was necessary for him to occupy the time of the magistrate with a speech, but he must apply for bail. —Mr. Bankes then formally committed the prisoner to the sessions, and granted bail, the prisoner in £4O and two sureties in £2O each.

NEW PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL FOR ROCK SAVAGE. LAYING OF MEMORIAL STONES. Since the world saw the dawn of Primitive Methodism on Moweop Hill, Cheshire' at the beginning of the present century, its adherents have greatly increased. Composed principally of the working classes, the success of its socie- ties has generally been attained only by hard plodding up- hill work, in which individual members took an active part. Almost invariably their first operations have commenced in the house of some zealous member, and meetings been held in the open air until by degrees they found themselves a sufficiently strong body to undertake the erection of a church. And in this way has the Primitive Methodism of Rock Savage developed, with which our present notice is more directly concerned. Though a very small village, Rock Savage was considered too important to be left without any religious instruction, and in January, 1876, a mission was established in the house of Mr. John Rowland, who, h conjunction with his son Henry, is at present the local preacher of the denomination. The labours of the members had varying success until 1879, when in consequence of the trade of the place being almost entirely suspended, and the village deserted, the mission had to be abandoned. But as the boulder in a stream serves only as a momentary check, over which the water flows with renewed energy, so the mission when resuscitated in 1880 went more vigour- ously to work. The result was seen on Tuesday last, when a good company gathered in the village to witness the lay- ing of the memorial stones of a new chapel. The structure will be built of red brick, with blue coursings, and will measure inside 16 feet 9 inches wide and 21 feet long. It is intended to light the chapel by four windows, two in front and two behind, which are to have slightly ornamented oval tops. At one end a rostrum is to be placed, and the furniture will be of pitch pine. The building is estimated to seat 77 people. The calculated cost is £l2O, towards which sum about £5O has been raised. The plans were prepared by Mr. John Wilson, jun., of Runcorn, and the builder is Mr. John Wilson, senr. From the Marquis of Cholmondeley the trustees of the chapel have 160 square yards of land on a lease of 999 years, and should it at any time be requisite to build a school there will be sufficient ground behind the chapel. At the ceremony there were present Mrs. S. White, Mrs. H. Rowland, the Revs. J. Pickwell and D. Schofield, Messrs. T. Stringfellow, H. Rowland, W. M. Salt, H. Hinde, J. Spruce, W. Booth, T. Yarwood, and J. Dar- lington. The pnceedings were commenced by the singing of a hymn; then a portion of scripture was read by the Rev. D. Schofield, and Mr. T. liarwood and Mr. J. Spruce offered up prayer. An address was then delivered by The Rev. J. PICKWELL, the circuit superintendent, who said they were met together that afternoon to lay the memorial stones of a new Primitive Methodist Chapel, and, perhaps, a few observations with regard to the history of the connexion might not be out of place. He wished to say that they were not a split from any other church, but were raised up by the special providence of God to perform a very important work in connection with the conversion of the world. On May 315t,1807,a very large company of persons assembled on a hill called Mowcop, situated partially in Cheshire and partly in Staffordshire, and held tire first English " camp meeting." A number of preachers on that occasion preached the Gospel with the power of the Holy Ghost sent down from heaven and many were saved. That meeting became a kind of type for other meetings, and after Shropshire, as well as Cheshire. For some time the a while the work spread throughout Staffordshire, leaders of the camp advised those people who had been aved through their labour to join the Wesleyan connexion. The Wesleyan body, however, refused to receive some of these converts as members, and consequently in March, 1810, the first Primitive Methodist Class was formed, con- sisting of ten members, none of whom, they were told, had ever been members of a church previously. Thus they had the nucleus of the Primitive Methodist Connexion in the ten members who composed that class. They (Methodists) were born in the open air, and they were not ashamed to hold their camp meetings and open air services yet, whilst they were happy to know that those who were opposed to them in the past, had actually taken up the same kind of work, and they were also glad to welcome them to tha open fold of the great chapel God had provided for them. To some of them it might be interesting to know that a mission was commenced at Preston Brook in the year 1819, by preachers from Tunstall in Staffordshire, and that Mr. Salt, their re- spected circuit steward, received his ticket dated February, 1820. He was among the first fruits of the labours of the Primitive Methodists in Preston Brook. In June 23, 1823, Preston Brook was made a circuit. At Runcorn, he believed a mission was started in the same year as that at Preston Brook, but so little was accomplished that in 1826 the labours were abandoned. A man named Mr. Richard Turner in 1834, offered the authorities at Preston Brook to again " mission " Runcorn. They told him they could give him no salary, but he determined to depend upon the generosity of the people, and the first quarter, he not only obtained his salary, but a surplus which he handed over to the circuit authorities. At that time Preston Brook was what was called an Irish mission; they sent their ministers, not only round England, but also to Ireland. Adverting to their doctrines, Mr. Pickwell said they toadied the doctrines taught by the Rev. John Wesley and his followers, and he believed they had done more to stop the torrent of iniquity in this country than any other at present existing. The polity of the connexion was very liberal, and was represented two years by laymen and every third year by a minister. Conference was composed of two laymen to one minister. In Rock Savage as yet there were only six menabdrs in society, but that number they expected would be largely increased. They had 40 Sabbath school scholars and three teachers. The connexional statistics as reported to the last conference showed that there were 1,140
PRESCOT BOARD OF GITARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day, Mr. Marsh presiding. There were also present Revs. T. Chambers, Finegan, Barnacle; Messrs. Meadows, Fidler, Paris, Tyrer, Newsome, Dobell, Hall, Birchall, Gerrard, Swift, Fisher, Sadler, Agnew, Penketii, Svder, Eatock, W. B. Longton, Leatherbarrow, Jackson, Griffiths, G. F. Paris, and R. Leigh.

div.head: travelling preachers, 15,597 local preachers, 10,709 class leaders, 185,312 members in society. He might state that
div.p: travelling preachers, 15,597 local preachers, 10,709 class leaders, 185,312 members in society. He might state that

they were likely to have a large increase for the connection during this year, for, according to reports sent in, they had an increase of 700 members for last month. (Hear. hear,) In the Liverpool circuit they had an increase of 499 for the year. (Hear, hear.) Last year there were deceased mem- bers to the number of 2,689, so that every year they had a good many gaps to fill. (Hear, bear.) The connection in- cluded 4,100 Sunday schools, 59,272 teachers, 383,350 scholars, 12,921 scholars over 14 years of age, who were members, and 12,042 who were pnder 14 years. They had 4,366 chapels, other places 1,855, among which was included Preston Brook, where they had had a house for about 63 years. They had engaged to do their best to obtain land for Preston Brook, and he hoped they would succeed. The church property was worth £2620,599, and they were in debt to the extent of only £1,042,466. Preston Brook station, it was pleasing to tell, reported an increase in all respects for 1882. There were 285 members in society, an increase on the year of 19; 2 ministers, 26 local preachers, 21 class leaders' 7 connexional chapels worth £4570, seven places at which services were held ; 8 Sunday schools, 96 teachers, 630 scholars, an increase of 60 for the year. The rev, gentleman concluded by asking those present for sym- pathy and help in their work at Rock Savage, and'Ails- pressed the hope that they would open the chapel free frill:a

____. A hymn having been sung, Mrs. S. White, of Runcorn, was called upon to lay the corner stone at the right hand side of the building. On behalf of the trustees Mr. Pick- well presented to her a silver trowel with an ivory handle, which to perform the ceremony. It was tastefully engraved, and bore the following inscription :—" Presented to Mrs. Samuel White, of Runcorn, by the trustees of the Rock Savage Primitive Methodist Chapel, on the occasion of her laying the memorial stone, 2nd May, 1882." In a cavity under the stone was placed a bottle containing a circular of the day's proceedings, a plan of Preston Brook circuit, the names of the trustees, The Runcorn Examiner, and another local paper. The memorial stones at each of the other corners were laid by Mrs. H. Rowland, Mr. H.Rowland, and Mr. Stringfellow. On behalf of the trustees the Rev. D. Schofie' d presented Mrs. Rowland with a book entitled " The life of Mrs. Robson ;" Mr. T. Yarwood presented Mr. H. Rowland with a . book containing a description of the proceedings of the first Wes- leyan Ecumenical Conference; and Mr. J. Spruce presented Mr. Stringfellow with a History of the Primitive Methodist Connexion. Mr. STRINGFELLOW addressed a few words to the gather- ing. He said it was more than 42 years since he joined the Primitive Methodists and from that day to the present he had consistently held their doctrines. His father was a Primitive Methodist local preacher many years before he joined the body, and he believed was one of the pioneers of that circuit. After being a Primitive Methodist for so long a period, it was his (Mr. Stringfellow's intention so to live that when came to die be might still be a Primitive Metho- dist. (Hear, hear). About the year 1875 he was requested by the Primitive Methodists of Rock Savage to open a mission there, and on January 21st, 1876, he preached in the house of Mr. John Rowland, a warm hearted friend. They had a glorious time. The house was filled. From that time to 1879 the services were continued and Rock Savage ap- peared on the Preston Brook Circuit plan as a mission. Unfortunately the inhabitants were compelled to leave the neighbourhood to seek a livelihood elsewhere, in consequence of work being difficult to obtain, and Rock Savage was almost deserted. As there were no people to preach t 9, the mission was withdrawn, but in 1880 services were again held,—indoors and outdoors and in all kinds of weather. He believed he had the honour of having conducted the first religious service in Rock Savage and he felt grateful to God for all his mercies towards them. He was glad to see the first stone laid towards the erection of the chapel and hoped the building would be reared without accident. Although dark clouds were continually passing over head, the weather was fine, and the proceedings were brought to a successful termination with the singing of a hymn, and the Rev. J. Pickewell offered up a prayer. We must not omit to mention that Mrs. White gave to the building fund a dona- tion of £2O, her daughter £l, Mrs. Rowland £5, her daugh- ter £l, Mr. Rowland £5, and Mr. Stringfellow £lO. A tea meeting was afterwards held in the mission house, and was well attended. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs. Basnett, Mrs. Oxwortb, Mrs. Rowland, Mrs. Coventry, and Mrs. Enkers. In the evening a public meeting was held, and a number of addresses were delivered.

IMPORTANT MEETING OF RUNCORN RATEPAYERS. On Thursday evening a meeting of the ratepayers of Runcorn was held in the Bethesda Congregational school- room, " to consider the desirability, or otherwise, of apply- ing to the Local Government Board for an order to fill up the vacancies in the representation of the parish on the Board of Guardians of the Runcorn Union." Mr. William Handley was voted to the chair, on the motion of Mr. Cole- burn. The CHAIRMAN having read the notice calling the meeting, Mr. G. S. HAZLEHURST said he dare say that most of them were aware that only, two guardians had been returned for Runcorn this year, the nomination having been made by Mr. Jones, draper, High-street, who merely nominated that number, instead of five. If none had been nominated, the former five would have been returned. It appeared that the ratepayers generally had not taken sufficient interest in the matter to nominate the number required, and when the point was brought before the attention of the Board of Guardians they merely laughed at Mr. Norman and himself, quizzed them for not having taken better care of their own interests, and said they deserved to smart for not having done so. It was an unfortunate thing that Runcorn would not during the the present official year have a better representation, as im- portant matters often came up for discussion, and having only two representatives, the parish would be sure to luffer. The CHAIRMAN read the form of - the order referring to the question. Mr. HAZLEHURST then moved the following resolution:— "That owing to the fact of there having been sent to the clerk of the Guardians to the Runcorn Union, acting as re- turning officer, the names of only two persons as Guardians for the township of Runcorn for the year 1882-3, and the said township is entiticd to five representatives on the Board of Guardians of the Runcorn Union, the Local Govern- ment Board be respectfully requested to grant a special election to fill up the three vacancies in the representation, and to issue an order accordingly." Mr. F. J. ADAMS seconded the proposition. Mr. CoLEnureN supported it, and said that as the rateable value of Runcorn was one-third that of the union, it was certainly entitled to even a considerably larger number than five guardians. He remF.rked that they would not be so badly off if Mr. Brundrit, Mr. Bankes, and Mr. Chadwick only attended the meetings at the workhouse, as they were entitled to do. The resolution was carried unanimously. AN IMPORTANT RESOLUTION. Mr. HAZLEHURST suggested that it would be well if some plan could be adopted which would prevent the recurrence of such an unfortunate state of things as the present. Might not the nomination ef Guardians be made at the annual vestry meeting, as was the case in other townships ? The CHAIRMAN said he bad observed that the adoption of such a plan frequently saved a contest. Dr. MCDOUGALL scarcely thought it would be well to well to adopt this plan and thus take in a sense, the matter out of the hands of the ratepayers. He suggested that Guardians might enquire shortly before the nominations ought to be sent in whether any one had seen to the matter. The CHAIRMAN thought that any Guardian possessed of ordinary delicacy of feeling would most carefully avoid taking any such step as that suggested by Dr. McDougall. Mr. HAZLEHURST moved "That with a view to secure a sufficiency of nominations in the future the overseers be requested to state the nomination of Guardians as one of the items of business to be transacted on the notice paper con- vening the annual township meeting." THE RATEPAYERS AND THE COMMISSONERS. Mr. COLEBURN said that a short time ago a large meeting of ratepayers was held in that room, and an important resolu- tion passed in regard to the public library. This motion was duly forwarded to the Commissioners, and he should like to know whether its receipt had been acknowledged? Mr. SurroN (assistant overseer) : No. . The CHAIRMAN: I have not received any such acknow- ledgement ;—I don't know whether Mr. Whittaker, my fellow overseer, has done so. Mr. WHITTAKER: I have not received any. The CHAIRMAN: Then there has been no notice taken of the communication, and I think it demands the courtesy, of a reply. I='Mr. COLEBURN said that perhaps the resolution might yet be acknowledged, if the reporters made a note of the re- marks which had been made. He, personally, certainly thought the Commissioners ought to have honoured the rate- payers with a reply to a resolution carried at what was cer- tainly a very large meeting. The ratepayers ought not to have the cold shoulder shown to them so directly. Perhaps the non receipt of it was due to omission on the part of the Commissioners or their secretary. Mr. ADAMS remarked that he felt a strong wish to support the observations which had fallen from Mr. Coleburn, as he certainly thought the conduct of the Commissioners had been marked by great discourtesy. He also noticed that "they said "some of those present at the meeting did not vote because they did not understand what was being done. Now, he (the speaker) was one of those who remained silent on the evasion as he sympathised, to some extent, with both the resolutions which were placed before the meeting. An observation, such as that to which he had referred, was a very great discourtesy to those who were present at the late meeting; and he certainly hoped that when the proper opportunity came the ratepayers would show by their con- duct how much the resented it. The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

Messrs. John Dun, of Rock Villa, Warrington, and Edward Greenall, of Grappenhail, Warrington, are now serving on the Grand Jury at Liverpool assizes.

RABBIT COURSING MATCII.—On Saturday afternoon a rabbit coursing match, in which the sporting fraternity of Warrington took some interest, was decided at the Abbey Hey Park, near Manchester, the contestants being Thomas Buckley's Nelson, of Warrington, and Mr. W. Rushton's Creeper, of Manchester, who were brought together to con- test the best of 21 courses for £3O. Creeper won by 11 courses to Nelson's 7. Henry Hayes, of Warrington, was referee.

div.head: BAD ACCOUNTS.
div.p: BAD ACCOUNTS.

A letter was read from Meesrr. Jos. Owen and Son threaten- ing the Board with legal proceedings if their account for supplying timber was not paid. The CLERK said the account was five years standing, and it was not right for the Board to pay it. He told the repre- sentative of Messrs. Owen that the Guardians were anxious to pay their debts, but they could not do so unless they were paid within a certain time. If the account had been sent in at the proper time it would have been paid. There was also one from Messrs. Brook & Co., ironmongers, St. Helens, but ho did not believe Mr. Brook would carry the thing further. The Local Government Board would not allow the payment of accounts after 12 months had elapsed since the contrac- tion of the debt.

div.head: IN IMPOSITION ON THE BOARD.
div.p: IN IMPOSITION ON THE BOARD.

The CLERK said that William Banks had written a letter stating that his daughter, who resides in Raglan-street, had been receiving relief from the Board under the pretence that her husband was in the hospital, but left in September, and had been receiving relief ever since. For that quarter she had received £9 195., and gave the relieving-officer to under- stand that her husband was in the hospital, whereas be was receiving wages as a watchmaker. He was given to under- stand that she was a worthless character, and the Guardians for Eccleston desired an example to be made of her. She had five children.

Mr. HALL and Mr. SADLER thought the relieving officer ought to be called in and questioned about this neglect of duty. Mr. HARRISON entered the room, and said that the woman always repeated to him that her husband was in the hospi- tal, and the neighbours, whom he had found out to be as bad as the woman herself, corroborated that statement. They told him that she liked her glasses, but was not a drunken woman. In answer to some guardians, Mr. HARRISON said he did not take the trouble to go to the hospital, but he would do in future. It was decided to prosecute the woman as an example to others.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER.

The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board acknowledging the receipt of letters informing them of the resignation of the assistant overseer for Widnes-with- 'Appleton district, in the Prescot Union, and requesting that under the circumstances mentioned, the Board would con- sent to the employment of an additional collector for a period of six months. The letter went on to say "that the orders of the Board in force in the Union con- tain no provision authorising the appointment, even with the consent of the Board, of a collector for the district. It appears, therefore, to be extremely desirable that no time should be lost in proceeding, after due notice, to appoint a successor to the assistant overseer who has resigned. With reference to the statement that the overseers of the poor of Widnes are in arrear with their contributions to the Com- mon Funds, the Board direct me to suggest for the con- sideration of the Guardians the question of the expediency of remunerating the assistant overseer about to be appointed by a poundage of the amount collected by him instead of a fixed salary. Experience satisfies the Board that the former mode of remunerating assistant overseers or collectors is to be preferred, inasmuch as it holds out to them a strong in- centive to perform their duties promptly, and efficiently. (Hear, bear.) A form of queries in which to report to the Board the particulars of the next appointment of assistant overseer is herewith transmitted."—ED. SUTTON.
Mr. LEATHERBARROW then moved that Mr. Goff, reliev- ing officer for Widnes district, be appointed at a salary of £l5O.

The CLERK said Mr. Goff was willing to acquiesce in any arrangements as to poundage afterwards. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS seconded the motion, which was carried. It was decided to advertise for a relieving officer at a salary of £lOO.

div.head: FATHER HENRY'S EXPLANATION.
div.p: FATHER HENRY'S EXPLANATION.

In regard to the Rev. Father Henry not using the new chapel which has been erected for the joint use of Protestant and Roman Catholic inmates, the following letter was read from that rev. gentleman : Portico. May 4th, 1882.—My dealings with your Board have been always of a friendly character and perfect mutual confi- dence. I gratefully acknowledge that this state of things has made it always a pleasure to me to come before the Board, and has lightened the burden of my responsible duties. The generous disposition of the Guardians, which has induced them to build a chapel in which the Catholic inmates of the house should have their religious services as well as the Protestants, was a new claim on my gratitude. For it procures the more numerous part of the Catholic inmates, who were hitherto without any service on account of their going to Portico, where there were scandalous abuses which could never be effectually prevented by any supervision. I should have, been untrue to my duties and the spiritual interest of the poor if I had not at once resolved to do all in my power to promote such a noble cause. Therefore I promised to undertake the services in addi- tion to my other duties. and I mean to fully keep the promise. It was greatly to my regret, then, that I could /la begin im- mediately after the opening. Before the foundation stone was laid I had started the objects which are partly prescribed by the rules of the Roman Catholic Church for the licit perform- ance of the services, and which I am consequently bound to observe, partly quite indispensable under the present circum- stances. These objects are—First, a decent furnished altar; second, an iron safs with two partitions, one for the sacred ves- sels and the other for the decent keeping of the consecrated host for the afternoon service; third, a press for the vestments. Moreover. I had pointed out that some arrangement had to be made to enable the Catholics to kneel during a part of the services. Since this is the recog- nised custom to assist at mass, it would hurt the religious feelings of the Catholics to oblige them to do it otherwise, and it would be cruel to let old and infirm persons kneel on the bare floor. As kneeling benches would have been very inconvenient for the Protestant paapers kneeling pads were suggested. These necessary requisites I naturally ex- pected to find ready on the day of opening. For I could not for a moment suppose that the Guardians, on accepting:my volun- tary offer, intended to tax me with any expenses necessary to set the chapel in working order. As the vestments and sacred vessels on acsount of their consecrated character, can not become the property of the Union, I undertake to procure them at my own expense. However, some days before the opening, I was, to my surprise, informed by the architect that there was no room to my demands to his estimate, and so I have the un- pleasant task to-day to acquaint the Board of the necessity of going to further expenses before my service can begin. Hop- ing that the generosity of the Board will enable me soon to begin the services.--JAS. HENRY, S. J. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said it gave him great pleasuse to hear the expression of Father Henry. He could not think that he intended to throw up the matter after taking such interest in the 'erection of the chapel. The Board decided that the requirements of Father Henry be conceded, and that the complete furnishing be done under the superintendence of Revs. Finegan, Chambers, Barnacle, Hall, Leatherbarrow, Fidler, and Swift. TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS.

Mr. TYRER moved that subject to the approval of the ratepayers, elections of guardians take place every three years instead of yearly in the township of Prescot. He observed that he would have done this earlier, but he had expected Parliament would have brought in a bill. The matter was as far off as ever, and he now made his motion, notice of which was given last meeting. It would be a saving of money, as there would only be one election in three years instead of three. Ultimately, he altered his motion to include all the townships of the Union, and that one-third of the members retire annually. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS seconded the motion, remarking that the change would probably do away with many frivo- lous ol.jections by a few animated ratepayers. Mr. SA.DLER said there would still be an election every year in Widnes as there were three members. Mr. TYRER said the members for one-third of the town- ships would retire annually, so that Widnes would be in- cluded in one batch. The motion was carried. Mr. TYRER moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Leatherbarrow for the handsome picture on the wall of the board-room, on which was inscribed the names of the members of the com- mittees. The picture is a handsome pen and ink sketch, with a splendid border of leaves and flowers ingeniously arranged, and in the centre of the lower border line is a pretty village sketch. Mr. FIDLER seconded the motion, and said this was the second time Mr. Leatherbarrow had presented the Board with such a skilful production from his nimble fingers. The motion was carried. Mr. LEATHERBARROW acknowledged the compliment, and said that etching was a labour of love with him.

LATEST NEWS.
Last night's London Gazette contains Lord Spencer's ap- pointment as Viceroy of Ireland.
Mr. Forster left Paddington station by the 5-10 train yesterday afternoon for Windsor, to have an interview with

Her Majesty. Dr. Arthur Sullivan has announced his intention of per- sonally conducting his new oratorio of "The Prodigal Son," at the Chester Musical Festival, in June. A Limerick correspondent telegraphs that Mr. Clifford Lloyd is reported to have received notice of the Govern- ment's intention to remove him from Limerick to some other county.

Intelligence has reached Newcastle that an explosion has taken place at the Shield Row Colliery, Durham, owned by Mr. Dickenson. Particulars are yet wanting, but it is be- lieved there was no loss of life. Major Hammersley, the chief constable of Cheshire, re- ports that pleuro-pneumonia has broken out in a violent form at Low Bebbington. Six animals have been attacked. One has died, and five have been killed.

A Central News telegram from Paris states that the Empress Eugenie is still staying at the Due de Mouchy's residence. M. Ronher visited her on Thursday, as did also the Due de Ba3sano, the Vicomtesse Aqualdo, and other friends.

Lord Frederick Ca vendish issued his address to the electors of North-West Yorkshire last night, in which, after expressing his deep regret at the resignation of his friend Mr. Forster, he appeals for a renewal of the confidence which he has enjoyed for the past fifteen years. A serious fire broke out in the large flour mills of Messrs.

Spill er and Browne, at Cardiff, late on Thursday night, and in spite of the efforts of the firemen the central building was completely destroyed. The damage is estimated at £200,000, which is fully covered by insurance. The hearing of the libel action Villiers v. The Referee was commenced in the Queen's Bench Division yesterday. The plaintiff is the proprietor of the London Pavilion Music Hall, which The Referee characterised as worse than the Argyll Rooms, which was suppressed by the Middlesex magistrates.

In consequence of the very heavy freshes in the Dee, salmon fishing has not been successful during the past week. Some large fish were captured by the trammel net men in the lower waters, and a few fish were caught by the Chester men near the Dee Mills. When the waters recede the fisher- men anticipate excellent sport, as measures have been taken to clear the river from impurities. The Hon. E. L. Stanley, M.P., in reply to a resolution passed by some of his constituents, says that members of Parliament were now the slaves of any member who elms° to waste time, and this systematic waste was not limited to one party. These tactics were now so common that the only remedy was that newspapers should call attention by name to the members who do these things. A death due to fright, caused by the thunderstorm of Wednesday afternoon, occurred at Blackburn yesterday morn ing. After one of the loud peals of thunder during Wednes- day's storm, Mrs. Hanson, wife of a fish dealer, fell down on the floor in her house, and, though two doctors were imme- diately summoned, and continued to attend her, she never recovered consciousness, and expired at a quarter-past seven o'clock yesterday morning. Mr. William B. Bryan, for four or five years borough en- gineer of Blackburn has resigned that position to accep t the appointment of chief engineer of the East London Water.. works Company, at a salary of £1,150 per annum. He stipulated that he should be allowed to superintend the completion of the Blackburn waterworks scheme, to which he has been devoting attention since its commencement. His present salary is £750. DESPERATE POACHERS.

Yesterday morning, at Stoke-on-Trent, Hugh Armstrong, John Beach, and Thomas Chatfield, were committed to the Stafford Assizes on a charge of night poaching on the 2state of Sir Lionel Pilkington, near Trentham, and threatening to shoot a gamekeeper. The keeper came across the prisoners and three men, not in castody, about three o'clock on the morning of the Ist inst., when they presented loaded guns, threatening to shoot if he advanced. To save his life he let them go, but the prisoners were subsequently arrested.

div.head: FARNWORTH TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE FARNWORTH TRAGEDY.

Yesterday morning, William Bradburn, the murderer of his stepdaughter and son, was pronounced by Dr. Parr, resident medical officer at the workhouse, to be out of danger. On Thursday he was removed from the padded room to a bedroom in which some half dozen invalids are confined, lie wainea the, wnole distance,' tout Mu:Hired yards. Bradburn is watched night and day. He is becoming very guarded in his conversation, particularly when a police- man is present. He said co a workhouse attendant that he hoped it would not be a hanging job, as that would break his mother's heart. The hands at Mr. Topp's mill, where the stepdaughter was employed, are makiag a subscription to defray the expenses of the funeral. The bodies will be in- terred to-day in the cemetary at Farnworth.

div.head: FRANCE AND TRIPOLI.
div.p: FRANCE AND TRIPOLI.

Thirty thousand Turkish troops are said to be stationed in Tripoli, and in order to be prepared for every eventuality which may arise from this uniooked-for concentration, the French flying squadron is reported to have received orders to be ready at a moment's notice to sail for the Barbary coast. HIGHWAY ROBBERY AT HEYWOOD.

On Thursday night, about fifteen minutes past nine, Jas. Smith, a young man, and Robert Fenton, a boy, employed in a branch shop of the Heywood Co-operative Society, whilst going home were accosted by a man unknown at Hooley Bridge. Fenton was carrying a box, but fortunately it only contained dividend cheques to the amount of £B. £B. The man hit Fenton on the head with a stick and and asked for the cash box. Smith says that he presented something at them like a pistol. They left the cash box, which the man took. Fenton was seriously cut by the blow.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY.
div.p: THE SALVATION ARMY.

In the Queen's Bench Division, yesterday, the Lord Chief Justice and Mr. Justice Grove made absolute a rule calling upon the magistrates of Kingsclere to state a special case for the opinion of the court in the case of the four members of the Salvation Army sentenced to one month's imprisonment with hard labour for a technical assault on the police, who were dispersing a procession. The question of costs was reserved. The prisoners have been released on bail.

div.head: RELEASE OF THE SUSPECTS.
div.p: THE RELEASE OF THE SUSPECTS.

Bonfires and illuminations to celebrate the release of Messrs. Parnell, Dillon, and O'Kelly were again general throughout Limerick and Cork on Thursday night. The police of Claremorris while endeavouring to disperse the number of peeple who assembled to celebrate the release of the suspects were fired upon, but escaped injury. The con- stabulary pursued several young men who were suspected of firing the shots, but did not make any arrest. At Skib- bereen further illuminations are being arranged to celebrate Mr. Davitt's release. Bonfires were lit on the hill tops last night, and people came in from all parts to share in the re- joicings.

div.head: CASE OF MR. BRADLAUGH.
div.p: THE CASE OF MR. BRADLAUGH.

In the Court of Appeal, Westminster, yesterday, the case of Clarke v. Bradlaugh came before Lord Justice Brett and Lord Justice Cotton. In this case jvstice had been entered for the plaintiff with costs, the action having been brought against the d efendant for penalties for sitting and voting in the House of Commons, without having subscribed the oath prescribed by law. The defendant now applied for leave to appeal against ceitain orders of the caurt, so far as they awarded the plaintiff the costs of certain motions.— Sir H. Giffard, Q.C. and Mr. Kidd appeared to propose the application, and the defendant supported it in person. —Mr. Bradlaugh in support of his motion said that in this action, their lordships had made four orders, three on de- murrers, and one on a rule nisi for a new trial, and that all those orders were made with costs. A petition of appeal had been presented to the House against the first two orders of the court on three grounds. First that there was no light for a common informer to seek for penalties; secondly that there was no cause of action on the record; and thirdly that a common informer had no right at all to costs, and that if the question of costs was left to the discretion of the court, the discretion had been wrongly exercised. He would remind their lordships that the point had already beed argued in the divisional court, on a motion for judgement, and the divisional court had reserved its judgement until after the decision of the House of Lords, on his appeal. He contended that there was no statute which gave a common informer power to recover costs, and unless costs were specifically given by statute, a common informer could not recover them. Ha was of a different opinion to Baron Huddleston, who, on the plaintiff moving for judgment and costs, said he did not feel pressed by his (Mr. Bradlaugh's) arguments, as to whether or not the court held in their discretion the power to give the plaintiff his costs, and that the Judicature Act gave the court discretion in all cases.— Lord Justice Cotton wished to know upon what special ground Mr. Bradlaugh applied for leave to appeal against the orders of the court, if the costs were in the discretion of the court.—Lord Justice Brett asked whether Mr. Bradlaugh desired leave to appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of this court that he should pay the costs of certain appeals.—Mr. Bradlaugh said he desired to appeal against their lordship's orders that he should pay the coats of the appeals.—Lord Justice Brett said that if Mr. Bradlaugh had a ground of appeal against the decision of the court, it was to the extent that they were not entitled by law to give costs against him. If the court had no such power, Mr. Bradlaugh's appeal would stand without leave; but if they had the discretion, they saw no reason for granting leave to appeal.—Lord Justice Cotton concurred.

Owen, Esq., Architect, &c., of Cairo- street Chambers, Warrington. Our firm witi therefore from this date be carried on at the above address as Architects, Sur- veyors, Estate Agents, and Valuers, under the style or title of PIERPOINT & ADAMS. JOHN PIERPOINT.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—At the request of an influential deputation, I have this day consented to beaeme a Candidate for the representation of the South-West Ward in the Town Council. For a considerable time past I have been of opinion that our Rates are very excessive, and that most energetic action will be necessary to ensure their reduction. Should you honour me with your confidence, I shall endeavour as your representative, to carry out these views, and will on all occasions do what lies in my power to secure the best Municipal Government at the least possible cost to the Ratepayers. I am, your obedient Servant, MATTHEW BOWDEN. 43, Wilson-Fatten-street, May 3rd, 1882.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE SOUTH-WEST WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—A vacancy having occurred in the representation of the South-West Ward owing to the resignation, through ill-health, of Mr. Josiah Pember- ton Williams, I have consented, at the urgent request of a large number of influential Burgesses, to become a candi- date for the vacant seat in the Town Council. I am, as most of you know, a large employer of labour, and a considerable ratepayer, and must consequently have the strongest personal interest in checking and keeping down the ever-increasing rates of the Borough, the pay- ment of which has become intolerably oppressive. Let me therefore assure you that, if you do me the honour of electing me as your representative, I will do everything I possibly can, compatible with the welfare of my fellow-townsmen, and with an intelligent recognition of our local requirements, to reduce the expenditure in every department controlled by the Town Council I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, • Your obedient Servant, JOHN ED. WRIGHT.
